2.3.6
JobIDs
Support for job-based communication introduces new verbs objects. A job object is a device-level object
that may be shared between processes. The configuration of a job object is considered a privileged
operation.
The maximum number of JobIDs that a device supports is advertised as an extended device attribute.
2.3.6.1
Job Attributes
A job object MUST be associated with a JobID value, port number, and source GID entry. The JobID value
maps directly to the JobID carried in the SES header. The source GID entry identifies the transport
protocol and source network address.
2.3.6.2
Address Table
An address table identifies a set of peer QPs belonging to a JobID. Each entry in the table contains the
extended address attributes used to target a remote service. Each address inserted into the table is
associated with an address index. The address index is specified when submitting send work requests to
identify the target QP.
The configuration of an address table within a job object is considered a privileged operation.
Operations include adding, replacing, removing, and querying an address at a specific index.
A JobID’s address table is automatically shared between all processes within the same job.
Support for address tables is optional.

PAGE 151

151

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
2.3.7
Job Keys
Job keys functionally import a device-level job object into a specific protection domain. A job key
provides a secure mapping between a user-accessible value and the corresponding transport JobID. QPs
may access JobIDs only where the job key and the QP share the same PD. Job keys enable processes to
share job information, including the address table, while maintaining separate memory registrations.
2.3.7.1
JKey
A JKey is a vendor-assigned value to a job key. A JKey is to a JobID as an LKey is to an MR. The JKey value
is submitted as part of a work request to target a specific job. When address tables are being used, a
JKey is paired with an address index to identify a target QP.
2.3.8
Work Requests
Work requests over UET QPs require additional information, including larger-sized data fields, than
those provided by RDMA verbs. UET verbs defines extended QP operations to configure work requests.
Extended operations are required to support:
•
64-bit immediate data
•
64-bit RKey and LKey
•
JobID (i.e., JKey)
•
Extended address handle
•
Address table index (i.e., index into the JobID’s address table when the extended address handle
is not specified)
2.3.9
Immediate Data Support
A NIC may support RDMA and UET protocols. Such NICs may implement transport neutral methods for
handling immediate data. To allow NIC implementations that are optimized for legacy RDMA protocols,
the UET verbs implementation may expose device restrictions on immediate data used by applications.
Restrictions may include:
•
Preventing an RDMA write with immediate data to consume a receive buffer at the target.
•
The maximum size of immediate data written to the CQ.
A new device capability is exposed that specifies if 64-bit immediate data is supported. If it is supported
and the underlying transport (i.e., UET) also supports 64-bit immediate values, then the application can
use 64-bit values. If not supported and the application uses a 64-bit value, the upper 32 bits will get
truncated. Similarly, if the transport does not support 32-bit immediate values, yet the device advertises
64-bit support, any 64-bit value used by the application over that transport will get truncated.
2.3.10 Work Completions
UET verbs defines extended CQ operations to report larger and additional completion data. Extended
operations are required to report:
•
64-bit immediate data
•
JobID

PAGE 152

152

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
SourceID
2.3.11 Memory Registration
UET verbs extends RDMA verbs memory registration with UET-focused capabilities. UET verbs memory
registration extensions are outlined below. Extended memory registration capabilities are aligned with
UET libfabric support.
There are three main configurations of MRs used to control the granularity of access:
•
MR + PD – This is the traditional PD model where only QPs that are part of the same PD can
access the MR.
•
MR + PD + JobID – This protects the MR even further, allowing an MR to be bound to a JobID.
Only operations within the JobID targeting a QP in the same PD can access the MR.
•
MR + PD + QP – This provides even further protection of an MR by attaching it to the QP. Only
that QP has access to the MR.
The above configurations provide different levels of MR protection for incoming requests at the target.
Alternatively, as an initiator, the only restriction for sending data from an MR in an outgoing request is
that the QP and MR must be within the same PD. An application can send data on a QP from any MR
under the same PD, to any JobID with a JKey allocated within that PD, regardless of whether the MR was
bound to a specific JobID.
2.3.11.1 Attach / Detach MR
UET verbs allows a vendor to expose an MR to the network as a separate operation from its creation. A
vendor can indicate this requirement through a QP usage flag. Exposing an MR to the network requires
attaching an existing MR to a QP. Network access can be revoked by detaching the MR. MR attach and
detach functions are UET verbs extensions to QP operations. The behavior of attaching an MR to a QP is
aligned with the libfabric FI_MR_ENDPOINT requirement (see Section 3.4.2.3.6).
2.3.11.2 Job Based MRs
An MR may optionally be associated with a specific job by specifying the job key when allocating the MR
(i.e., job-restricted). When a job key is specified, only incoming requests within that job will be allowed
to access the MR. The QP, MR, and job key must all belong to the same PD.
2.3.11.3 Derived MRs
Derived MRs are new memory regions that are wholly contained within an existing region but may have
different access rights or other attributes. A derived region must be within the same PD as the existing
region. Deriving a region allows a vendor to share page mappings or other hardware resources between
the two regions. UET verbs extends memory registration to support derived memory regions. Derived
MRs are an optional optimization that a vendor may support. UET devices MAY support the semantics of
derived regions, even if underlying optimizations are not available.

PAGE 153

153

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
2.3.11.4 User RKeys
UET verbs will allow for application selected RKey values. Support for user RKeys is device-specific and
exposed through a device capability flag. An application that makes use of user RKeys is responsible for
ensuring that the RKey value is usable for any transport that may access the MR.
2.3.11.5 64-bit LKeys and RKeys
Devices that support UET MUST return a 64-bit RKey value that adheres to the UET specified RKey
format. A multi-transport device may also return a valid 32-bit RKey for use with legacy RDMA
transports. A 64-bit LKey MUST be returned if a 64-bit RKey is returned. The number of LKey bits that
are non-zero is vendor-specific.
2.3.12 QP Semantics
QP semantics define a set of device queryable attributes, which can be modified by the application and
provided into QP creation. QP semantics define message and data ordering semantics implemented by a
QP type over a specific transport. This includes various combinations of:
•
[Send | Read | Write] after [Send | Read | Write]
RDMA verbs require that a developer reference RDMA specifications to understand data transfer
ordering. UET verbs exposes data ordering as new QP attributes. Additionally, applications can remove
unneeded ordering requirements prior to creating a QP. Vendors that are able can optimize transfers
around necessary ordering semantics.
UET devices SHOULD use the QP ordering semantics to guide protocol selection between ROD or RUD.
UET verbs QP semantics are aligned with libfabric endpoint attributes.

Beaverton, OR, USA, 2025.

2.4 In-Network Collectives (INC)
High-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) workloads frequently require multiple
accelerators to coordinate as groups of cooperating processes that accomplish computational
objectives. In the message-passing interface (MPI) and most collective communication libraries (CCLs),
we refer to these groups as communicators, with each process in a group called a rank. Each rank
receives an integer ID, ranging from 0 to r-1 for a group of r ranks. Ultra Ethernet (UE) adopts the same
abstraction for the purpose of facilitating collective operations.
Ultra Ethernet In-Network Collectives (INC) enables network switches to perform computational tasks
directly for a range of group operations. These switches can accelerate key collective operations defined
by the MPI and various CCLs. While this overview does not comprehensively list all such operations, the
MPI specification has additional details. This INC specification focuses on a subset of collective
operations from MPI and CCLs, demonstrating the adaptability and extensibility of the INC framework
for high-performance computing environments.
INC can reduce the bandwidth required for large-message reduction operations by a factor of two, as
established in the literature [1]. This reduction in data movement immediately decreases energy
consumption at the endpoints. By executing computations within the network, INC also lessens the
computational burden and alleviates memory load on accelerators located at the endpoints.
Additionally, INC can significantly reduce latencies for small operations, further enhancing performance
and efficiency in high-performance computing environments.
Collective operations are initiated by application software on a communicator. They are considered
active from when the first call issues by a rank in the communicator until the final completion
notification is received by a rank in the communicator.
INC offers support to accelerate the following collective operations in switches:
•
Barrier
•
Broadcast
•
Allreduce
•
Reduce
These basic operations can be used to accelerate more complex operations such as reduce-scatter.
2.4.1
Assumptions
UE makes several assumptions about the definition and deployment of INC operations:
1. UE INC operates on a single logical switch with a single switch endpoint (SEP) in the network.
Vendors may offer solutions where this single logical switch consists of a distributed set of
switches, provided it adheres to the behavior specified herein.
2. UE INC MUST operate over a lossless fabric (using PFC or CBFC) over the UET ROD transport
between the FEP and the SEP. Each FEP MUST be directly connected to a port associated with a
SEP.

PAGE 155

155

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
3. Packets carrying INC reduction operations (allreduce and reduce) MUST carry full elements of
the specified datatype (i.e., a single element of the operation must be carried in one packet).
4. All FEPs in an INC communicator are associated with the same job.
5. The operands carried in the payload MUST use little-endian byte order. Operands MUST NOT be
padded1.
INC is composed of the following components:
•
INC manager (IM): A daemon that facilitates collective offload.
•
UET.
o SES deferrable send.
o PDS reserved ROD service.
o Non-interleaved messages.
o TFC (optional).
o TSS (optional).
•
Group(s) of UET fabric endpoints (FEPs) called communicator(s).
•
One or more logical SEPs.
o Each SEP supports the INC switch.
The INC switch requirements are defined in Section 2.4.10.
2.4.2
Theory of Operation
The IM establishes a communicator by grouping member FEPs and associating the group with a SEP,
assigning a unique collective ID (CID) upon creation. The INC switch uses the CID to disambiguate
communicators. The INC switch filters packets based on JobID/CID combinations.
Some applications require specific orders of operator application. Optionally, each communicator can
have constraints on the order of operations.
Upon communicator creation, the CSN is set to 0. The establishment of the required transport resources
is coordinated by the IM, as described in Section 2.4.12.
When a new operation is started, a rank uses the current CSN and increments it by one, wrapping from
the maximum 12-bit value back to 0. To start a collective operation, a rank issues a
UET_DEFERRABLE_SEND with the defined INC field (see Section 2.4.11.1) that encodes the CSN, type of
operation, and necessary parameters.
The SEP receives the input data, performs the operation defined by the INC field on the group identified
by the CID, and sends the output data to the recipients. The recipients of the output data depend upon
the operation.  For example, the allreduce collective requires the SEP to send the data to all ranks of the
communicator. The reduce collective requires the SEP to send the data to only one specified root node.
The broadcast collective requires the SEP to send the data to all ranks except the root node. Optionally

1 Composite operands, such as those used for MINLOC and MAXLOC, may contain padding. No padding is added to
the payload before or after any of the operands.

PAGE 156

156

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
the root node can also receive the output data if forced output is requested in the INC operation. INC
communicator ranks MAY post a receive buffer that is identified using a tag with the inc_info format
(see Section 2.4.11.1) before sending their input data. Ranks asynchronously issue their operations, and
a switch will block an operation until all ranks have contributed their data.
The maximum number of outstanding collective operations (i.e., operations that a rank may initiate
without waiting for a completion) is subject to the SEP’s capabilities and MUST NOT exceed the size of
the CSN space (i.e., 4096 total outstanding collective operations).
Informative Text:
While this specification does not define how to implement a logical INC switch with multiple smaller
switches, one could use simple tree topologies and a similar protocol to achieve this. The fact that the
collective root is carried in the matching bits simplifies that implementation.

2.4.6
Operator Ordering Modes
INC implementations MUST support at least one of the following operator ordering modes when
configured through the IM:
•
No ordering: No guarantee of the reduction order.
•
Consistent ordering in the same communicator: For the same communicator, the switch always
applies the same order of reduction operations.
•
Consistent ordering across different communicators: For different communicators with
identical attributes in the same job, the switch always applies the same order of reduction
operations.
•
Consistent ordering across different communicators and jobs: For different jobs with identical
node allocations and different communicators with identical attributes in those jobs, the switch
always applies the same order of reduction operations.
•
Natural ordering: The switch reduces in the order of ranks beginning from 0 to p-1. For example
p=4: sum(sum(sum(0,1),2),3); note that this mode limits parallelism and may lead to lower
performance.
2.4.7
Operator Rounding Modes
INC implementations MUST support the following floating-point rounding modes:
•
Round to nearest, ties to even.
INC implementations MAY support any of the following floating-point rounding modes:
•
Round to nearest, ties away from zero.

PAGE 159

159

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
Round toward 0.
•
Round toward plus infinity.
•
Round toward minus infinity.
2.4.8
INC Libfabric
The creation of a communicator is initiated by the ranks calling fi_join_collective() with matching
arguments. Figure 2-22 shows the sequence of exchanges between the IM, an exemplary rank, and an
INC switch during INC communicator creation.
After all ranks send a CommunicatorJoinRequest, the IM allocates fabric resources for the operation of
the INC communicator, subject to immediate availability and, optionally, any vendor-specific policies.
The IM configures each switch individually and sends a CommunicatorJoinReply to the communicator
ranks with the information required to communicate with their adjacent SEPs.
The rank then allocates an initiator PDS and performs a UET_INC_BARRIER collective, which forces the
establishment of both the initiator and target PDCs.

Figure 2-22 - Example INC Communicator Creation

PAGE 160

160

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The communication between the libfabric provider and the IM is specified in Section 2.4.15. The
communication between the IM and the switch is specified in Section 2.4.17.
After all collective operations of the communicator have completed, the ranks request that the IM tear
down the INC communicator. Figure 2-23 depicts the sequence of steps taken by the IM, a rank, and an
INC switch.
The IM first waits for all ranks to produce a CommunicatorLeaveRequest to allow for all collectives to
complete. Afterward, it starts independent procedures at both the rank and the switch.
The rank receives a CommunicatorLeaveReply, whereupon the initiator PDC is closed.
The INC switch is directed to terminate the INC communicator. Following this, the switch adjusts its
internal configuration, disabling INC offload for the communicator, and closes the SEP’s initiator PDC.
The libfabric provider MAY implement a mechanism to release target PDCs that the switch failed to
close. Such a mechanism is beyond the scope of this document.
The IM can also tear down an INC communicator for any of the following reasons:
•
A rank signals an error.
•
Conditions are detected that preclude continued INC communicator operation (e.g., link
failures).
•
Administrative action or policy.

2.4.8.1
Composite Collective Operations
The libfabric provider decomposes an offloaded collective operation into multiple INC operations in the
following cases:
1. Allgather operations (fi_allgather()) are performed as a series of broadcast operations where
each member is designated as the source of the input data for one of the broadcast operations.
2. Reducescatter operations (fi_reduce_scatter()) are performed as a series of reduce operations
where each member is designated as the destination for the output data for one of the reduce
operations.
2.4.9
Libfabric Provider Extensions
An application utilizing INC collectives provides a 16-byte unique ID when the address vector (AV) set is
created, by passing a structured communication key (comm_key) parameter of the AV set attributes.
The communication key is passed in the fi_av_set() API call within the attr parameter.
The structure of the comm_key for INC collectives is:
/*
 * UET INC comm_key
 */
struct uet_inc_comm_key {
    uint8_t version;
    uint8_t unique_id[16];
} __attribute__((packed));


For INC collectives, the INC comm_key MUST be used and the comm_key_size parameters MUST be set
to the key’s size (i.e., sizeof(struct uet_inc_comm_key)). The communication key MUST be filled as
follows:
•
version: set to 1.
•
unique_id: set to a Unique ID chosen for the communicator.

•
PDS functions:
o Reserved ROD PDCs
▪
ROD_REQ,  ACK, NACK, CP (close commands)
o UET CRC
A switch MAY support the following capabilities:
•
CMS functions: TFC

2.4.11 INC Transport
INC leverages existing UET services and introduces a compact extension field to a semantic sublayer
header to carry INC‑specific information. This extension field conveys fields such as the communicator
ID, collective sequence number, and operation type.
2.4.11.1 Semantic Operation
INC uses UET_DEFERRABLE_SEND and UET_DEFERRABLE_RTR operations for data exchange. All
necessary information for the collective operation is encoded in the 64-bit ses.inc_info field (see Figure
2-24).
The UET_HDR_REQUEST_STD (Figure 3-11 and Figure 3-12) is used for deferrable send operations. In
UET_HDR_REQUEST_STD packets, the ses.match_bits field is replaced by the 64-bit ses.inc_info field.
While the ses.match_bits fields in traditional send operations inform the destination where to place
data and match messages, the ses.inc_info field informs the SEP how to process the data.
Informative Text:
The ses.inc_info field is overlayed upon the ses.match_bits field and it is difficult for an independent
third party (e.g., a wireshark packet capture) to disambiguate the contents of these fields.  A switch
understands how to process the ses.inc_info because it is aware of the {FA, JobID, PIDonFEP, RI} tuple
in the request.

Table 2-50

The CSN is incremented by broadcast collective operations even if no message is received, ensuring
global synchronization. Non-root FEPs in a broadcast collective operation increment the expected CSN
without receiving a message, ensuring subsequent CSNs align. The CSN is incremented by all ranks for
each new collective operation.
If data arrives at the receiving FEP and a buffer is not available, the FEP generates a response indicating
the event (see Section 3.4.5.4).
Because deferrable send is used, packets are retransmitted with new pds.psn values when delivered to
SES and acknowledged. A NACK is not generated when a message is deferred; the defer is
communicated via the SES response in an ACK.
Sending the RTR message optimizes latency as compared to waiting for a pre-configured time. If the
buffer is posted more quickly than the ‘buffer-not-ready’ timer, the RTR message will trigger
retransmission faster than waiting for the configured time period. The timer becomes a backup to the
RTR message, as not all FEPs support generation of UET_DEFERRABLE_RTR.
SEPs receiving a message with an unknown ses.inc_info.ver MUST ignore the rest of ses.inc_info, reject
the message and return RC_UNSUPPORTED_OP (see Table 3-25).
2.4.11.2 Packet Delivery and Congestion Management
INC uses ROD PDCs, which provide in-order delivery of requests and responses. Reserved PDCs are used
to simplify the SEP. Each INC communicator is allocated an individual PDC.
INC PDCs may optionally use UET transport flow control (TFC–See Section 3.6.15), allowing the receiving
SEP or FEP to constrain in-flight data on a PDC based on buffer availability.
No special PDS or CMS features are required to support INC. UET profiles supporting INC MUST support
reserved PDCs.
2.4.11.3 Transport Security
No special TSS features are required to support INC.

PAGE 164

164

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
2.4.12 INC Data Plane Overview
This section specifies the INC data plane protocol. The IM controls the initial creation phase of the INC
communicator. Once the INC communicator is created, collective operations may be issued repeatedly
without additional setup. The IM also controls the destruction of the INC communicator. Refer to
Section 2.4.8 for an overview of the command flows.
2.4.12.1 Data Plane Sequences
Once the communicator is active, with all PDCs established, collective operations can be performed.
Figure 2-25 shows an example of executing a CCL allreduce operation. Each packet carries an integer
number of elements and sufficient information for the SEP to perform the operation autonomously. The
state required at the SEP is primarily the INC communicator membership and root FEP for reduce
operations.
TFC may be used if the switch has limited buffering and needs to limit the amount of data each member
FEP sends. In some deployments, CBFC may be adequate and TFC is not necessary.
The initialization phase is not shown in Figure 2-25.
In an allreduce operation, every member FEP receives output data. Other collective operations, such as
reduce, may produce output data only for a designated root FEP. In those cases, the acknowledgement
from the SEP that all input data has been received indicates completion of the collective operation.
Figure 2-26 shows the flow when a member FEP receive buffer is not available. This condition causes all
traffic on the INC communicator to pause.

2.4.13 Error Handling
INC errors fall into the following categories:
•
Transmission error (e.g., unrecoverable packet loss or link loss)
•
Format error (e.g., unexpected CSN, datatype mismatch, unsupported data type, etc.)
•
Member failure (e.g., timeout)
•
SEP failure (e.g., timeout)
•
IM failure (e.g., timeout)
In most cases, transmission errors are avoided using a lossless transport alongside FEC and LLR. Errors
that are not recovered by FEC and LLR are recovered by PDS retransmission.
Link loss can be avoided using redundant links or other mechanisms, which are out of scope for this
specification.
Uncorrectable errors encountered by the ranks or switches are reported to the IM. In such a case, the
IM destroys the INC communicator and notifies all ranks and switches involved.
2.4.14 INC Manager
The INC manager (IM) coordinates the setup and teardown of collective offload to INC switches. It uses
switch capability information to allocate switch resources for collective offload.
The IM requires network connectivity to the ranks of a job and INC switches. It can operate in the same
network as the INC data plane, or in a separate management network.
The IM exposes a gRPC server to the ranks of a job, which act as clients. The ranks are configured with a
URL to the IM’s gRPC server. The IM, in turn, uses gNMI as a client to communicate with the INC
switches.
2.4.15 UET Libfabric Provider and IM
The IM exposes a gRPC server supporting a UE-defined protocol that interacts with a UET libfabric
provider on behalf of an application that intends to use INC.
The protocol supports the following operations:
•
Capability query
•
Communicator creation/destruction
•
Communicator status query
2.4.15.1 The gRPC API
The full .proto file specifying the API exposed to the UET provider can be found at the following URL:
<https://github.com/ultraethernet/uec-inc/blob/main/proto/uec-uet-inc-im.proto>
It is reproduced below:
syntax = "proto3";

PAGE 167

167

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

import "google/protobuf/empty.proto";

package uec_uet_inc_im.v1;

service INCMembership {
  // Register a rank with the IM.
  rpc Register(RegistrationRequest) returns (RegistrationReply);
  // De-register a rank from the IM.
  // Also leaves any communicators that the rank is part of.
  rpc Deregister(RegistrationRequest) returns (google.protobuf.Empty);

  // Query the INC capabilities of the fabric.
  // Until a specific communicator is formed, the final capabilities may not
  // be known if the fabric consists of switches with different
  // capabilities.
  rpc GetCapabilities(google.protobuf.Empty) returns (CapabilitiesResponse);

  // Join a communicator.
  // A communicator is established after all ranks have attempted to join.
  // Communicator creation MUST fail if the required network resources and/or
  // capabilities is not provided.
  // This RPC is idempotent and safe to call again in case of a timeout.
  // The rank must be registered before calling this.
  rpc CommunicatorJoin(CommunicatorJoinRequest) returns
(CommunicatorJoinReply);
  // Leave a communicator.
  // This is irrevocable and kills the communicator.
  // The rank must be registered before calling this.
  rpc CommunicatorLeave(CommunicatorLeaveRequest) returns
(CommunicatorLeaveReply);

  // Fetch the list of failed communicators.
  // The rank must be registered before calling this.
  rpc CommunicatorStatus(AddressingInfo) returns (CommunicatorStatusReply);
  // Fetch the list of failed communicators and receive streaming updates as
  // communicators fail.
  // Leaving the stream open is the suggested way of generating heartbeats.
  // The rank must be registered before calling this.
  rpc StreamingCommunicatorStatus(AddressingInfo)
    returns (stream CommunicatorStatusReply);
}

2.4.15.2 Semantics of the Capabilities Fields for the CommunicatorJoin RPC
During the CommunicatorJoin RPC, the Capabilities message appears in the CommunicatorJoinRequest
as both required_capabilities and desired_capabilities, and in the CommunicatorJoinReply as capabilities.
The fields in the Capabilities message have the following semantics based on where they are located:
•
collectives, operations, which contain items that are non-exclusive:
o Required: the list of required items
o Desired: the list of desired items, in addition to the required items
o Reply: list of supported items
•
protocol_types, rounding_modes, which contain items that are exclusive on a per-group basis:
o Required: the list of items in order of preference, any of which are considered sufficient
o Desired: the list of items in order of preference, if none are required
o Reply: the item chosen by the IM for the communicator
•
ordering, payload_mtu, bandwidth, which contain the minimum values:
o Required: the minimum required value, if any
o Desired: the minimum desired value, if any
o Reply: the value chosen by the IM for the communicator
2.4.16 IM Management
An IM management interface is required for the job launcher to configure the IM at job launch and
termination. A control protocol is also required to establish INC communicators and configure
components for collective operations. Vendors can implement a control protocol of their choosing; this
document provides an example gRPC API.

2.4.17 IM and INC Switches
The IM communicates with INC switches to perform the following operations:
•
Query INC capabilities.
•
Allocate and free switch resources for an INC communicator.
•
Query the configuration that is in place.
•
Monitor the status of an INC communicator.
•
Collect statistics for troubleshooting.
For this purpose, each switch exposes a gNMI server to the IM. The mechanisms by which the IM
discovers the INC switches and establishes connectivity to them are beyond the scope of this document.

The YANG model of the data communicated between the IM and INC switches is made up of two
modules:
•

uec-uet-inc-types.

2.4.17.2                     ’
The capabilities node holds information regarding switch capabilities. The IM uses these capabilities to
determine if an INC switch is eligible to be used for INC offload for a particular communicator. The IM
reads the switch capabilities and performs the following:
•
The IM ensures that at least one of the protocol types included in the available-protocol-types
node is supported by all the other switches used by the communicator.
•
The IM verifies that the set of capabilities provided by the switch matches the set of capabilities
required by the ranks. The capabilities are listed in Table 2-54.
•
The IM verifies that the resources listed in Table 2-55 are available on the switch.

2.4.17.3 Configuration of an INC Communicator
This section describes the process of configuring an INC switch for an INC communicator. To perform
this process the following information is produced by or provided to the IM:
•
The CID.
•
The data plane protocol2.
•
The set of involved SEPs and their fabric addresses.
•
The peering relationships of the SEPs.
•
The data MTU size to be used by the communicator.
•
The scalar integer by which the results are divided when performing sum and scale operations.
•
The TC_low and TC_high traffic classes used by the UET protocol.
•
The bandwidth at which collectives are to be run.
•
The operator ordering mode for the communicator.

2 This specification defines a single data plane protocol (see section 2.4.11); however, other vendor-specific
protocols are possible.

PAGE 176

176

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
The floating-point rounding mode for the communicator.
The series of steps makes no assumption about the atomicity of how gRPC requests are handled. An IM
implementation performs the following steps.
The INC communicator node is created as follows:
•
The admin-status is initialized to DOWN.
•
The communicator-id is set to the CID.
•
The job-id is set to the INC communicator’s JobID.
•
The payload-mtu is set to the Payload MTU to be used for the INC communicator.
•
dscp-low and dscp-high are set to the codepoints mapped to the low and high traffic classes to
be used for INC traffic.
•
scale-factor is set to the number by which data for sum and scale is divided.
•
protocol-type is set to the protocol type selected for the communicator.
•
ordering-mode is set to the chosen operator ordering mode for that communicator.
•
rounding-mode is set to the chosen rounding mode for that communicator.
•
The bandwidth node is set to the rank bandwidth allocated by the IM for the INC communicator.
The interface and subinterface nodes reference the chosen IETF interface and subinterface,
respectively.
•
The local addressing information, namely the values for local-pid-on-fep and local-resource-
index, are chosen arbitrarily by the IM.
•
The peers list node is populated with the interfaces participating in the communicator.
A peer node is created as follows:
•
The id is set to a value that is unique within the list.
•
The remote-fabric-address is set to the peer’s fabric address.
•
The role is set to LEAF.
•
The flow-control-info node includes the cell-size and packet-overhead nodes. This information
was provided as part of the rank’s RegistrationRequest::flow_control_info.
•
If natural operator ordering mode is used, the assoc-index node indicates the position in the
natural order taken up by the peer’s input data.
•
The remote addressing information, namely the values for remote-pid-on-fep and remote-index,
are extracted from the rank’s RegistrationRequest::rank_addr, namely pid_on_fep and index,
respectively.
The IM MUST set the INC communicator’s admin-status to UP only after all of the data structures have
been initialized.
Once the admin-status is set to UP, a switch that cannot or will not comply with the initialized data
structures MUST set the INC communicator’s oper-status node to FAILED.

PAGE 177

177

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The switch otherwise waits for the necessary INC resources to become ready for use and sets oper-
status to UP.
The IM considers the switch configuration to be finished when the communicator’s oper-status is set to
UP. It is RECOMMENDED that the IM set a gNMI subscription to the oper-status node at this point.
2.4.17.4 Monitoring INC Communicator Status
Switches report communicator failures by setting the oper-status node to FAILED. The IM monitors the
oper-status node and reports the INC communicator as failed if any switch reports a failure. It is
RECOMMENDED that the IM set a gNMI subscription to the oper-status node.
When an INC communicator’s oper-status node changes to FAILED, the failure-description leaf SHOULD
contain a human-readable description of the failure.
2.4.17.5 INC Communicator Destruction
The IM can destroy an INC communicator by deleting the communicator node.

3 UE Transport Layer
The Ultra Ethernet Transport (UET) layer is designed to handle the most challenging application scale,
deliver packets reliably and securely, manage and avoid congestion within the network, and react to
contention at the endpoints. Its goals are minimal tail latency and highest network utilization. At the
same time, UET is designed to enable simple hardware and software implementations—such as what
might be required for accelerator-integrated endpoints. UET can be programmed through the OFI
libfabric standard interface. It sets out to address the shortcomings of RoCEv2 [1], specifically its
semantics, transport layer, wire operations, implementation complexities, and scale limits.
UET leverages semantics and reliability techniques from HPC to enable extreme scale while providing
advanced congestion management that employs the breadth of techniques and telemetry rising from
hyperscale datacenters for traditional Ethernet environments. The transport supports up to millions of
endpoints (NIC ports) with the ability to address up to billions of processes. Scalability is built into every
aspect of its design—from the state required in the semantic layer down to the way encryption keys are
managed and the way reliability and ordering are achieved.
To enable simplified implementations, subsets of the capabilities are defined in specific profiles that
support specialized use cases in AI domains. The HPC profile offers the most comprehensive
functionality. Some of it is optional to implement; two of the AI profiles define subsets of HPC. The AI
Full and AI Base profiles enable full or partial offload of *CCL-like messaging functions to hardware. The
AI Full profile offers deferrable sends, which save up to 1 RTT compared to the AI Base profile in the case
when the receive buffer is not ready. The AI Full profile also provides exact match offload to identify a
specific receive buffer. The AI Base profile requires a prior message exchange to communicate a desired
target buffer, which enables slimmer AI Base profile implementations. The Unified Local profile extends
UET to support local scale-up networks. Optimized for wire efficiency, small transactions, and compact
implementation, the Unified Local profile supports write/read/atomic operations.
This overview section has been used by the working group to define the goals and the overall
architecture of UET as well as to design the specifics of the sublayers. It contains an overview of the
architecture and each sublayer as well as some historic context to ease the understanding of readers. It
does not contain normative text outside of Section 3.3.
3.1 UET Scope, Scale, and Reach
This section outlines the original design guidelines for UET to limit its scope and enable optimized design
choices. This background information helps readers understand decisions and architectural choices.
UET focuses on the backend scale-out and local scale-up networks. UET opportunistically considers
support for frontend networks while not preventing applications in the scale-up network. UET does not
define details of the hardware interface to the endpoints.
UET is designed to operate within one administrative domain. This means that, where necessary, a
single provisioning system is presumed for the assignment of identity and policy.
The workload and use cases are focused on generic AI, HPC, and storage traffic.

PAGE 179

179

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Single applications are expected to span the entire system, single-node jobs filling up the system, and
the full spectrum in between. The objective of UET is to serve the breadth of all those use cases with a
single transport.
3.1.1
Virtualization
Virtualization hides the details of the physical infrastructure from tenants and tenants from each other.
Although there are “bare metal” instances, host virtualization is common, and network virtualization is
almost universal in cloud deployments. This level of virtualization presents a stark contrast between
traditional HPC and clouds: Traditional HPC deployments typically focus on performance first with a
more trusted user base.
Most virtualization technology sits in direct tension with performance objectives. For example,
traditional network virtualization requires O(N) state per endpoint, which UET tries to avoid.
Additionally, using network tunnel techniques introduces substantial packet overheads. In many
environments, however, the added security and isolation provided by virtualization is a fundamental
requirement. UET assumes the following with respect to virtualization:
1) Network tunnel techniques that are used today work in the context of UET, because UET uses IP
packets. UET packets can be encapsulated within VXLAN and similar tunnels; similarly, UET
packets can carry packets of tunneled protocols. Detailed implementations of virtualization
techniques are currently beyond the scope of UET. If UET packets are encapsulated in other
protocols, care must be taken to support UET’s signaling.
2) Host virtualization can be accomplished using traditional techniques—such as SR-IOV, SIOV,
unique fabric addresses (IP) per tenant, or others.
3) Deployments focused on the largest scales leverage techniques that simplify the tunnel logic
(e.g., structured addressing techniques).
4) Deployments that need to focus on network packet efficiency may choose to not use
encapsulation.
Nonetheless, some basic support is needed to support tunneling in a network using UET. For example,
systems carrying UET packets inside a tunnel would provide congestion information, such as explicit
congestion notification (ECN), to the encapsulated packets. Solutions such as IETF RFC 6040 [2] are
available to provide this functionality. Furthermore, such systems would copy the entropy value of
encapsulated UET packets to the encapsulating packet to ensure ordering and load balancing. UET does
not currently define details for tunneling and leaves it up to the system administrator to ensure correct
encapsulation and decapsulation.
3.2 UET Layers, Components, and Capabilities
The Ultra Ethernet transport layer is built on four largely independent sublayers: semantics, packet
delivery, congestion management, and security. See Figure 3-1. Each piece is designed to be separable
from the others; however, implementations may choose to build and integrate the functionality in any
way.

PAGE 180

180

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The semantics sublayer (SES) defines addressing, authorization, message types, protocols, and semantic
header formats between endpoints. SES works at the level of transactions, such as messages or remote
memory accesses (RMA), and breaks those into multiple packets to be transmitted by the packet
delivery sublayer. The packet delivery sublayer (PDS) transports a stream of packets reliably to the
destination FEP and passes them to the target’s SES layer for processing. It generates and interprets ACK
and NACK packets to ensure reliable transmission and uses ephemeral state to track outstanding
packets in the network. The congestion management sublayer (CMS) ensures that the packets are
transmitted at highest rate while minimizing network congestion. The transport security sublayer (TSS)
defines scalable encryption and authentication mechanisms for peer-to-peer as well as client-server
communications.
Figure 3-1 shows an overview of the overall UE stack and the UET sublayer structure. The key
architectural features of each sublayer are summarized, including how they are composed to form UET.
Full details of the specification are defined in the respective sections of this document.


Figure 3-1 - Overview of UET
Each sublayer uses specific header fields in the packet. The UET payload is the data portion of a UET
packet beginning immediately after the SES header fields and of length specified by the length field of
the SES header. The length field of the SES header does not include the UET trailer if present. The total

PAGE 181

181

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
size of a UET packet is the sum of UET header, UET payload, and UET trailer. The UET packet structure is
shown in Figure 3-2.

3.2.1
Semantic Sublayer (SES)
The objective of UET’s semantic sublayer is to provide high-performance and highly scalable messaging
to enable specialized AI and fully featured HPC deployments. The SES bridges between the user-facing
libfabric API and the PDS by mapping libfabric API calls to a set of UET communication operations, such
as tagged and untagged send/receive, RMA read/write, and atomics. Utilizing libfabric inherits benefits
from a wider ecosystem in which user-facing libraries using libfabric already exist and are portable even
beyond UE devices. SES is optimized for common end-user-facing APIs—from *CCL to MPI to
OpenSHMEM. It provides optional message ordering and various optional initiator or target completion
notifications (e.g., global observability). SES supports libfabric’s connectionless API to allow the
underlying hardware to support a large number of endpoints.
SES translates libfabric communication calls into messages that transmit data from or to buffers at the
initiator or target process, respectively. It transmits message transactions by utilizing PDS functionality,
packetizing messages and mapping packets into messages at the destination. PDS interactions include
the packets of the message but also control packets for reliability and status exchanges.
SES defines two protocols for (large) message transmission: rendezvous and deferrable send. The
rendezvous protocol is used for messages that exceed the available temporary eager buffer limit at the

Figure 3-2 - UET Packet Structure

PAGE 182

182

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
target. The target waits (“rendezvous”) until the receiving process has posted a matching receive and
then triggers a read from the source. The deferrable send protocol simply sends messages of any size,
and a target that cannot receive it yet sends a message to stop the sender. Later, once the buffer is
posted, the target sends a resume message to continue the transaction. The main difference is that with
the rendezvous protocol, a sender decides before sending the message whether it is sending it using an
eager or a rendezvous transaction, while the deferrable send behaves the same at the sender, and the
receiver reacts dynamically and defers the send if the receive has not been posted and the message
cannot be buffered.
SES supports two fundamental addressing types: relative addressing for peer-to-peer communication in
large compute jobs and absolute addressing for client-server connections. Once a message endpoint is
identified, a buffer is selected with optional matching criteria (based on a packet-carried initiator ID,
e.g., an MPI rank and additional match bits).
OFI libfabric is an open-source ecosystem with wide adoption—from ISV-certified MPI implementations
to ML communication libraries like *CCL. UEC does not specify how user-facing libraries use libfabric, but
many mappings are natural. For example, *CCL semantics map naturally to fi_tagged(send/recv) with
exact matching semantics, MPI-1 semantics map to fi_tagged(send/recv), and MPI-3 RMA as well as
OpenSHMEM semantics map to fi_rma(read/write) in libfabric. Collective operations can map to
fi_collective() for acceleration. Of course, it is always possible to implement any messaging semantics
(e.g., *CCL) over any lower-layer semantics (e.g., fi_rma()), but this may add additional software
overhead and prevent full offload.
3.2.2
Packet Delivery Sublayer (PDS)
PDS implements reliable packet transmission for the SES. It receives packets from the SES at the initiator
and delivers packets to the SES at the target, which the SES resolves to messages that may update target
memory. It also delivers SES return codes and return data (read and atomics) back to the initiator. The
PDS offers various ordering modes for packet delivery. All packets of a UET message, excluding the last
packet, are of size MTU.
Achieving a scalable reliability solution requires that the state retained in the NIC be based on the
number of simultaneously active (concurrent) communications—not the total number of endpoints in
the application. The reliability layer is designed to cover three key requirements:
1. Extreme scalability
2. Ordered delivery of some packets
3. Unordered delivery of some packets—particularly of bulk payload
Those requirements enable efficient support for packet spraying. PDS defines three packet types:
request, response (aka ACK/NACK), and control packets. PDS request packets flow from the initiator of a
message to the target (reads are an exception). PDS responses flow in the opposite direction. Request
packets usually carry data; ACKs carry SES codes to complete the message or defer it. As an
optimization, PDS responses may also carry small read data directly. Larger reads are handled
differently. The SES response code for a read request indicates “read accepted,” and a separate SES

PAGE 183

183

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
response with data is sent using a PDS request from the target to the initiator. Control packets are used
for management purposes, e.g., to request the status of a request packet or to probe a path’s
congestion situation.
In support of the ordering objectives and the use of multiple, concurrent, independent paths, the
reliability layer is designed with five packet delivery modes. Those modes support the semantic needs of
both HPC and AI, while enabling highly optimized, highly scalable implementations. In some use cases,
the same message may utilize more than one packet delivery mode. For example, an MPI
implementation might use an ordered mode to ensure header ordering together with an unordered
delivery mode for the payload. The five packet delivery modes are:
1. Reliable, unordered delivery for operations (RUD): The RUD packet delivery mode is designed
to enable operations that are passed to the semantic sublayer only once but can tolerate
reordering in the network (e.g., atomic add operations). This allows all bulk data to be routed
unordered across the network. The reliability sublayer detects duplicate packets so that each
packet is delivered to the semantic sublayer only once (i.e., operates on host memory only
once).
2. Reliable, ordered delivery (ROD): The ROD packet delivery mode maintains the order for all
packets between two endpoints. It is designed for applications that require message ordering,
e.g., MPI’s match ordering or OpenSHMEM put-with-signal semantics. As an example, MPI can
transfer a header using an ordered delivery protocol and then transfer the body of the message
using a different protocol. This provides ordering at the message level and unordered bulk data.
The reliability sublayer detects replays and ensures that the operation within each packet
interacts with host memory only once.
3. Reliable, ordered delivery for local networks (RODL): The RODL packet delivery mode is a
variation of the ROD packet delivery mode that is optimized for networks using the Unified Local
profile. RODL allows implementations to omit PDS‑layer retransmission for efficiency, relying on
mechanisms such as LLR for reliability. The header format is optimized for wire efficiency.
4. Reliable, unordered delivery for idempotent3 operations (RUDI): The RUDI packet delivery
mode supports special applications where very small messages need to be delivered between an
extreme number of endpoints. It takes advantage of the fact that some data—like bulk payload
delivery—can be written into memory multiple times up until the final message completion is
delivered at the initiator. RUDI packets can be reordered in the network and replayed due to
loss, leading them to be delivered more than once to the semantic sublayer and in any order.
Because end-user semantics can be complex, this protocol may not be appropriate for all use
cases; yet, due to its stateless nature at the receiver, it is the most scalable of the delivery
modes because it requires no state at the receiver.
5. Unreliable, unordered delivery (UUD): As with most transport layers, UET provides an
unreliable packet delivery mode. Unreliable packets (or datagrams) can be used if guaranteed
delivery is not required.

3 Idempotent operations give the same result with the no additional side effects when performed multiple times.

PAGE 184

184

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Both RUDI and UUD traffic are not subject to UET congestion control and therefore it is not
recommended for their traffic to share the same traffic class with either ROD or RUD traffic.
Informative Text
UET does not use connections but defines various packet transport modes. UET first distinguishes
between reliable and unreliable packet transmission, then between ordered and unordered delivery.
The reliable unordered mode differentiates between idempotent (RUDI) and non-idempotent (RUD)
operations, where the former can be applied multiple times in the context of the same message
transmission (e.g., write or read). Examples for non-idempotent operations are atomic operations and
operations that have other side effects at the target (e.g., delivering header data to a completion
queue). The ability to apply a packet operation multiple times has implementation benefits.
Idempotent packet operations may not change the message transmission or matching state when
they are applied multiple times.

UET supports in-order message delivery while allowing the majority of the associated bulk data
placement to be out of order. This includes ordered buffer addressing. For example, many AI
applications rely on in-order buffer matching semantics in *CCL libraries. This can be implemented with
UET using user-level message sequence numbers as matching tags. This way, incoming multi-path RUD
messages can be matched at the receiver in the order they were issued at the sender. If wildcard
matching is required by the user code (e.g., in MPI), a combination of ROD and RUD can be used to
deliver rendezvous messages: The initial part of the message would be delivered in order through ROD,
and the remainder could be delivered as part of rendezvous or deferrable send through RUD.
Extreme scalability is also supported by using dynamically created packet delivery contexts (PDCs). This
means that reliability state is required only between peers with ongoing communications. PDCs can be
created as part of normal packet transmission without incurring additional round trips. Depending on
resource availability, PDCs can be kept alive for extended periods of time (up to 231 packets) as well, and
the mechanism supports cache-like PDC management.
3.2.3
Congestion Management Sublayer (CMS)
UET’s congestion management involves the combination of mechanisms for window-based congestion
control and load balancing that is performed at each FEP. UET defines various congestion-control
algorithms to enable interoperability between vendors. Specific load balancing techniques and
mechanisms to ensure fairness of congestion control in the presence of multiple FEPs are outside of the
scope of UET, as they are not required for FEP-FEP interoperability. By necessity, different vendor
solutions operating in the same fabric plane are required to co-exist. UET exemplifies various possible
algorithms.
CMS reacts to endpoint contention (e.g., incast) and network congestion (e.g., in oversubscribed
scenarios). CMS defines two fundamental congestion control algorithms: Network-signal based
congestion control (NSCC) that runs primarily at the sender and receiver-controlled congestion control
(RCCC) that runs primarily at the receiver. Either can be used in isolation, or deployments can combine

PAGE 185

185

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
both. NSCC is designed as a generic stand-alone algorithm supporting arbitrary deployments and traffic
patterns. It relies only on round-trip time and ECN, while RCCC explicitly monitors incoming flows at the
receiver. RCCC is expected to work best on fully provisioned (nonblocking) fat trees and can be
complemented with NSCC in oversubscribed fat trees. UET also specifies optional packet trimming
support for more rapid congestion information provided to both algorithms.
Both algorithms limit the amount of pending data (in unacknowledged packets) in the network. UET
defines a congestion control context (CCC) that contains the state required to implement the congestion
control algorithm(s). The CCC state controls the window size that limits the number of data packets in
the network for the one or more PDCs associated with the CCC. This efficient scheme supports multiple
PDCs between the same two FEPs that share the same traffic class (TC). CCCs may be helpful to
coordinate multiple PIDonFEP endpoints, for example, or different logical types of traffic sharing the
same TC. Such a set of PDCs is called a PDC group and is matched to a single CCC such that all traffic on
the same TC between the same pair of FEPs is coordinated. Multiple CCCs may exist between the same
FEPs to enable co-existing RUD and ROD flows.
Path load balancing algorithms choose which path to utilize for a specific packet. UET does not mandate
any path selection or load balancing algorithm to enable vendor differentiation. It provides examples
where path selection is implemented using equal-cost multi-pathing (ECMP) and is controlled through
changing the entropy in the packet headers. Those example algorithms aim to reduce hash collisions and
congestion and improve performance. The UDP source port is used as the common field in the packet
headers to specify entropy. ECMP forwarding behavior of switches is assumed to guarantee (in the
absence of failures) that packets with the same entropy use the same path.
Ultra Ethernet offers programmable congestion management (3.6.18) allowing administrators to define
their own congestion control and load balancing algorithms in software.
3.2.4
Transport Security Sublayer (TSS)
Security is a first-class citizen in UET and designed in from the start. UET’s security solution provides the
option to encrypt and authenticate all data payload and most of the transport headers while being
designed to enable packet spraying. The security solution provides a scalable solution using a single key
across an entire parallel application and no per-peer security state for large parallel jobs. It also provides
a scalable mechanism to secure many clients that communicate with a server using key derivation. The
PDS is designed in conjunction with the TSS to enable the detection of replays. TSS is robust against
known attacks on other low-level transport schemes, such as various exhaustion attacks [3].
3.2.5
Layering Summary
UET can run on top of IP/UDP or experimentally on top of IP directly; implementations may be
configured with a protocol number as described in IETF RFC 3962 [4]. When wire efficiency is important,
UET can run directly over UFH. Detailed packet header formats can be found in the SES, PDS, CMS, and
TSS sections of this specification. Packet formats include an entropy value field in the UDP source port to
enable compatibility with existing switches and common ECMP path selection approaches.

PAGE 186

186

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Because UET uses a standard IP packet carried over Ethernet, it is implicitly possible for UET to be
tunneled using standard technologies such as VXLAN and NVGRE.
Within a UET packet, there is an optional encryption header followed by a reliability header and then a
semantic header. The encryption and reliability headers both leverage a next-header encoding so as not
to prohibit the UET definition from evolving to allow other traffic—including RoCE or TCP—to be layered
within the encryption and reliability mechanisms. While the initial design of UET does not consider such
encapsulations, the packet layering is provisioned to enable this as a future option.
3.2.6
Sublayer Interfaces
The sublayers of UET are modularized to specify roles and responsibilities of functionality rather than
indicate implementation requirements. Actual implementations are free to choose whatever modularity
is appropriate, as long as the external observable behavior of the implementation is compliant with the
normative directives in the specification. Interfaces between the UET components and the users of UET,
both above and below, are described in the specification to further delineate the roles and
responsibilities of the modular functionality.
Figure 3-3 depicts the UET components and component interfaces. The UET libfabric provider is the
primary application-facing layer of UE. It is responsible for mapping libfabric API calls to the UET
semantic sublayer to support the communication needs of the libfabric endpoint. Send and completion
queues are the primary means of interfacing between the UET libfabric provider and the semantics
layer.

SES connects the UET libfabric provider to the PDS. SES packetizes messages at the source of the data
and deposits the received data into memory at the target. In addition, it implements various higher-level
protocols, such as rendezvous or deferrable sends, to synchronize initiator and target. SES in turn makes

Figure 3-3 - Component Interface Overview

PAGE 187

187

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
transmission requests to the reliability component of PDS, which (if needed) creates and assigns a
packet delivery context (PDC) and a congestion control context (CCC) for those packets. PDS is
responsible for delivering packets from sender to receiver. PDS implements reliability and is designed to
operate on both lossless and best-effort networks. CMS is optimized to support best-effort networks. It
manages the assignment of packets to traffic classes. The PDS interfaces with the congestion
management sublayer on each packet to determine whether new packets can be sent into the network,
as well as an entropy value to be used. Send completion notifications and congestion signals from
received packets and ACKs are passed to the congestion management sublayer to manage transmission
windows. The TSS performs encryption and authentication at the sender, and decryption and
authentication at the receiver, of each packet. The data is then forwarded to the output ports of the
fabric interface.
3.2.7
Error Handling
Each layer may generate errors that are either to be passed to the application through the libfabric
bindings (see libfabric mapping Section 2.2.5.6) or to the system administrator through logging or other
alert mechanisms. In UET, only the SES layer interfaces to the application directly; other layer errors are
either passed through SES to libfabric or logged in a vendor-specific form.
3.3 Profiles and Capabilities [normative]
UET covers various application use cases utilizing different communication libraries and services with
differing communication requirements for both HPC and AI. Not all use cases require all semantics, and
simplified semantics offer opportunities to specialize and optimize hardware. Thus, UET defines four
profiles called HPC, AI Base, AI Full, and Unified Local respectively. The HPC profile supports full-fledged
HPC semantics and supports a wide range of applications. The AI Base profile is specialized to support
*CCL and unreliable datagram communication focusing on minimal implementation complexity. The AI
Full profile is intended to support all AI training and AI inferencing requirements to serve that emerging
market most effectively. The Unified Local profile defines an efficient header format for high efficiency
over the wire in local scale-up networking contexts. A specific endpoint implementation can support any
single profile or any combination of the four profiles. However, communication between two endpoints
requires that those endpoints both support the same profile.
Within each profile, specific features of the protocol may be defined as being optional. For example, all
profiles define encryption as optional. This means that devices choosing to implement a profile would
implement the upper layers of semantics with or without encryption, and then a deployment could
decide whether to enable encryption. A device that does not implement encryption can be compliant to
a profile, and deployments using that device could not enable encryption. Yet, communication between
devices of the same profile shall be possible through the least common denominator feature set.
The following specifies the UET features included in each of the profiles. The keyword “MUST” indicates
that a feature must be implemented. If a cell is empty, it means that the feature does not have to be
supported, but vendors are free to support it in enhanced profiles (e.g., AI Base + Read). In this case,
vendors should be sure to track all dependencies. Optional features may be disabled at runtime. That
means that an implementation declaring support for AI Base may implement all features (which would

PAGE 188

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
make it also HPC and AI Full compliant). The following tables assume familiarity with the respective UET
subsections. All requirements apply to both best-effort and lossless deployments unless otherwise
specified.

3.3.9
Encapsulation
Many of the transport components of all profiles inherently rely on consistent lower-level protocol
encapsulation (e.g., IPv4 vs. IPv6 as network layer encapsulation, UFH_16 vs. UFH_32 for the Unified
Local Profile, and native UET vs. UDP encapsulation at the transport layer). For example, TSS uses
confidentiality and encryption offsets for the secure domain specific to the encapsulation type, and CMS
uses a nominal packet size to calculate bandwidth. An implementation SHOULD use consistent
encapsulations on all packets on a FEP, PDC, and TSS security domain.

3.4 Semantics Sublayer (SES)
UET specifies a semantic sublayer (SES) with support for a range of use cases. The first use case is
traditional scale-out networking for AI and HPC using the AI Base, AI Full, and HPC profiles. A subset of
these semantics is adapted and extended to support local scale-up use cases as part of the Unified Local
profile.
3.4.1
Semantic Use Cases
The UET SES supports multiple use cases.  These include:
•
The OFI libfabric API
•
Networks using the Unified Local profile.
3.4.1.1
Support for the OFI libfabric API
UET specifies a semantic sublayer (SES) that supports the OFI libfabric API. To support libfabric, the
semantic sublayer uses concepts that have been deployed in HPC networking products as part of
libfabric implementations. This specification defines optimized profiles for AI and HPC deployments that
allow seamless interoperability between the common features of the profiles. Mappings of the popular
send/receive semantics in *CCL to the proposed AI semantics are discussed in Section 3.4.10.
The products that have seeded this initial effort are inspired (to varying degrees) by the semantics
exposed through the Portals 4.x API [5]. In particular, various pieces of nomenclature are similar to what
is found in Portals 4, as is much of the addressing and authorization model. Portals 4 is mentioned here
as a resource for additional insight into some of the concepts.

Because libfabric was modeled after Portals 4, a strong semantic match remains between the two.
However, libfabric does not define how to handle various challenges for a wire protocol that lie beneath
the API (e.g., unexpected messages). Portals does not define a wire protocol either, and many of the
Portals semantics relate to NIC or software behavior that is beyond the scope of UET (e.g., event
delivery). By necessity, UET defines some behaviors of network hardware and software, but only to the
extent necessary to build compatible devices. The UET on the wire protocol does not intend to achieve
compliance with any existing semantics (neither IBTA nor Portals 4) and interoperates only with a peer
UET device.
SES defines the behavior of processing the wire protocol only to the extent that is necessary to achieve
interoperability between implementations of the libfabric API over the wire. FEP semantics and
implementation details are left to individual implementation choices, and the split of the
Informative Text:
SES uses the terms “initiator” and “target” in various places. Whereas many implementations use
“sender” and “receiver” respectively, those terms are often difficult when talking about transactions
like “read” or even more complex transactions like rendezvous. For example, in a rendezvous
transaction, an initial request is sent from the initiator to the target. The target then issues a “read” to
pull the data from the initiator.

PAGE 194

194

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
implementation between hardware and software is not defined. Several details of the libfabric
implementation requirements are not defined by the wire protocol. The libfabric mapping specification
covers some additional requirements for achieving interoperable providers.
3.4.1.2
Support for Local Scale-up Networking
To support local scale-up networking within a consistent framework, SES leverages concepts, header
fields, and opcodes from the semantics defined to support libfabric. Specific adaptations are
incorporated to reduce header overhead while meeting the semantic requirements of the Unified Local
profile.  UE does not specify any particular API above SES to support the Unified Local profile.
Local scale‑up use cases typically require much lighter‑weight endpoints than scale‑out deployments.
This is often because they leverage endpoints incorporated into processing units to deliver substantially
higher bandwidth. To support lightweight endpoints, scale‑up use cases typically sacrifice multi-tenancy
and scale (operating in the hundreds or thousands of endpoints rather than tens or hundreds of
thousands). Throughout the SES definition, semantics concepts are defined in the context of libfabric
and then specialized for the Unified Local profile.
3.4.2
Definition of Semantic Concepts
This section articulates the semantics provided by the UET to support AI and HPC applications. Fields
within the header are articulated in this section, and the proper semantic handling of those fields is
described; additional normative text is found in Section 3.4.4. The section starts by describing
addressing: how is a buffer selected. This is followed by a discussion of authorization: the process of
determining whether a message is allowed to access a buffer. In addition, this section covers the
network operation types, how the ordering modes interact with the semantics provided, and network
protocol security.
3.4.2.1
Operations, Messages, and Transactions
A “transaction” is composed of all of the packets needed to eventually deliver the payload desired by
the user and implement the libfabric request. A “message” consists of a set of packets sharing a single
message ID. A transaction consists of one or more messages and supporting packets. As an example, a
32 KB libfabric fi_send() would be transmitted in eight packets, all sharing the same message ID that
identifies the send transaction. A send transaction would include the acknowledgments and semantic
responses to the send message packets. A more complex example would be a large fi_send() using
rendezvous (3.4.5.3). This would consist of one or more packets as part of an eager message plus one or
more packets as part of the read message (a second message). Each of those messages would have
Informative Text:
Throughout the semantic section, the text refers to “buffers” or “data buffers.” In this specification,
the term buffer is used generically to refer to an addressable section of memory. This includes a
libfabric “memory region” (i.e., the target of an RMA operation) as well as the pointers passed into an
fi_tsend()/fi_trecv() that refer to memory to send from or receive into. It includes areas described by a
scatter/gather list as well.

PAGE 195

195

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
associated responses and acknowledgments. All of these together would make up the rendezvous
transaction.
The term “operation” is reserved for the behavior implemented at the endpoint. The operation is
encoded in the opcode (3.4.7.2) and specifies operations such as reads and writes to memory, sending
of messages, and atomic operations on memory. Operation is also used in a handful of cases when
referring to libfabric concepts (e.g., a receive operation).
3.4.2.2
Services and Resources
A “service” is a libfabric-level construct that encapsulates all of the resources associated with a higher-
level library (e.g., *CCL, MPI). Resources can include constructs such as buffers, completion queues, and
completion counters. A “Resource Index” is an addressing construct used to select an addressable set of
resources within a service. Three Resource Index spaces exist, corresponding to three operation types:
RMA, SEND, and TAGGED. That is, Resource Index 0 for an RMA opcode (e.g., UET_WRITE) has a
different meaning from Resource Index 0 for a SEND opcode (e.g., UET_DEFERRABLE_SEND). Similarly,
TAGGED opcodes (e.g., UET_RENDEZVOUS_SEND) have a third meaning for Resource Index 0.

3.4.2.3
Addressing
Addressing describes the entire process of selecting a target and identifying a data buffer at the target.
This may be the destination of data (e.g., for a Send (3.4.2.5.1)– or a Write (3.4.2.5.2), the source of the
data (e.g., for a Read (3.4.2.5.3), or both a source and destination of data (e.g., for atomic operations).
There are three types of addressing: relative addressing, absolute addressing, and direct memory
addressing. The first two types rely on a Fabric Address (FA), PIDonFEP (3.4.2.3.2), and set of Resource
Index (3.4.2.3.3) values to select a libfabric endpoint. They differ in how a PIDonFEP is interpreted. In
relative addressing, the PIDonFEP is relative to the JobID (0). In absolute addressing, the PIDonFEP is
interpreted without a JobID. The libfabric endpoint has a variety of resources that can include such
things as a receive queue for send/receive operation, a set of matching buffers, RMA resources, and
completion delivery—both completion queues and counters. This list does not attempt to be exhaustive,
and the exact types and nature of the resources are not intended to be prescriptive.
For each matching, nonmatching, or RMA operation that an implementation supports, separate
resources are identified by the combination of a Resource Index and operation type. Buffers provided
for different operation types are addressed independently, as illustrated throughout the following
examples.
Informative Text:
Tagged and untagged messages inherently require two different “lists” at the target, which requires
two different addressing points. The original mechanism considered was to have a single opcode (e.g.,
UET_PUT) for all, with the target resources addressed based on the configuration of the target
resource. An alternative mechanism considered was to have each resource index be configured for
what type of operation could be performed on it and reject operations of other types.

PAGE 196

196

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The addressing hierarchy begins with a Fabric Address. An FA selects a fabric endpoint (FEP). Once a FEP
is selected, two addressing modes are defined. Relative addressing is intended to enable scalable
addressing for parallel communication within a distributed application, which is called a job. Absolute
Addressing is intended to enable scalable addressing for client/server operations where the server is not
required to be part of the application. In both cases, the initiator of a transaction is assigned a JobID (0)
that is inserted in each packet in a trusted way (3.4.8.1). The JobID is an identifying property of the
initiator only, and then is used as part of addressing and authorization (3.4.2.4) at the target.
In relative addressing, the FEP uses JobID to define the scope of the PIDonFEP. Within the PIDonFEP, a
Resource Index (RI) is associated with a “service”. A service can correspond to a specific use case or
library. In libfabric, a libfabric endpoint is opened for the service, and the number of Resource Index
values used depends on the service. The details of the usage of the Resource Index is hidden beneath
the libfabric endpoint4 that was opened in association with the service. The mapping of services to
Resource Index values is covered in the libfabric mapping specification [6]. Within a service, each
Resource Index creates a unique addressing space where a send operation, tagged send operation, or
RMA operation can select a buffer. This is highlighted in Figure 3-4. Figure 3-4 specifically illustrates the
operation of send/receive and tagged send/receive, where there is a pool of buffers behind a Resource
Index. For send/receive, the first buffer is consumed from the queue by an incoming message. For
tagged send/receive, the buffer is selected using the matching criteria. An initiator identifier is provided
as part of the matching criteria (3.4.2.3.4). Note that send/receive and tagged send/receive have a
different pool of buffers—even when they use the same Resource Index.
While Figure 3-4 provides an overview of how the addressing might be used in a complete HPC software
stack—where multiple complex applications might share a node—it is also possible to implement a
simplified version of this hierarchy for more purpose-built use cases (e.g., an integrated FEP in an AI

others which are not (e.g., a completion queue). Within a space selected by a PIDonFEP and Resource

Absolute addressing differs from relative addressing in that the PIDonFEP is an absolute number that
spans the process space on the target node instead of being relative to a JobID. This allows a service to
exist that is not associated with any job and allows addressing of those services within the UET

job, and the authorization model (3.4.2.4.1) enables scalable authorization using the JobID. For example,
a client can use this approach to access a service residing at a well-known PIDonFEP (or a PIDonFEP
obtained through some form of address resolution) on a server node. The JobID at that point is used

Direct memory addressing is associated only with transactions using the Unified Local profile. These

address space is associated with the entire JobID at the target FEP. System-level software is responsible
for managing addresses in this context. Translations (or, lack thereof) and protection mechanisms other
than the JobID are outside the scope of UET. The target FEP MUST utilize the JobID for isolation. It may
do this in one of two ways:
1. Allowing only a specific job to access memory at a given FEP.
2. Making the address relative to a base address associated with the JobID.
