3.6.14.7.2.2 RCCC Aggregate Rate Control Algorithm
When RCCC Aggregate Rate Control is enabled, the following OnRX(pkt) code must be run on each
packet arrival in addition to the OnRX(pkt) packet processing described in Section 3.6.14.6. The code
updates the credit_rate (a FEP global variable, see Table 3-102), which is used to control the frequency
of credit creation at the receiver as specified in the OnCreditTimer() pseudocode in Section 3.6.14.6).
OnRX(pkt):
    if (pkt.csig.t== “max(Delay)”):
        //UPDATE average delay based on CSIG signal maxDelay
        average_delay = g * quant_reverse_lookup_for_maxDelay(pkt.csig.s) +
                       (1-g) * average_delay
    else:
        est_delay = 0
        if (pkt is trimmed):
            est_delay = trim_delay
        elif (pkt.ECN marked):
            est_delay = max_thresh_delay
        else :
            est_delay = min_thresh_delay

        average_delay = f * est_delay + (1-f) * average_delay

    delta = now() - last_update

    if (delta > CC_INVOCATION_DELTA):
        DoOversubscribedCC()
        last_update = now()


DoOversubscribedCC():
    u = average_delay / base_rtt + 1

    update_interval = UPDATE_INTERVAL * base_rtt +
                      max(average_delay, base_rtt)
    updateWc = now() >= next_rate_change

    if (u >= target_u || increment_stage >= MAX_INCREMENT_STAGE):
        credit_rate = reference_rate / (u / target_u) + rai

        if (credit_rate > 1):
            credit_rate = 1
        if (credit_rate < min_rate):
            credit_rate = min_rate

        if (updateWc):
            increment_stage = 0
            reference_rate = rate
            next_rate_change = now() + update_interval
    else:
        credit_rate = reference_rate + rai

        if (credit_rate > 1):
            credit_rate = 1
        if (credit_rate < min_rate):
            credit_rate = min_rate

PAGE 505

505

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

        if (updateWc):
            increment_stage++
            reference_rate = rate
            next_rate_change = now() + update_interval

3.6.15 Transport Flow Control (TFC)
Transport Flow Control is provided to allow a destination to control the amount of data transmitted
from one or more sources. TFC uses a point-to-point credit mechanism, with the destination allocating
credit and the source consuming credit. A source MUST NOT transmit a packet if it does not have credit.
For the purposes of transmission of credit from the destination to the source, TFC is aligned with the
RCCC credit mechanism and uses the same header fields. It uses a 24-bit pds.credit field that is carried
from the destination to the source in either PDS Credit CPs or using the pds.cc_type=CC_CREDIT header
in PDS acknowledgements. When using pds.cc_type=CC_CREDIT with TFC, pds.ooo_count MUST be set
to 0xFFFF, indicating the field is invalid and pds.ooo_count MUST be ignored on receipt.
As with RCCC, the pds.credit field is a monotonically increasing number that wraps at its maximum
value. An increase in the value of the pds.credit field provides additional credit to the source. This is
used to provide tolerance to packet loss. A single bit in the pds.credit field represents 256 bytes of
credit. When a Credit CP or an ACK conveying credit arrives at the source, the source’s state is updated
in a similar way to RCCC:
TFC.OnCreditUpdate(Credit):
if Credit > ccc.cumulative_credit:
ccc.credit += (Credit - ccc.cumulative_credit) >> 8
ccc.cumulative_credit = Credit

As with RCCC, the source is permitted to send if ccc.credit > 0. Note that being able to send is not
dependent on packet size, so if ccc.credit is greater than zero, the destination MUST be able to accept an
MTU-sized packet.
TFC differs from RCCC credit in that a TFC source can retransmit without using credit. The rationale for
this difference is that the role of TFC credit is to prevent the source from sending data that the
destination cannot buffer, whereas the role of RCCC is to manage network bandwidth. With TFC, a
packet can be safely retransmitted without needing additional credit because the corresponding buffer
at the destination must have already been allocated for the original packet.
Note that retransmission at the PDC level is conceptually separate from any retransmission that may
occur at the link level using link-layer retry (LLR).
Because TFC controls access to receive buffers, different destinations may have different requirements
when it comes to buffer management. Some destinations may allocate buffers for entire MTU-sized
packets, so the transmission of a packet must then consume an MTU of credit. Other destinations may

PAGE 506

506

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
allocate buffers in cells, whereby the arrival of a smaller packet will consume fewer cells than the arrival
of a larger packet.
To accommodate different buffer allocation strategies, the approach taken by TFC is to allow the
destination to manage a receive buffer as a number of “cells,” where each cell is of size
tfc_dest_cell_size. As credit is allocated in units of 256 bytes, a range of cell sizes from 256 bytes to 9 KB,
in multiples of 256 bytes, MUST be supported. The tfc_dest_cell_size variable defaults to 256 bytes, the
same as a unit of credit. When the source transmits a packet, the number of cells required to store the
packet is calculated, and hence the number of bytes of credit consumed, credit_used, is calculated.
A TFC source can send if TFC.CanSend() returns TRUE:
TFC.CanSend(rtx):
if rtx or ccc.credit > 0:
return TRUE

else
return FALSE
Sending a packet reduces ccc.credit as follows:
TFC.OnSend(credit_used, rtx):
if rtx == FALSE:
ccc.credit –= credit_used
In CanSend() and OnSend(), rtx indicates whether the packet is a retransmission. Retransmissions do
not require credit to send and do not consume credit when sending.
Because it may be possible for packet sizes to change in transit, and as destinations may wish to store
additional data along with an arriving packet, tfc_pkt_size is defined as the UET payload size +
tfc_pkt_overhead bytes. The source and destination must use the same value of the constant
tfc_pkt_overhead. Constant tfc_pkt_overhead defaults to 256 bytes, the same as one unit of credit. It is
RECOMMENDED that tfc_pkt_overhead is configurable between 0 and 256 bytes, but an
implementation MAY use a constant size of 256 bytes — in which case a destination may need to
allocate additional buffering if larger encapsulations are used.
The tfc_pkt_overhead parameter is intended to cover any additional memory required at the destination
to store the arriving packet. This may include space to store the Ethernet, IP, UDP, and SES headers; FCS;
and any additional metadata the destination may store along with the packet. The destination MUST be
able to store any valid arriving packet for which it has allocated credit.
TFC manages a unidirectional flow of data from a sending FEP to a receiving FEP. As the requirements
for tfc_dest_cell_size and tfc_pkt_overhead are primarily determined by the destination FEP, when
PDCs are established in both directions between a pair of FEPs, the values of tfc_dest_cell_size and
tfc_pkt_overhead may be different in one direction from the other.

PAGE 507

507

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The values of tfc_dest_cell_size and tfc_pkt_overhead cannot be modified on an active PDC. Either their
default values MUST be used, or any non-default values MUST be configured or communicated out of
band prior to data being sent on the PDC.
3.6.15.1 Examples of credit_used calculation
The values of UET payload size, tfc_dest_cell_size and tfc_pkt_overhead determine the amount of
credit required to send a packet.
For example, to send an UET payload size of 4096 bytes with a tfc_dest_cell_size set to 512 bytes and
default tfc_hdr_size, then:
tfc_dest_cell_size = 512B (configured value)
tfc_pkt_overhead = 256B (default value)
tfc_pkt_size = UET payload + tfc_pkt_overhead
credit_used = ROUNDUP(tfc_pkt_size/tfc_dest_cell_size)*tfc_dest_cell_size

Thus with a 4096 byte UET payload, tfc_pkt_size is 4096 + 256 = 4352 bytes.
Sending a tfc_pkt_size of 4352 bytes requires 4352/512 = 8.5 cells; rounded up this requires 9 cells, and
so credit_used = 4608 bytes.
Alternately, a destination may wish to maintain data structures for packet buffers on a per-packet basis.
In such a case, tfc_dest_cell_size would be set to the maximum value of 9216 bytes. Sending the same
4 KB packet would use the same tfc_pkt_size of 4352 bytes, but this would require only one 9126-byte
cell. The credit_used would then be 9216 bytes. Such a destination would then allocate n * 9216 bytes
of credit for n packet buffers.
3.6.15.2 TFC Credit Initialization
When a TFC PDC is created, the ccc.credit value MUST be set to tfc_pkt_overhead or a larger configured
value, but it cannot be less than tfc_pkt_overhead. The intent of setting the initial credit to
tfc_pkt_overhead is to permit the source to send an SES NO_OP packet that contains a credit request in
the pds.req_cc_state.credit_target field, allowing the source to request enough additional credit to
send data. If an implementation reports a tfc_pkt_overhead of 0, a larger configured value should be
used. The rationale for using an SES NO_OP instead of a Credit Request CP to request initial credit is that
an SES NO_OP can bring up a PDC, whereas a Credit Request CP cannot. The ACK for the SES NO_OP may
carry the available credit, or a separate Credit CP may be used.
Once a PDC is established, if more credit is required than initially requested, the source can convey this
to the destination using the pds.req_cc_state field in PDS Request packets or the pds.payload field in
Credit Request CPs. The pds.payload field and Credit Request CP is used in the same way as RCCC. It
carries a pds.payload.ccc_id to identify the CCC context at the source and a pds.payload.credit_target
field, which carries the cumulative amount of credit requested since the CCC was created.

PAGE 508

508

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
As with RCCC, multiple TFC PDCs may be controlled by the same CCC, or each PDC may be given its own
CCC. It is RECOMMENDED that the decision to share a TFC CCC between PDCs be a configurable option.
When a CCC controls multiple PDCs, credit allocated to one of the PDCs controlled by the CCC may be
used by any of the PDCs controlled by the CCC.
The source controls whether multiple PDCs share a CCC. The PDS Request header carries the
pds.req_cc_state.ccc_id field. If multiple PDCs between a pair of FEPs are assigned the same CCC_ID,
then the destination MUST associate these PDCs with the same CCC. If different CCC_IDs are used, then
the PDCs MUST be associated with independent CCC instances.
3.6.15.3 TFC CCC Shutdown
When the last PDC sharing a TFC CCC is shut down, the CCC is also shut down. Any credit allocated for
the CCC is no longer usable by the source to send new data, and any buffers at the destination reserved
for the use of that credit may be freed for other uses.
At the source, a CCC MUST NOT be reused for a new PDC after the last PDC using that CCC has entered
the QUIESCE state in the Single PDC Close State Machine of Figure 3-57. This procedure prevents a
potential race where the destination thinks the last PDC using a CCC has been shut down and frees
buffers, but the source attempts to start a new PDC using that CCC.
3.6.15.4 TFC CCC Credit Timer
Like RCCC, TFC CCC requires a credit timer at the source to cover a corner case where packets containing
credit can be lost. When a sender enters an active state — that is, it has no credit available, but has data
to send — it starts a timer with a timeout equal to the retransmit timeout. When the timer expires, the
TFC.OnSourceCreditTimer() pseudocode is executed.
TFC.OnSourceCreditTimer():
#either we don’t have any work to do, we have pending packets which
#will trigger timeouts or we already have credit.
if ccc.state != READY:


return

send_credit_request(ccc.credit_target)
3.6.16 Multipath Path Selection
This section describes the path selection algorithms used to load-balance the network. It is
RECOMMENDED that a UET endpoint performs multipath load balancing for RUD and RUDI traffic, but
the choice of precise implementation is left to implementations.
The protocol relies on multipath forwarding to distribute packets from flows across multiple network
paths. With the exception of the single-path ROD service, packet spraying is typically done using per-
packet ECMP, which uses hashing of network header fields to spray packets across many paths. This
approach can achieve higher throughput and lower flow completion times than what can be achieved by
a single path.

PAGE 509

509

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Some network switches can perform packet spraying themselves, rather than hashing the header fields
to determine the path. It is RECOMMENDED that such behavior not be enabled for UET traffic if path-
aware multipath spraying (Section 3.6.16.4) is used, as it prevents UET getting a clean signal as to which
paths are congested.
Despite attempts to evenly distribute the traffic, some path-specific congestion is likely to occur.
Hashing is not guaranteed to spread the packets evenly. The presence of other traffic that is not sprayed
may impact available bandwidth on some paths. In addition, failures may render a path unavailable.
Improved throughput and reduced flow completion times can be achieved if the sources actively
balance traffic.
3.6.16.1 Path Entropy
When packet spraying is employed, packets are sprayed across multiple paths by varying the value of an
entropy field that carries the Entropy value (EV) in packet headers (see Section 3.6.10.1). The entropy
field is used by switches to determine which ECMP path each packet takes to the destination.
Three modes of operation are permitted:
•
Single path (used only by ROD). All packets in a CCC use the same EV for some period of time,
before the EV is changed.
•
Oblivious spraying. The packets of a CCC are sprayed across many paths by changing the EV
through a large space (typically at least 256 values). EVs are chosen pseudo-randomly with the
goal of spreading traffic evenly across all possible paths.
•
Path-aware spraying. The packets of a CCC are sprayed across many paths by adaptively
changing the EV to avoid congested paths, based on feedback provided by the destination as to
which EVs saw congestion.
3.6.16.2 Single-Path Entropy
At PDC startup, the reliability module generates an AllocateCCC() event with sprayed=FALSE. The CCC
chooses an entropy value to use for the packets of the flow. To ensure that, in the absence of route
changes or packet loss, packets arrive in order, only a single entropy value is used at one time for this
CCC.
If network congestion is observed and it is determined that the congestion is not occurring at the final
link to the destination (which cannot be avoided by re-routing), then the CCC MAY change the entropy
value it uses. To minimize the impact of reordering and any potential retransmission, it is
RECOMMENDED that the CCC either change the entropy value when the flow has become idle, or if
there is no idle period, that it does not change the entropy value more often than every t_reroute RTTs.
How long a flow should be idle before changing entropy value is a configuration choice. It is safe to
switch whenever there are no packets in transit, but such a conservative choice will not necessarily lead
to improved performance. It is RECOMMENDED that the default value of t_reroute be set to at least 10
RTTs and that this value be configurable.

PAGE 510

510

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
When more than one single-path PDC exists between a source and destination, PDS should request the
allocation of different CCCs for them. The different CCCs between the same pair of FEPs SHOULD
coordinate to allocate different entropy values to reduce the frequency that CCCs use the same single
path.
Informative Text:
The motivation for using different but coordinated CCCs is to reduce the impact of flow collisions. A
flow collision on one PDC is unlikely to affect another PDC if they use different EVs, and congestion
state from one single-path EV is not a good predictor of available capacity using a different single-
path EV.

3.6.16.3 Oblivious Multipath Spraying
The source maintains a space of entropy values to use for the CCC, but it does not keep information
about which entropy values are less congested than others. A typical size for the entropy space is 256
values, but other sized spaces MAY be used. The source SHOULD use entropy values from the entropy
space in a pseudo-random order, with the goal being to use all the entropy values once before
repeating. It is beneficial for each source to independently re-randomize the pseudo-random sequence
periodically to reduce the probability of multiple sources synchronizing on sequences that hash to
similar path sequences.
How the source chooses a pseudo-random sequence is implementation defined. A simple modular
counter, while not pseudo-random, suffices for protocol interoperability and so is permitted, but it relies
on switch ECMP hash functions to provide pseudo-random load balancing. This may be sufficient in
many deployments. If so, the counter SHOULD be initialized randomly to avoid synchronization.
Oblivious spraying is most effective when combined with packet trimming. With packet trimming, on
congestive loss, the source will receive a NACK quickly from the destination and will retransmit the
packet as soon as congestion control permits. The retransmitted packet will, with high probability, take a
different path. The use of a relatively low trimming threshold of around one BDP prevents queues
growing unnecessarily large, and as trimmed packets use little capacity at the congestion bottleneck and
elicit fast retransmissions on a different path, oblivious spraying with trimming can do a good job of
actively load balancing the network.
Oblivious spraying without packet trimming is discouraged, as it will result in load balancing that is less
even than path-aware spraying. However, in a network without packet trimming, a source MAY choose
to employ oblivious spraying if it cannot hold enough per-path state.
3.6.16.4 Path-aware Multipath Spraying
As with oblivious spraying, the source maintains a space of entropy values to use for the CCC and uses
those entropy values in a pseudo-random order. The size of this space SHOULD be chosen adaptively so
that each value used can be considered for reuse within less than two RTTs. This approach is to ensure
that load balancing is not responding to out-of-date path congestion information.

PAGE 511

511

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
In reverse-direction ACK and NACK packets, the destination feeds back the Entropy from the received
packet together with the pds.flags.m (“marked”) flag that indicates that this path experienced
congestion. The pds.flags.m is set when the arriving packet that triggers an ACK or NACK has the
ip.ecn.ce bit set.
The destination MAY use other forms of telemetry to determine whether a path is congested.
On receipt of an ACK or NACK packet with the pds.flags.m flag set, the source SHOULD ensure that the
indicated Entropy is not reused for at least one round-trip time. An exception is when ACKs or NACKs
indicate that the majority of paths are congested. Under such circumstances, the load balancing signal
has become saturated, and skipping paths will no longer be effective. The fraction of paths that must be
congested before the destination decides the load balancing signal is saturated SHOULD be a
configuration option. A reasonable default value for this configuration option is 50% of paths congested.
This value is a tradeoff: It is undesirable to reduce the entropy pool unnecessarily during network
oversubscription or incast; however, it is desirable to maintain load balancing for as long as reasonably
possible when congestion occurs.
How the source chooses to avoid reusing the path is implementation specific. For example, two possible
approaches are:
1. Entropy from ACKs received that do not indicate congestion via the pds.flags.m flag can be re-
used for outgoing packets, as in REPS [12]. This self-clocking mechanism essentially stores the
Entropy values “on the wire.” If a packet is lost, the packet is not ACKed, so the Entropy is not
reused; similarly, if the packet is ACKed but the pds.flags.m flag indicates congestion, then the
EV is not reused. REPS can be extended with a small local circular buffer (significantly smaller
than the supported EV space, e.g., eight values) to cache good entropies. These entropy values
are then consumed when sending out data packets. If an outgoing packet requires an EV but the
buffer is empty, a new (random) EV can be used.
2. Maintain a bitmap where each bit in the bitmap corresponds to an Entropy value used [10].
When feedback indicates a path selected by an Entropy value is congested, the corresponding
bit in the bitmap is set. The source rotates through the entropy space using values in a pseudo-
random order. When the source is choosing an EV for a packet to send, if the corresponding bit
is set, it skips that EV, clears the bit, and tries the next EV in sequence. To ensure feedback is
recent, the size of the active Entropy value space may be dynamically changed, so that
uncongested entropy values are reused within approximately two RTTs.
Combinations of these methods or other methods are also permitted. Path-aware spraying permits
more active load balancing across the paths selected by the entropy values.
3.6.16.5 Detecting and Handling Path Failure
CMS is primarily aimed at networks with switches that perform ECMP load balancing based on a hash of
the Entropy in the packet header. In such networks there is a mapping of a single path to a destination
with an Entropy value. Path-aware multipath spraying can use this mapping, together with ECN feedback
and NACKs generated due to packet trimming, to improve load balancing beyond what the switches

PAGE 512

512

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
achieve by themselves. Most such networks will use a dynamic routing protocol to determine the ECMP
set for a destination address. When a failure occurs in such a network, it is expected that dynamic
routing will eventually remove failed paths from consideration, and so EVs that previously mapped to a
failed path will then be remapped to a working path. Such dynamic rerouting may take many round-trip
times, and all UET connections that spray across the failed path will suffer packet loss until rerouting has
taken place.
How UET-CC load balancing handles such transient failures is an implementation decision. For example,
if path-aware load balancing is being performed by UET-CC and packet trimming is enabled, then actual
packet loss should be relatively rare. In such circumstances, a UET-CC source might choose to avoid
reusing an EV that resulted in a timeout or SACK-based loss inference decision for some significant
period of time, long enough for routing to have reconverged. However, if trimming is not used, then
such inferred packet loss may be more common. An implementation would therefore need to take care
removing too many EVs from the entropy set it is using.
Some networks may have a static mapping of EVs to paths with no dynamic routing protocol used to
route around failures. UET-CC’s path-aware multipath spraying can be used in such networks to actively
route around failed paths by not reusing EVs that result in timeouts or SACK-based loss inference. In
such networks, such active path choice takes on greater importance, because routing will not remove
the paths from use. How to do this is again implementation dependent.
When a UET-CC endpoint does not perform path-aware multipath spraying, it is not a requirement for
the network to maintain a stable mapping between EVs and paths. In such networks, switches may
perform local load-balancing decisions on a per-packet basis. When this is being performed, UET-CC load
balancing SHOULD NOT attempt to remove from use any EVs corresponding to packet loss, as there will
not be a stable correspondence between an EV and a failed path.
3.6.16.6 Multi-port and Multi-plane Operation
UET supports multi-port NICs, and the CCC can spray traffic across multiple ports that are simultaneously
used for a single PDC. There are many ways multiple ports can be used, and not all of them are
supported by this specification. Among the possibilities are options numbered as follows:
1. Each port connects to a separate plane and uses the same FEP address. No inter-plane routing is
provided.
2. Each port connects to a separate plane and uses a different FEP address.
3. Each port connects to a single plane and uses the same FEP address. Anycast routing is used to
route packets to one of the destination ports with the same FEP address.
4. Each port connects to a single plane and uses a different FEP address.
Options 1 and 3 are supported by this specification.
In this specification, the CCC does not maintain addressing information, so multiple ports with different
addresses are not directly supported.

PAGE 513

513

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Option 2 is not directly supported by the CCC, but once the CCC has chosen an EV and port, an
implementation could map the destination FEP/port to an appropriate IP address using an additional
mapping table for destination IP addresses. This specification does not cover this use case.
Load balancing for option 4 requires the CCC to choose an EV/port/FEP address combination, and load-
balance between the different possible source ports and destination ports between the same pair of
FEPs. This specification does not cover this use case.
3.6.16.6.1 Multiple Separate Planes, One Shared FEP Address for All Ports.
This use case is option 1 listed above. UET RUD PDCs can be created between a pair of multi-port FEPs
configured in a multi-plane topology where each plane is logically or physically separate, such that a
packet sent from FEP A using its port on plane P will be received by the port at FEP B that is also on
plane P. In such cases, a single IP address is used by all the ports of each FEP. In such configurations, a
CCC can load-balance traffic between planes and within planes by spraying traffic across a range of
entropy values, where each EV is mapped to a specific outgoing port, and hence to a plane. Each EV for a
PDC is used on only one plane. UET ACK and NACK packets specify the EV from the respective data
packet, so it is unambiguous from the EV which path the feedback refers to.
Multi-port operation is supported via the GetSendParams() interface between the PDS scheduler and
the CCC.
GetSendParams(free_port_list) -> port, Entropy, Credit_Target

When GetSendParams() is called, the scheduler supplies a list of the ports that currently have spare
capacity to send a packet. There MUST be at least one free port in this list.
The CCC will choose an EV that is associated with one of the free ports in the free_port_list, performing
load balancing using ECN feedback to avoid congested paths, as in single-port operation.
3.6.16.6.2 Multi-port, Single Plane, One IP address for All Ports
This use case is option 3 above. In this case multi-port NICs are connected to a single plane, but all ports
of the same FEP share an IP address. Anycast routing can then ensure that all the ports can be part of
the ECMP set used to route packets. In such cases the CCC will choose the outgoing port (if more than
one free port is available), but the incoming port is determined by the switches hashing the EV from the
packets. From the point of view of the CCC, option 2 behaves in the same way as option 1, in that the
CCC MUST consistently map a chosen EV to a single outgoing port so that the EV in ACKs and NACKs
refer to an unambiguous path.
3.6.16.6.3 Single-port Spraying on a Multi-port NIC
An implementation MAY map a FEP to a single port on a multi-port NIC.  For this specification, options 2
and 4 SHOULD be handled in this manner. In such cases, each port is visible to the application as a
separate FEP, and it is then the application’s responsibility to load-balance traffic between FEPs and
hence between ports. In this case the PDS and hence CCC are unaware that other ports exist; the CCC

PAGE 514

514

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
SHOULD map its entire entropy space to the port managed by its PDS. The free_port_list in
GetSendParams() can then indicate only a single port, so the choice of port by the CCC is a no-op.
3.6.17 Switch Configuration for UET CC
UET-CC uses ECN both for load balancing and as the congestion signal driving NSCC. UET-CC also
optionally uses trimming for oblivious load balancing and to provide early loss indication. Thus, the
correct configuration of network switches is important for UET-CC performance.
Plane_BDP is defined as the bandwidth-delay product of the lowest bandwidth path between a source
and destination, measured without queuing, where the network path traverses the core of the network.
In most networks this will be:
Plane_BDP = min(sender.linkspeed, receiver.linkspeed) * config_base_rtt

For a multi-ported NIC on a multi-rail topology, the linkspeed is typically the linkspeed of a single port,
not the aggregate bandwidth of all ports.
Informative Comment
Plane_BDP may differ from the BDP value used in CCC algorithms over a multi-ported NIC in a multi-
rail topology. In this scenario, the CCC BDP value is based on the sprayed capacity across all ports in
the spraying set, but Plane_BDP considers only a single port or rail. For a single-port NIC, Plane_BDP
and BDP are the same.

UET can be used with two or three traffic classes (3.6.4.7) for each UET PDC. In the three-traffic class
case, these are:
•
Low priority (TC_low)
Queue setting for this TC is referred to as queue_low.
•
Medium priority (TC_med)
Queue setting for this TC is referred to as queue_med.
•
High priority (TC_high)
Queue setting for this TC is referred to as queue_high.
•
When two traffic classes are used, the medium priority TC (TC_med) will not be used.
The RECOMMENDED default settings for ECN when using probabilistic marking are:
queue_low.min_thresh = 0.2 * Plane_BDP
queue_low.max_thresh = 0.8 * Plane_BDP

ECN can also be set using a deterministic marking threshold. The recommended deterministic ECN
marking threshold is 0.5 * Plane_BDP. In general, probabilistic marking is preferred.

PAGE 515

515

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
ECN SHOULD be disabled for queue_med and queue_high.
When trimming is enabled, the RECOMMENDED default settings are:
queue_low.trim_threshold = Plane_BDP
queue_med.drop_threshold = Plane_BDP
queue_high.drop_threshold = Plane_BDP

If the DSCP_TRIMMABLE_RTX codepoint is used to protect retransmitted packets, the
queue_low.trim_threshold for these packets is RECOMMENDED to be 1.5 * Plane_BDP.

In the absence of trimming, the UET congestion management algorithm supports widely deployed
shared switch buffer architectures. Although the algorithm is capable of handling highly variable
latencies caused by the shared buffer, it is recommended to bound the tail drop threshold. The
RECOMMENDED drop threshold for a given queue should be at least 2 * Plane_BDP and at most
5 * Plane_BDP.
Rather than using strict priority, a deployment MAY choose to use the same priority for queue_med and
queue_low, but instead use weighted round robin or a similar scheduling scheme to ensure that when
the trim rate is high, queue_med gets a large share of the bandwidth. In such cases a reasonable default
is for queue_med to be weighted to receive 75% of the capacity when competing with queue_low.
3.6.17.1 CSIG Configuration
The overall bucket boundaries for the max(Delay) signal quantization SHOULD be configured based on
the trim or drop threshold recommendations, regardless of whether the compact or wide CSIG header
format is used.
The recommended queue_low.trim_threshold, queue_med.drop_threshold, and
queue_high.drop_threshold are specified as factors of Plane_BDP, which is derived from the link speed
and config_base_rtt. This information is used to derive expected maximum packet queueing times per
trim or drop threshold, which equates Plane_BDP to config_base_rtt as follows:
Plane_BDP = min(sender.linkspeed, receiver.linkspeed) * config_base_rtt

However, this equation assumes that only a single queue is active per port. To account for scenarios
where other, higher-priority queues are active and may increase maximum queueing times, it is
RECOMMENDED to apply a 2-times multiplier to the threshold-derived maximum packet queueing time.
Informative Text:
These queue threshold settings are based on simulated results to date. Lower drop thresholds may
lead to additional loss of high-priority traffic. Additional tuning of deployed implementations may be
required.

PAGE 516

516

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Based on the above methodology, the recommended trim and drop thresholds with their derived,
RECOMMENDED bottom-of-the-bottom-bucket to top-of-the-top-bucket boundaries are:
•
With trimming:
o
queue_low.trim_threshold: 1.5 * Plane_BDP
o
Bucketization range: [0, 3 × config_base_rtt]
•
Without trimming:
o
queue_med.drop_threshold, queue_high.drop_threshold: At least 2 * Plane_BDP and at
most 5 * Plane_BDP
o
Bucketization range: at least [0, 4 × config_base_rtt] at most [0, 10 × config_base_rtt]
Intermediate bucket boundaries SHOULD be distributed linearly between the minimum and maximum
values.
When CSIG is enabled for multiple traffic classes, it applies the settings uniformly across all of them. The
maximum trim or drop thresholds among all affected traffic classes within the port SHOULD be used as
the reference values for bucket boundary calculation.
3.6.18 Programmable Congestion Management
Ultra Ethernet programmable congestion management (PCM) provides support for alternative
congestion control (CC) and load balancing (LB) algorithms within the transport architecture. PCM is
designed to support algorithms that reduce congestion and efficiently utilize network resources across
multiple paths.
CC support in UE PCM is categorized into two primary mechanisms. The first mechanism governs the
sending of data within the network by restricting the number of bytes in flight, through either a send
window or credit scheme. The second optional mechanism limits the send rate. While hybrid
approaches are possible, the baseline congestion control specified herein limits the number of bytes in
the network only by using windows for NSCC and credits for RCCC.
LB support is provided through two approaches: per-packet load balancing, where algorithms are
invoked for every transmitted and acknowledged request packet, and EV table-based load balancing,
which relies on a hardware-maintained table of entropy values (EV table). PCM algorithms manipulate
this table to optimize traffic distribution dynamically.
A robust congestion management framework must be capable of operating across endpoints handling a
diverse range of traffic types. Large AI systems frequently encounter mixed workloads consisting of both
AI and storage traffic. These mixed workloads necessitate an approach that provides fundamental
quality-of-service (QoS) mechanisms not only within the network at each switch buffer, but also at the
endpoints to ensure appropriate traffic differentiation and prioritization.

PAGE 517

517

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Furthermore, distance-aware congestion management is a critical requirement in Ultra Ethernet (UE) to
accommodate the growing diversity of traffic patterns across modern network deployments. Storage
traffic is frequently mirrored across multiple datacenters, often spanning distances of thousands of
kilometers. The replication process requires congestion management techniques that account for
latency and bandwidth constraints associated with mixed short- and long-distance transmission.
Similarly, AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems increasingly operate across distributed
datacenter infrastructures [55]. These architectures generate network flows that traverse both short
intra-datacenter paths and long inter-datacenter links [56]. To optimize performance and minimize
congestion, endpoints are required to differentiate between short-distance and long-distance flows.
This distinction enables adaptive congestion control mechanisms that adjust transmission behavior
according to the network distance, ensuring efficient data transfer across varying deployment scenarios.
By integrating distance-aware congestion management, UE can address the specific needs of storage
replication and AI/HPC workloads while maintaining network stability and performance.
While baseline algorithms such as NSCC and RCCC provide strong defaults, they are fixed. Evolving site
conditions create a need for forward-compatible mechanisms. Operators may need a way to adopt new
methods, swap in alternative algorithms, or apply targeted modifications for the new conditions.
PCM addresses these gaps by providing a programmable way to extend and adapt congestion policies in
the network. PCM provides configurability to network administrators. This approach enables fine-
grained control over congestion management policies, allowing adjustments to optimize network
performance in response to specific deployment requirements and evolving traffic conditions.
PCM offers functionality similar to the congestion control mechanisms implemented in the QUIC
protocol [54]. However, unlike QUIC, where congestion control operations are managed in software at
the transport layer, PCM enables designers to offload these functions entirely to the network hardware
at the endpoint. This hardware-based approach ensures low-latency congestion management, reduces
computational overhead on hosts, and enables highly efficient and scalable control mechanisms that
operate seamlessly within high-performance networking environments.
3.6.18.1 PCM Architecture
The UE PCM architecture is designed as a logically structured framework composed of four distinct
components:
1. Incoming signals: Signals that gather information about the current state of the network as well
as relevant operational state from the endpoint, form the first component. These signals
provide data necessary for congestion analysis and management.
2. Congestion control (CC) algorithm: The algorithm, including its state, that processes the
collected signals to compute appropriate control actions. By interpreting network conditions
and endpoint states, the algorithm determines precise adjustments required to optimize data
flow and mitigate congestion. The CC algorithm defines congestion control.
3. Load balancing (LB) algorithm: The algorithm that assigns entropy values to transmitted request
packets and reacts to network signals when responses for transmitted requests are received.

PAGE 518

518

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
4. Control table: A structured table that stores computed adjustments by control mechanisms
associated with each congestion control context (CCC). This table dictates transmission
scheduling behavior based on dynamically updated control variables, ensuring efficient traffic
regulation.
Both CC and LB algorithms use local and global state to store and exchange variables between
invocations.
This logical architecture is designed to be independent of any specific physical implementation, allowing
for compatibility with NSCC and RCCC congestion control schemes, as well as optional load balancing
mechanisms. The following sections provide a detailed definition of each architectural component and
its role in congestion management. Figure 3-3 shows an overview of the architecture.

FEPs that implement PCM support one or more active congestion control algorithms bound to different
CCCs. Algorithms operate independently of other active algorithms and can coordinate through global
variables. The PCM runtime is responsible for delivering signals to, and applying algorithm-initiated
operations to, hardware.
A possible algorithm lifecycle can be as follows:
•
Load: Algorithms are loaded by an implementation-specific PCM tool to a specific FEP.
•
Instantiate: The PCM tool creates an instance of the algorithm.
•
Configure: Parameters are setup for an algorithm instance.
•
Assign: The algorithm instance is assigned to a subset of network traffic.
•
Activate: The algorithm instance is activated and controls network traffic.

Figure 3-135 - PCM Logical Architecture Overview

PAGE 519

519

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
Stop/Deactivate: The instance is quiesced and no longer controls data traffic.
•
Destroy: The instance is torn down and all per-instance resources and state are released.
•
Unload: When all instances of the algorithm have been stopped, the algorithm may be
unloaded.
These steps illustrate a typical algorithm lifecycle. It is not mandated that these steps are explicitly
followed by any particular implementation. Tools may merge or skip steps (e.g., stop and unload).
This specification defines how to use floating-point datatypes. Implementations MUST offer integer
datatypes and MAY offer floating-point types. If floating-point types are not supported, the compilation
of a program using floating point MUST fail. Integer datatypes MAY be used to approximate floating
point.
3.6.18.2 Congestion Management Algorithm Specification and Invocation
Congestion management algorithms are a fundamental component of the UE PCM framework,
responsible for dynamically regulating congestion through interactions with system signals and CC
controls. They can be triggered by defined signals or timers, potentially allowing invocation for each
incoming acknowledgment (ACK) packet to ensure prompt responsiveness to network conditions. These
algorithms can both read and modify signals and controls, enabling adaptive congestion management
strategies.
At the time of algorithm invocation, the system captures a snapshot of all relevant signal values. These
values remain fixed for the duration of the algorithm’s execution. Signals arriving after the invocation
timestamp do not affect the current execution and are queued for processing during the next invocation
cycle.
Informative Text:
PCM programs may assume that the algorithm is invoked immediately after the timed or control
trigger occurs. Delays could lead to inconsistent signal observations and reduced algorithm fidelity.
The exact details depend on the implementation.

3.6.18.3 Load Balancing Algorithm Specification and Invocation
Like congestion management algorithms, load balancing algorithms are invoked by data path transmit,
ACK/NACK, and retransmit timeout events. Implementations may use triggers to modulate the
frequency of these events on a per-CCC basis. LB algorithms are logically distinct from CC algorithms and
are expressed as independent programs with their own entry point, accumulators, and triggers.
PCM supports two distinct LB implementation models: per-packet and EV table.
3.6.18.3.1 Per-Packet
In the per-packet model, LB algorithms are invoked for every transmitted and received packet, and the
data path does not maintain any EVs or EV state. Algorithms can associate per-packet private state with

PAGE 520

520

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
transmitted packets; this state is available to the algorithm when the corresponding ACK or NACK for the
packet is received.
3.6.18.3.2 EV Table
In the EV table model, the HW maintains a logical table of EVs for every active CCC. For each transmit,
the hardware LB algorithm selects an EV, and for every received ACK or NACK packet the HW may invoke
the PCM algorithm, depending on runtime configuration.
In this model, each HW LB algorithm is described by a YAML schema under an lb_algorithm stanza. This
scheme is used to:
•
Specify and validate the per-CCC and per-EV configuration.
•
Generate LB API bindings to enable the algorithm to manipulate per-EV and per-CCC state.
Using this mechanism, implementations can achieve hardware performance while still maintaining
software control.
The detailed YAML schema and fields for EV table LB algorithms are described in Section 3.6.18.8.5. The
key concepts and primitives are described in Table 3-105:
Table 3-105 - YAML Schema Concepts and Primitives
Primitive
Description
hw_algo
Names the hardware LB implementation for the instance.
hw_config
Algorithm-specific, static configuration consumed by the HW algorithm.
ev_fields
Per-EV fields; defines EV values and state accessible or modifiable by SW. Multiple fields may
be defined for every EV; each field is defined by a unique name, type, and whether it can be
modified or accessed by SW.
ccc_fields
Per-CCC fields; used for CCC wide parameters. Like ev_fields, multiple fields may be defined for
every CCC.

In the EV table model:
•
Each CCC has an EV table of fixed depth, E, addressed by an index into a per-CCC logical table of
range [0, E].
•
For each transmit:
o The hardware LB algorithm selects an EV in the EV table.
▪
The selection process is algorithm-specific.
o The hardware LB algorithm derives the on-wire entropy from the EV (as stored in the EV
table), the values of exposed per-CCC and per-EV fields, and private state and logic.
•
The LB algorithm:
o The algorithm uses the PCM LB API to read and update (where allowed) ev_fields and
ccc_fields.
o The algorithm interacts with the hardware LB algorithm via the same trigger and signal
mechanisms as for congestion management.

PAGE 521

521

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Informative Text:
The path-aware multipath spraying algorithm (3.6.16.4) is an example of a sophisticated scheme that
can be supported in the EV table model. It maintains CCC-level path configuration and per-EV
penalties and exposes the hardware-computed on-wire EV (including both path index bits and higher-
order randomness) to PCM.
The YAML syntax for the algorithm is outlined below:

lb_algorithm:
  op_model: ev-table
  lb_entry: uet_lb_uet_bmp
  hw_algo: uet-bmp

  hw_config:
    path_random_reinit:
      type: uint
      comment: "interval in microseconds between recomputation of
path_random (upper EV bits)"

  ccc_fields:
    - name: no_of_paths
      type: uint
      sw_access: ro
      init: hw_init

    - name: ev_max_penalty
      type: uint
      sw_access: ro
      range: [0, 15]
      init: cfg_provided

    - name: ev_skip_count
      type: uint
      sw_access: ro
      range: [0, 0xFFFF]
      init: zero

  ev_fields:
    - name: entropy
      type: uint
      role: ev_value
      sw_access: ro
      range: [0, 0xFFFF]
      init: hw_init

    - name: ev_skip_penalty
      type: uint
      sw_access: rw
      range: [0, 0xFF]
      init: zero

3.6.18.4 Congestion Signals
Congestion signals are key metrics gathered either from the network or directly at the endpoint to
inform congestion management decisions. These signals provide critical information regarding current
network conditions and performance. For instance, incoming acknowledgment (ACK) packets contain
service time information and an indication that the associated request was explicit congestion
notification (ECN) marked. Additionally, endpoint time measurements can be utilized to measure round-
trip time (RTT) for each packet, offering insight into latency variations and network responsiveness.
Updates to such congestion signals often occur at a higher frequency than the invocation of the CC or LB
algorithm itself. As a result, signals may undergo multiple updates before being processed, with
accumulated values maintained according to predefined rules such as summation or maximum
aggregation. This ensures that the CC and LB algorithms operate on an appropriately synthesized set of
data, allowing for accurate congestion control adjustments while maintaining computational efficiency.
Ultra Ethernet categorizes congestion signals into three distinct types: mandatory signals, optional
signals, and vendor-specific signals. Mandatory signals form the core set that all PCM implementations
MUST support to ensure baseline compatibility and functionality across deployments. Optional signals
provide additional capabilities that MAY be implemented selectively based on specific requirements,
allowing flexibility in adapting congestion management behavior to different use cases. Vendor-specific
signals MAY be used to enable further extensibility, permitting individual vendors to introduce
customized metrics tailored to proprietary networking solutions. While the mandatory signals ensure
interoperability across all UE implementations, optional and vendor-specific signals offer adaptability to
specialized workloads and infrastructure configurations. Any UE PCM implementation MUST support the
default signal set, MAY include any subset of the optional signals, and vendors MAY extend the available
signal set with their own enhancements.
Signals are configured through a YAML definition specified at algorithm load time as outlined in Section
3.6.18.8.5.
3.6.18.4.1 Signal Accumulation Operators
PCM defines a set of accumulation operations for processing congestion signals. These operations
determine how multiple signal updates are combined over time. The specific accumulation functions
used in UE are formally specified in Table 3-106, providing a structured approach to handling signal
updates within the congestion management framework. Any implementation MUST support all defined
accumulation operations. Table 3-110 lists mandatory and default accumulators for all signals.
Table 3-106 - Mandatory Signal and Global Variable Accumulation Operators
Accumulation Operation
Description
uet_op_sum
Running sum
uet_op_max
Running maximum
uet_op_min
Running minimum
uet_op_last
Simply store last update (overwrite)

PAGE 523

523

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

In addition, the optional accumulation operators are defined in Table 3-107.
Table 3-107 - Optional Signal Accumulation Operators
Accumulation Operation
Description
uet_op_ewma
Exponentially weighted moving average for newly samples x defined as
ewma = x * s + ewma * (1-s)
with s being a configurable smoothing factor

This accumulation operator conceptually requires floating point support, and all
variable types are float. Implementations MAY use integer or fixed-point to
approximate the floating-point computations.

When a new update to a congestion signal is received, the update is integrated into the current signal
value using the predefined accumulation operation. The update occurs atomically, meaning that each
signal update is applied without interruption, preserving data integrity and preventing partial
modifications. Additionally, the update order is undefined, as PCM assumes associative operators,
allowing updates to be applied irrespective of sequencing constraints. This may affect the accuracy of
some operators that are not actually associative such as uet_op_ewma().
Furthermore, all signal updates originating from a specific source, such as an acknowledgment (ACK)
packet, are processed atomically. This guarantees that multiple updates contained within a single packet
are applied simultaneously before any subsequent packet influences the corresponding signals. For
instance, if a packet carries updates to both an explicit congestion notification (ECN) signal and a round-
trip time (RTT) signal, both updates are applied at the same instant, ensuring consistency before any
other packet modifies either of those signals. This atomic handling mechanism maintains consistency in
congestion signal processing within UE's congestion management framework.
Multiple accumulation operations (e.g. uet_op_last() and uet_op_sum()) may be defined for the same
signal.

Signal Mnemonics: Even though the signal_index fields are all integers for simple compiler
optimization based on constants, it is recommended to use mnemonic representations such as
macros to refer to signals in the source code. The function interface allows compiler developers to
easily replace any function invocation, e.g., with a simple load or store to a special address. Those
functions may be defined in the header file as inline functions to permit implementation-specific
optimization. Replacing such function invocations is significantly simpler than replacing accesses to
structures, for example.

wraparound is not acceptable, algorithms may be supported by using counters wide enough to
guarantee wraparound will not occur for the lifetime of any given connection in the use case.

3.6.18.4.5 Optional Signals
Table 3-112 defines the set of optional signals that MAY be supported. If a YAML definition uses a signal
that is not supported by the specific implementation, the compiler MUST fail.
3.6.18.4.5.1 CSIG Signals
Ultra Ethernet defines congestion signaling (CSIG) in Section 4.2. CSIG is an in-band telemetry method to
collect information on the fabric’s congestion state as the packets traverse the network. Each switch
along the path applies a simple aggregation function to a locally measured congestion value and the
value carried in the CSIG tag of the received packet. The result of the aggregation function at each
switch is that the packet egresses with a single, path‑summary result. In many useful cases, the relevant
metric is the minimum or maximum of a signal across the path—i.e., the value where the signal is most
constraining (e.g., the minimum available bandwidth or the maximum queueing delay).
Within PCM, CSIG signals are accumulated to provide a standardized source of congestion signals that
algorithms can consume for their decisions. The CSIG specification defines multiple signal types (e.g.,
available bandwidth and delay), but each packet carries exactly one CSIG signal at a time, encoded as a
quantized value. CSIG information can be consumed at the receiver (termination) or reflected back to
the sender, enabling sender- or receiver-based PCM algorithms to react by adjusting windows, rates, or
path selection.
If a switch performs packet trimming, then a CSIG-tagged packet’s csig.d bit (do-not-modify flag) is set.
This leaves the tag unchanged thereafter and preserves the congestion signal as before the trimming.
This information is to be made available to the PCM algorithms when CSIG support is enabled in PCM.
The PCM interface exposes these readings as optional CSIG signals delivered to the algorithms.
CSIG always does tag termination at the receiver if it receives a CSIG packet. If NSCC is enabled, the
CSIG-Reflect() function is mandatory, which populates the CSIG Reflection Header within ACK/NACK
packets. However, an algorithm can have only one source of the data at any given time–The CSIG-Term()
function is the natural input for receiver-based CC, whereas CSIG-Reflect() would provide the input to
the sender-based CC.
A per-group set of signals could be defined, but invocations can be easily controlled by checking if the
CSIG signal type received is terminal or reflected.
PCM exposes a boolean uet_rx_csig_type where 0=TERM and 1=REFLECT. Algorithms SHOULD validate
the origin on each sample and then operate on the unified fields {uet_rx_csig_t, uet_rx_csig_s,
uet_rx_csig_m, uet_rx_csig_d}.

PAGE 531

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

when extracted from the 8-byte wide CSIG tag. The CSIG signal returned to PCM is of a fixed width that
can support both 5-bit and 20-bit values.
CSIG values exposed in PCM for algorithms SHALL carry the quantized bucket index s as an opaque
unsigned integer together with {t, m, d}. PCM implementations SHALL supply de‑quantization
parameters via a YAML file, and SHOULD provide a utility function csig_dequantize(t, s) that returns the

3.6.18.4.6 Vendor-specific Signals
Any implementation MAY support vendor-specific signals. Their names MUST be prefixed with <vend>, a
vendor-specific alias encoded in the variable name, e.g., uet_tx_ack_vend_<signal_name> or
uet_rx_req_vend_<signal_name>. The <signal_name> MAY encode any additional information such as
vendor name.
3.6.18.5 Triggers
Algorithms request invocation when an accumulator matches their criteria, as determined by triggers.
Every trigger is associated with a single accumulator instance and is identified by a trigger identifier. The
set of triggers available to an algorithm, and their association with accumulation functions and signals, is
defined by the algorithm’s YAML configuration profile. Triggers cannot be created or deleted at runtime,
but an algorithm can modify them to change their configuration and match criteria.
Triggers are defined in the YAML specification and given a macro name to reference them from the
algorithm code.
3.6.18.5.1 Trigger Definition
Triggers are state machines that determine when to take an action based on a unified count-or-time
condition.
Each trigger is defined by the following configuration fields:

PAGE 532

532

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
trigger_id: Unique identifier for the trigger within the CCC
•
accumulator_value: Value of the accumulator being evaluated
•
op: Comparison operator used to evaluate a predicate against an accumulator value. Allowed
operators are: ==,!=, >, >=, <, <=, *
Informative Text:
The ‘*’ operator is a “wildcard match,” used when the algorithm should always be triggered; it is the
logical equivalent of the compound operator: (==||!=)
•
mode: Trigger evaluation mode. Only one mode is supported: COUNT_OR_TIME. In
COUNT_OR_TIME mode, the trigger may fire due to accumulated TRUE evaluations or due to
elapsed time since the trigger last fired.
•
mode_ref_val: Tuple specifying count (mode_ref_count_val) and time (mode_ref_time_val)
thresholds for determining whether a trigger has fired. Predicates tests against this tuple of
reference values are defined as:
  time_predicate = accumulator_value (op) mode_ref_time_val
  count_preficate = accumulator_value (op) mode_ref_count_val
A true evaluation is any evaluation for which at least one predicate evaluates to true.
Semantics of mode_ref_val tuple are defined as follows:
mode_ref_count_val
mode_ref_time_val
Semantic Behavior
0
0
No evaluation: No evaluation is performed; trigger fires
immediately if armed
0
≠0
Time-only mode: Trigger fires when elapsed time since the
trigger last fired is greater than or equal to mode_ref_time_val
≠0
0
Count-only mode: Trigger fires after mode_ref_count_val true
evaluations of the predicate
≠0
≠0
Combined mode: Trigger fires after mode_ref_count_val true
evaluations of the predicate or when elapsed time since the
trigger last fired is greater than or equal to mode_ref_time_val,
whichever occurs first
•
arm_mode: Controls trigger evaluation and behavior after firing. Allowed values:
o DISARMED: Trigger does not evaluate predicate and cannot fire
o ONCE: Trigger evaluates predicate; when it fires it automatically transitions to
DISARMED and MUST be explicitly re-armed to fire again
o CONTINUOUS: Trigger remains armed after each fire; after firing, the count of true
evaluations and elapsed time since last fire are reset and evaluation continues
•
action: Action taken when trigger fires. Allowed values:
o INVOKE: Invoke the PCM algorithm
o RECORD: Record the trigger fired in the trigger bitmask; do not invoke algorithm
•
invoke_deadline: Upper bound on how long an invoke action may be deferred after trigger fires.
Applies only if action is INVOKE

3.6.18.5.3 Trigger Evaluation
Triggers are logically evaluated as follows:
•
When a packet is received, all armed triggers associated with accumulators tracking uet_rx
signals are evaluated
•
When a packet is transmitted, all armed triggers associated with accumulators tracking uet_tx
signals are evaluated
•
When a time event occurs, all armed triggers associated with accumulators tracking uet_time
signals are evaluated
The algorithm MUST be invoked exactly once to deliver all fired (non-deferred) triggers; piecemeal
delivery is not allowed. Algorithms determine the set of fired triggers by examining the trigger bitmask
delivered with every invocation.
Multiple deferred invocation triggers are reconciled as follows:
•
A per-CCC deadline variable maintains the minimum deadline to the next invocation.
•
For every evaluated trigger, if the trigger has a non-zero invocation deadline, the per-CCC
deadline is updated as follows:
CCC.invoke_deadline = min(CCC.invoke_deadline,now() +
trigger.invoke_deadline)
3.6.18.5.4 Trigger Updates
On successful application of a trigger update, the PCM subsystem MUST reset all trigger working states.
After resetting, the trigger MUST be immediately eligible for evaluation and firing under the new
configuration. All trigger reference value fidelities match those of the associated signal.

The function uet_trigger_mask() returns an unsigned integer that can be used to identify the trigger that
invoked the algorithm. It can be compared to macros defined for each defined signal in the YAML
configuration corresponding to the signal.
Informative Text (example for uet_trigger_mask()):
Imagine an algorithm is set up with two triggers with the following YAML file:
- signal:
  name: “uet_time_current”
  macro: “t_time”
  accumulator: “uet_last”
     trigger:
       op:wc
       op_val: 0
      ...

- signal:
  name: “uet_rx_ack”
  macro: “c_acks”
  accumulator: “uet_sum”
     trigger:
      op: gte
      op_val: <integer>
     ...

void algorithm() {
  uet_trigmask_t fired_triggers;
  uet_trigger_mask(&fired_triggers);
  if(fired_triggers & t_time) {
    // algorithm was triggered by timer
  }
  if(fired_triggers & c_acks) {
    // algorithm was triggered by ack count received
  }
}

Informative Text:
Implementations SHOULD ensure that the function uet_trigger_mask() is implemented in a fast and
lightweight manner appropriate for the platform. The specific mechanism used to achieve this
efficiency is implementation-defined.

3.6.18.5.7 Load Balancing Support
3.6.18.5.7.1 Per-EV Triggers
Per-EV triggers enable LB algorithms to react to events associated with specific EVs in the CCC EV table.
By evaluating conditions and updating state locally in hardware, these triggers eliminate the overhead of
frequent software callbacks.
Per-EV triggers are defined using the YAML signal construct configuration schema; the scope field MUST
be set to EV for every per-EV signal. Multiple EV triggers are supported within a single algorithm
configuration. Triggers defined in this manner are automatically attached to every EV index in the CCC
EV table. It is not possible to bind triggers to individual EV indices; the association is uniform across all
slots in the EV table for the lifetime of the CCC.
Per-EV signals are evaluated whenever a packet associated with a given EV is transmitted or received.
On invocation, an algorithm can determine whether any per-EV trigger has fired by checking the macro
name against the output of uet_trigger_mask().
Algorithms can further iterate through the set of fired per-EV triggers using the functions below:
Table 3-116 - Per-EV Access and Manipulation APIs

3.6.18.6.3 PCM Telegrams
PCM algorithms can exchange out-of-band messages with software running on the local node as well as
the peer CCC using optional telegrams. The structure and use of telegrams is algorithm-specific; they
may be used in any situation in which coordination or information exchange between the algorithm and
the host or remote peer is required.
Telegrams are fixed-size structures of up to 30 bytes in length, composed of one or more fields. An
algorithm can define multiple types of telegrams. There is no definition-level distinction between
telegrams exchanged locally or with peers, although support is provided for an algorithm to distinguish
between the source of received telegrams. Telegrams are defined using the YAML schema provided in
Section 3.6.18.8.5. Telegrams of different types are uniquely identified both locally and remotely by the
value of the structure type_id field.

Informative Text:
The 30-byte length constraint for telegrams results from specific design decisions: telegrams are
transmitted as control packets, the total payload is limited to 32 bytes, ensuring the complete

PAGE 538

538

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
packet—including all protocol headers—remains small. Of this total, 2 bytes are reserved for the
telegram type header and other control fields, leaving 30 bytes available for actual payload data.

The PCM runtime delivers received telegrams to algorithms through the algorithm’s registered callback
function. A single telegram is delivered per invocation. Algorithms determine the telegram type using
the uet_get_tgm_type() function and the invocation context using the uet_invoke_ctx() function.
Telegram field values are accessed using the telegram field access functions. Fields MUST be delivered
to the algorithm in the PCM implementation’s native endian order.

3.6.18.6.3.1 Processing Telegrams
The PCM runtime is responsible for forwarding sent telegrams to the local host or remote peer as
follows:
Local telegrams are forwarded to the host in an implementation-specific manner. The mechanism used
to receive logs and alert host software is configuration-specific. Example mechanisms include:
•
Kernel logs (e.g., dmesg).
•
Device-specific control APIs (e.g., netlink/sysfs/debugfs).
•
Vendor-specific user-space daemons.
Peer telegrams are forwarded to the remote PDC via Telegram CPs (see Section 3.5.16.8). Telegram
structures are encoded as payload in these control packets with the following format:
•
Fixed header (2 bytes):
o type_id (8 bits): Identifies the telegram type and determines the interpretation of the
payload. This field MUST be populated with the telegram type identifier as defined by the
corresponding telegram YAML specification.
o reserved (8 bits): Reserved for future use. This field MUST be set to 0x0 by the sender and
MUST be ignored by the receiver.
•
Fields (up to 30 bytes):

PAGE 540

540

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
o Contains the telegram-specific field values associated with the indicated type_id.
o The encoding, ordering, and semantics of these fields are defined by the telegram type.
o If the telegram-specific payload is shorter than 30 bytes, the remaining bytes MUST be set
to 0x0 by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver.
Regardless of whether the telegram is forwarded locally or to a peer, field values MUST be transmitted
in big-endian format and packed in accordance with the YAML specification for the structure

3.6.18.7 Error Handling and Recovery
This section defines mandatory behavior for signaling, containing, and recovering from fatal errors
originating from the data path or PCM subsystem.
The error handling and recovery model is defined to enforce the following invariants:
1. A CCC MUST NOT operate in an uncontrolled, undefined, or partially corrupt state.
2. Any condition that compromises correctness, safety, or determinism of CCC operation MUST
result in immediate and permanent disablement of the CCC by transitioning it to the ERROR
state.
3.6.18.7.1 Fatal error conditions and state transition
A CCC in the ACTIVE state MUST atomically transition to the ERROR state if any of the following fatal
conditions occur:
•
The hardware detects an internal fault while generating PCM signal updates, evaluating triggers,
invoking an algorithm, or applying algorithm-initiated operations
•
A PCM algorithm performs an invalid operation as defined by this specification, including (but
not limited to) illegal PCM API usage or out-of-range index access
•
A PCM algorithm explicitly requests fatal termination of the CCC by invoking uet_ccc_fatal()
Upon detection of a fatal condition, the implementation MUST make the ACTIVE→ERROR transition
atomically visible to all components that can observe the CCC or PDC state.
When a CCC transitions to the ERROR state:
•
All PDCs serviced by the CCC MUST simultaneously transition to an ERROR condition consistent
with the CCC ERROR state.
•
There MUST be no transition out of ERROR except via explicit reinitialization or reset performed
outside the PCM subsystem.
3.6.18.7.1.1 Algorithm API
Algorithms choose to cope with unexpected events or conditions by performing algorithm-mediated
control actions (e.g., setting the congestion window to a single packet). When an algorithm encounters
an (algorithm-defined) unrecoverable error, it can transition a CCC into ERROR state by using the
function defined in Table 3-126.



PAGE 542

542

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Table 3-126 - ERROR State Transition Function
Function Name (Argument(s))
Description
void uet_ccc_fatal(int reason)

Transition the CCC into ERROR state. The value of reason
is algorithm-defined and is used to signal the cause of the
error for debug and telemetry purposes; it is not
interpreted or used by the PCM subsystem.

3.6.18.7.2 ERROR state semantics
3.6.18.7.2.1 Data path
Once a CCC has entered the ERROR state, the implementation MUST ensure the following:
•
The CCC is logically disabled.
•
No new packets associated with the CCC are admitted to the data path.
•
All in-flight, acknowledged, and queued packets associated with the CCC are logically dropped.
•
No further PCM events or telegrams are generated for the CCC.
•
No API operations invoked by the algorithm are applied.
3.6.18.7.2.2 PCM subsystem behavior
After the CCC enters the ERROR state:
•
Any PCM algorithm invocation already in progress MAY be aborted or MAY complete execution;
however, regardless of completion or abortion, it MUST NOT produce any externally visible side
effects of any kind.
•
No mutation of the CCC or PDC state is permitted after the CCC enters the ERROR state,
including mutations attempted by an in-flight algorithm invocation.
•
Any PCM API invocation targeting the CCC (including those issued by an in-flight algorithm
invocation) MUST fail and MUST return the error code -ENOTRECOVERABLE.
•
Further PCM algorithm invocations for the CCC MUST NOT occur.
3.6.18.7.3 Error reporting and observability
When a CCC transitions to the ERROR state, the implementation MUST record a single CCC-scoped fatal
error indication with the following information:
•
Error source. One of:
o IMPLEMENTATION: Fatal error detected by the implementation.
o PCM_ALGORITHM: CCC transitioned to ERROR due to a PCM algorithm action.
•
Error value:
o If IMPLEMENTATION: Value is implementation-defined.
o If PCM_ALGORITHM: Value MUST equal the reason supplied to uet_ccc_fatal().
Once a fatal error indication is recorded for a CCC, subsequent fatal causes for that CCC MUST NOT
overwrite, append, or accumulate additional fatal indications. The fatal error indication MUST remain
available for software inspection until CCC reset or reinitialization.

PAGE 543

543

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The implementation SHOULD emit a diagnostic message identifying the CCC instance and the recorded
fatal error indication.
The implementation MUST provide a software-visible mechanism to determine, for each CCC, whether it
is in ACTIVE or ERROR state and, if in the ERROR state, to retrieve the recorded fatal error indication.
This mechanism MUST satisfy all the following:
•
The ERROR state MUST be observable by software no later than the point at which the
ACTIVE→ERROR transition becomes atomically visible within the implementation.
•
Retrieval of CCC state and fatal error indication MUST be non-destructive (i.e., it MUST NOT
clear the indication).
3.6.18.7.4 Reset and reinitialization
Recovery from the ERROR state is outside the scope of PCM. An implementation MAY provide a
platform-specific mechanism (e.g., driver, firmware, or device reset) to reinitialize a CCC. If a CCC is
reinitialized, the implementation MUST ensure the reinitialized CCC appears as a fresh instance with no
retained PCM state.
3.6.18.8 Algorithm Lifecycle Management
Logically, PCM algorithms are loaded, instantiated, configured, assigned to a subset of data traffic, and
activated to provide congestion control capabilities. The remainder of this section outlines this flow.
3.6.18.8.1 Loading Algorithms
PCM algorithms are dynamically loaded using implementation-specific tools. Algorithm implementors
specify required PCM features for a particular algorithm by providing a load-time specification along
with the algorithm that is consumed by the load tool to determine if the implementation can support
the algorithm and to configure the PCM subsystem for the algorithm. Load-time specifications provide
the following information on an algorithm basis:
1. The set of configuration parameters and associated default values.
2. All signals and their mapping to indices, and initial values for new CCCs.
3. All outputs and their mapping to indices.
4. All local storage variables and their initial values.
5. The invocation callback function.
6. The set of initial triggers for new CCCs.
7. The default cwnd and send_rate values for new CCCs.
Load-time specifications are expressed in a hierarchical YAML format as described in Section 3.6.18.8.5.
3.6.18.8.2 Algorithm Instances
Algorithm instances are specific, independent realizations of a loaded PCM algorithm, complete with
configuration and state, and are used to manage congestion control for an administrator-defined subset
of bulk data generated by the FEP.

PAGE 544

544

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
3.6.18.8.3 Configuring Algorithm Instances
Algorithm instances are configured using implementation-specific tools. The set of configurable
parameters are algorithm-specific and provided to the PCM subsystem as YAML definitions as described
in Section 3.6.18.8.5.
3.6.18.8.4 Assigning Algorithm Instances to Network Traffic
PCM supports assigning algorithm instances to network traffic on a UET-instance basis. In this model it is
assumed the FEP is configured to operate over one or more UET instances. Every instance has two or
three traffic classes as outlined in the Section 3.6.4.7. All the traffic in a PCM-managed UET instance
MUST be controlled exclusively by a single CC and a single LB algorithm instance.
3.6.18.8.5 Load-time Algorithm Configuration YAML Format
PCM algorithms, their signals, accumulations, local state, and control outputs are configured via a
specified YAML format. The YAML file contains the following top-level keys:
•
Algorithm: Details of the algorithm specification
•
Signal: Configuration of the used signals, accumulations, and triggers
•
Control: Output control definitions
•
Variable: Definition of local-state variable and its initialization
•
Parameter: Constant algorithm configuration parameters
The YAML template below defines the format of the file and its valid fields. Optional fields are in square
brackets. The type of <c-identifier> is a string that adheres to the C programming language definition of
an identifier. The type <enum> refers to names in the referenced table. The types uint, int, float refer to
the corresponding C types expressed in usual C string syntax (float values in scientific notation, e.g.,
“1.3e5”). A <scalar> is any of those.

# ── CC Algorithm metadata (mapping node) ──
cc_algorithm:
  name: <c-identifier>     # Algorithm name (entry point of the function)
  description: <string>    # Algorithm description (free text)
  max_ack_coalescing: <uint>   # max number of ACKs to be coalesced
  [uint_min_bitwidth:  <uint>] # minimum required bitwidth for unsigned integers
  [int_min_bitwidth:   <uint>] # minimum required bitwidth for signed integers
  [float_min_bitwidth: <uint>] # minimum required bitwidth for float numbers

# ── Input signals (sequence node) ──

      mode_refval: <uint> <uint>     # Fire mode reference value tuple
      arm_mode: DISARMED|ONCE|CONTINUOUS   # Trigger armed mode
      action: INVOKE|RECORD          # Action performed on fire
      invoke_deadline: <uint>        # Invocation deadline

Parameters can be used to differentiate multiple instances of the same algorithm. For example, there
could be two instances of NSCC—one for AI and one for storage traffic—with different parameters. The
