4.2 Congestion Signaling (CSIG)
Contemporary machine learning (ML) training and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads
compute across a switched network fabric in closely coupled, synchronous fashion. As a result, they
demand short flow completion times, even at the tail of the distribution. For these workloads, overall
application progress can stall when even a single flow’s completion is delayed.
When a flow completes, it abruptly releases the capacity it had previously consumed at links along its
path. Other flows that share those links must be able to increase their rates rapidly to put that newly
idle capacity to use promptly. Moreover, achieving low tail flow completion times requires effective
multi-path spreading of flows across the fabric’s many paths.
In oversubscribed workloads, stretching of tail completion times for “losing” flows can become a
bottleneck for overall application performance. These performance constraints demand unprecedented
responsiveness from congestion control protocols, and in turn call for new inputs to congestion control
that offer fine-grained and timely information about the congestion state of the network fabric.
End-host congestion control has long employed simple end-to-end signals, such as round-trip time (RTT)
and packet loss events, to summarize the extent of congestion on a full path. Using explicit congestion
notification (ECN) marks, switches directly provide a simple, Boolean indication to end hosts of whether,
short of a drop, a packet encounters more than some threshold queue length at one or more hops along
its path. These established signals are coarse grained: as end-to-end, path-summary metrics, RTT, and
packet-loss event counts reflect the total congestion along a full path and do not reveal conditions at
any individual switch.
An ECN mark offers only a single-bit quantification of congestion, and as a path summary, reports only
the presence of congestion along any extent of the full path, or its absence along all of it. These signals
do not meet the finer-grained congestion control needs of contemporary ML and HPC workloads. For
example, to increase a flow’s sending rate rapidly to match the abruptly released capacity on a link
precisely, a sender would benefit from discovering the available bandwidth at the single most
constrained link along a path: the link with the minimum available bandwidth.
While per-link available bandwidth is readily measurable by individual switches, it is not directly
observable by end hosts. Absent finer-grained signals, status-quo congestion control approaches are
limited to searching conservatively for a path’s available bandwidth by increasing their sending rate and
detecting when they congest the path—a slow process.
As another example, end-to-end delay measurements mix together queueing delays from all congested
hops along a path, such that in delay-based congestion control, the number of congested hops
determines a sender’s perceived extent of congestion, which can yield bandwidth unfairness between
flows. Only the queueing delay at a flow’s single most congested hop (its true bottleneck) should
determine a sender’s sending rate. This quantity, again, is not directly observable by end hosts using
today’s coarse-grained, path-summary signals.

PAGE 601

601

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
These ML training and HPC workloads present further challenges in network fabric monitoring and
performance analysis. Traditional forms of network telemetry, such as time series of link utilizations or
packet drop rates across all links in the fabric, often fall short in explanatory power because they are
decoupled from application context. They are labor-intensive to correlate with specific application flows
at specific time points, and often are recorded at too coarse a resolution in time to reveal the pathology
experienced by a flow (e.g., during an extremely brief traffic burst). Effective performance diagnosis and
monitoring at scale require fine-grained network telemetry, both in time and at a per-switch granularity,
that closely correlates in-network measurements with a workload’s context—ideally, with the
 xp ri nc  of  n  pplic  ion’s individu l p ck  .
This specification describes congestion signaling (CSIG), a simple and efficient in-band network
telemetry method that collects fine-grained signals that describe the network fabric’s congestion state.
The central insight underlying CSIG’s design is that for many telemetry signals useful in congestion
control and performance analysis, the result of a simple aggregation function computed over the
congestion state at switches along a packet’s path is of interest. For example, for several signal types,
the congestion state only at a single switch along a path is of interest, where the switch of interest is the
one where a signal’s value is an extremum (maximum or minimum) among the signal’s values at all
switches along the path. By leveraging this insight, CSIG offers the following desirable properties:
•
Targeted, per-switch signal granularity: CSIG can return a signal from the single bottleneck
switch along a path and thus exposes congestion state not generally available from end-to-end,
whole-path signals.
•
Space-efficient telemetry collection: While CSIG measures signal data at each switch along a
path, a measurement adds only a short, 4-byte (or for increased measurement precision, 8-byte)
tag to a packet’s header, regardless of path length in hops. This space efficiency is possible
because CSIG tags carry only a single aggregated value (e.g., maximum or minimum value
observed thus far along a path, depending on the signal type being measured).
•
Compute-efficient telemetry collection: The operations a switch must perform to process a
CSIG tag are simple and latency-efficient.
•
In-band collection that captures application/transport context: Because CSIG tags are low in
space overhead and in processing overhead at switches, an application or transport may attach
them to every packet it transmits. The congestion signals collected by these packets will reflect
how switches process that application’s and transport’s actual packets (and not how distinct
packets sent by a measurement system, which arrive at different points in time than “native”
application traffic, are processed).
•
Transport- and encapsulation-agnostic: CSIG tags are carried in layer 2 headers and thus switch
processing of CSIG tags does not involve processing of transport headers, nor does it incur any
complication when used with encrypted transports.
•
Extensibility: CSIG provides for future specification of additional signal types within the
protocol’s framework.

4.2.2
Overview
This specification defines CSIG, a simple in-band network telemetry method in which packets collect
fine-grained measurements at switches as they traverse a network path. CSIG incurs low telemetry
collection overhead by limiting in-packet state to a single, fixed-size CSIG tag that stores a signal value
measured at a single switch (independent of the number of hops the packet traverses).
Each switch along a path inspects and (where appropriate) updates this single tag in accordance with a
signal type encoded in the tag and policies configured by the network administrator (e.g., choices of
parameters that govern quantization and time granularity of measured values). Network endpoints can
consume arriving CSIG signals for use by in-band functions such as congestion control and load
balancing. Monitoring entities at network endpoints can also process arriving CSIG signals for use in such
out-of-band functions as performance analysis, debugging, and SLA assurance. When included in packets
that comprise applications’ usual traffic flows, CSIG tags gather in-context telemetry that indicates the
state of the network path as experienced by an application’s packet. In addition, monitoring frameworks
can include CSIG tags in dedicated probe packets to measure the network’s state.
The CSIG tag is a link-level Ethernet tag that carries telemetry information end to end. Its definition is
independent of any specific layer 3 network encapsulation or layer 4 transport. Although a CSIG tag does
not itself specify the higher-layer transport and/or application for which it carries a signal, that signal
must nevertheless be interpreted in context. This specification discusses means to associate the signal in
a CSIG tag with the appropriate higher-level transport context (in Ultra Ethernet Transport [UET], the
appropriate congestion control context [CCC]), and means for reflection of the signal in a tag on a UET
packet arriving at a destination endpoint back to the source endpoint in the header of a UET layer 4 ACK
or NACK.
Informative Text:
Note that because CSIG is an optional UE feature, for CSIG tags to be carried end to end in a UE fabric
all switches in the UE fabric must support CSIG, and the fabric must be configured to enable the use of
CSIG. Please refer to further discussion of these deployment considerations in Section 4.2.10.

PAGE 603

603

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Each switch along the path traversed by a CSIG-tagged packet identifies the signal type encoded in the
tag and updates the associated value within the tag using a simple aggregation function. The switch can
also write locator metadata within the tag to indicate properties of the network hop that updated the
signal.
CSIG supports three signal types in its base profile:
•
The max(Delay) signal finds the delay bottleneck along a path. When each switch along a CSIG-
tagged packet’s path receives the packet, it conditionally updates the queueing delay signal
value stored in the CSIG tag using the maximum function, where the switch overwrites the delay
signal value in the CSIG tag with its own local delay value if it exceeds that in the CSIG tag.
•
The min(ABW) signal finds the available bandwidth bottleneck along a path. When each switch
along a CSIG-tagged packet’s path receives the packet, it conditionally updates the available
bandwidth signal value stored in the CSIG tag using the minimum function, where the switch
overwrites the available bandwidth value in the CSIG tag with its own local available bandwidth
value from the egress port if it is less than that in the CSIG tag.
•
The min(ABW/C) signal does the same, but for each switch’s relative available bandwidth,
normalized by output port capacity.
(Full definitions of these CSIG signal types may be found in Section 4.2.4.1.2.)
Figure 4-2 illustrates through a simple example how CSIG telemetry functions on endpoints and in the
network fabric. It depicts a high-level schematic of a CSIG-tagged packet, showing both the CSIG tag
carried on a packet’s forward path and the reflection of the signal from the destination endpoint back to
the source endpoint in an layer 4 transport header. (Examples of the placement of the CSIG tag in other
layer 2 frame types may be found in Figure 4-8 and Figure 4-9.) It further shows the local signal value at
each hop for three signal types—max(Delay), min(ABW), and min(ABW/C)—and the distinct bottleneck
locations for each of these signal types along the path. Upon receiving a CSIG-tagged packet, each switch
along the path conditionally updates the signal value in the CSIG tag according to the signal type
specified in the CSIG tag, the min() or max() function specified in the signal type’s definition (and name),
and the local value for that signal type at that switch.
This specification defines the CSIG telemetry method in an application-agnostic fashion. It further
discusses CSIG’s relevance to multiple use cases relevant in the UE setting.

PAGE 604

604

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

Figure 4-2 - Example of CSIG Endpoint and Fabric Processing
4.2.3
Use Cases
The collection of network telemetry with CSIG benefits multiple UE-relevant use cases.
4.2.3.1
End-to-End Congestion Control
When a sender’s transport protocol includes CSIG tags on its packets, the returning information about
the congestion state at switches along each packet’s path can be used to improve congestion control’s
performance. This information can include the least available bandwidth at any link along a packet’s
path (useful for promptly and precisely claiming newly released link capacity in NSCC and RCCC; see
sections 4.2.9.1.3 and 4.2.9.2.3) and the greatest queueing delay at any queue along a packet’s path
(useful for improving the bandwidth fairness of delay-based congestion control schemes, such as NSCC,
and for responding to oversubscription in RCCC; see Section 4.2.9.3.4).
4.2.3.2
Multi-Path Load Balancing
CSIG signals describing the least available bandwidth at any link along a packet’s path are also useful for
choosing higher-spare-capacity paths in multi-path load balancing, as applied in NSCC and RCCC (see
sections 4.2.9.1.3 and 4.2.9.2.3).
4.2.3.3
Telemetry
The signal collected in a CSIG tag provides useful telemetry information describing the congestion state
of a path through the fabric.
These signals can help developers understand the extent to which their applications’ packets encounter
congestion (e.g., service delay, normalized queue depth) or available link capacity. This insight can be
used to inform application design changes or debugging efforts.
CSIG tags can assist in localizing congestion points within the network fabric and evaluating how
effectively the fabric’s provisioning meets workload demands.

PAGE 605

605

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
For telemetry purposes, signals from CSIG tags can be collected by software running on FEPs, either by
forwarding the CSIG signal directly to the receiving application or by routing it to a dedicated telemetry
collection application.
Methods for collection of telemetry from received CSIG signals are outside the scope of this
specification.
4.2.4
CSIG Tag Formats
This specification defines two CSIG tag formats: a 4-byte compact CSIG tag and an 8-byte wide CSIG tag.
The compact CSIG tag (Figure 4-3), is a 4-byte header field identical in frame offset and field width to an
IEEE Std 802.1Q-2022 clause 9-compliant VLAN tag (hereafter referred to as “VLAN tag” for brevity) [2] .
This choice of compact CSIG tag format simplifies adding CSIG functionality to the many switches that
can leverage VLAN tag match-action support to recognize and update CSIG tags.
All UE-compliant switches and hosts that support CSIG MUST support the compact CSIG tag format.
In comparison, the wide CSIG tag format (Figure 4-4), 8 bytes in length, targets deployments in which
switches have native CSIG support. The wide tag contains the same fields with the same functions as the
compact tag, but by virtue of the greater number of bits available for data fields in the wide tag, the
wide tag supports more signal types (csig.t: 16, vs. 8 for compact tags), finer-grained signal value
measurements (csig.s: 1 million quantized values vs. 32 buckets for compact tags), and more detailed
locator metadata (csig.lm: 15 bits vs. 6 bits for compact tags). The csig.t constants defined for signal
types are identical for the compact and wide tag formats, but the wide tag format supports additional
(as yet unused) signal type definitions that have no corresponding definitions in the compact tag format.
The compact and wide tag formats apply different transformations in their csig.s signal value
representations. The definitions of the csig.d (Do Not Modify) bit and csig.lm (Locator Metadata) fields
in the wide CSIG tag format are the same as those for the compact CSIG tag format, apart from the
greater width of the LM field in the wide CSIG tag format.
UE-compliant switches and hosts that support CSIG MAY additionally support the wide CSIG tag format.

4.2.4.1.1 CSIG Tag Protocol Identifier
The CSIG tag protocol identifier (csig.tpid) is a fixed, constant, two-octet EtherType that identifies the
CSIG tag. The compact and wide CSIG tags are identified by distinct EtherTypes to distinguish between
the compact and wide CSIG tag formats, to simplify hardware, and to make best use of the tag formats’
limited bits.
This specification refers to the EtherType value identifying compact CSIG tags as csig.csig_tpid_compact,
and the EtherType value identifying wide CSIG tags as csig.csig_tpid_wide.
Until permanent assignments of CSIG EtherTypes are obtained, CSIG implementations MUST support
configurable EtherType values for the compact and wide tags. EtherType values used for the compact
tag and wide tag (if supported) MUST be distinct and MUST NOT conflict with any other EtherTypes in
use in the CSIG deployment domain.

CSIG implementations SHOULD support configurable EtherType values for the compact tag and wide tag
(if supported) even after a permanent assignment has been obtained, subject to the same constraints as
above on configured values.

When updating the signal value in a CSIG tag, the switch pipeline compares its local value for that signal
type to the signal value in the CSIG tag using this aggregation function. Table 4-4 and Table 4-5 shows
the supported signal types and associated aggregation functions.

4.2.4.1.3 Signal Value (csig.s)
The signal value field carries a switch-measured value for the signal type encoded in the CSIG tag. It is
quantized into buckets with explicit, configured [min, max] ranges in the compact tag format, and
encoded in a base-relative, uniform bucket-size representation in the wide tag format.

PAGE 608

608

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The switch computes the signal’s local value and quantizes it. The entity within the switch that computes
a signal’s local value may vary with the signal type; the definitions of individual signals in this
specification discuss the entity(ies) that compute a signal’s local value. The pre-quantization locally
computed value and quantized value MUST both be integers; this constraint simplifies implementation
by avoiding the complexity of floating-point arithmetic, both in the computation of local signal values
and in their quantization. Individual signal type definitions can straightforwardly enforce this integer-
value constraint by specifying units accordingly. The switch pipeline compares the quantized local signal
value with the incoming CSIG tag’s quantized signal value according to the aggregation function
associated with the CSIG tag’s signal type.
4.2.4.1.4 CSIG Tag Quantization Algorithm
Figure 4-5 illustrates how a switch’s hardware might maintain signals’ local values and quantize them. In
accordance with the signal type in an arriving packet’s CSIG tag, the switch pipeline compares the
quantized signal value in the packet’s CSIG tag with the quantized local value for the signal of the same
type and, as appropriate, updates the signal value in the packet. The use of a background thread to
compute a signal’s local value in Figure 4-5 is a non-normative example; other implementations, such as
ones based on per-packet updates, are possible. The details of local signal computation, within the
confines of the per-signal definitions in this specification, are implementation-specific. An
implementation will compute a local signal value, quantize it, and perform CSIG-Compare-and-Update()
of the quantized value per the compact or wide tag.

4.2.4.1.5 Compact CSIG Tag Quantization Algorithm
The quantization applied to values stored in compact CSIG tags is a simple mapping of the raw,
unquantized value into one of several buckets. Each bucket is parameterized by minimum and maximum

signal values set by the switch control plane during configuration. The buckets MUST not overlap in their
ranges and their ranges MUST be contiguous. Bucket ranges are inclusive.
Because different signal types often carry values of differing magnitudes, quantization bucket ranges for
compact CSIG tags are configured separately for each signal type. The switch control plane sets buckets’
minimum and maximum values during configuration.
The compact CSIG tag includes 5 bits of signal value. There are 25 = 32 quantized values, each
corresponding to one bucket. Before quantizing a raw signal’s value, the switch hardware MUST ensure
that the raw signal’s value is of a precision (length in bits) that matches the precision of that signal’s
quantization bucket ranges. If the precision of the raw signal’s value exceeds that of the signal’s
quantization bucket ranges by e bits, the hardware right bit-shifts the raw signal’s value by e bits. No bit-
shift is performed if the precision of the raw signal value is less than or equal to that of the signal’s
quantization bucket ranges. The hardware then performs a simple range check on the resulting signal
value to map the raw value to the bucket in which it falls. The index of that bucket is the quantized
value.
If a raw signal value is less than the minimum bound of bucket index 0 (the least raw signal value
represented in the quantization’s configuration), it is out-of-range low, and the switch hardware MUST
quantize that raw signal value as falling within bucket index 0. If a raw signal value is greater than the
maximum bound of bucket index 31 (the greatest raw signal value represented in the quantization’s
configuration), it is out-of-range high, and the switch hardware MUST quantize that raw signal value as
falling within bucket 31. Switch implementations SHOULD keep event counters for out-of-range low and
out-of-range high occurrences during quantization. The reporting and use of these counters is
implementation-specific and outside the scope of this specification.

4.2.4.1.6 Wide CSIG Tag Quantization Algorithm
The wide CSIG tag includes 20 bits of signal value. There are 220 = 1048576 quantized values, each
corresponding to one bucket. For a given signal type, the quantization is parameterized by a bucket
range exponent e >= 1 and base value b >= 0, where b MUST be either zero or a power of two. 2e
contiguous unquantized signal values map to each bucket. To quantize an unquantized signal value v, a
device computes (v – b) and maps the result to the index of the bucket in which it falls—a simple shift

PAGE 610

610

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
right by e bits, as each bucket spans 2e unquantized values. The resulting bucket index is the quantized
value.
The switch control plane sets e and b per signal type during configuration.
Each bucket index i represents the range of unquantized values:
[𝑏+ 𝑖2𝑒, 𝑏+ (𝑖+ 1)2𝑒−1]
And thus, for a given b and e, the full range of unquantized values representable in quantized form is:
[𝑏, 𝑏+ 2𝑒+20 −1]
To quantize an unquantized signal value v, yielding bucket index i, the corresponding quantized value, a
device computes:
i = (𝑣−𝑏) ≫e
The result of the quantization function is undefined for input unquantized signal values v that fall
outside the full range.
This quantization function is efficient to implement in hardware, given the simplicity of the subtraction
and shift-right operations.
As with the handling of out-of-range values in the quantization for the compact tag, if a raw signal value
is less than b in the wide-tag quantization, the switch hardware MUST quantize it as falling in bucket 0,
and if a raw signal value is greater than (𝑏+ 2𝑒+20 −1), the switch hardware MUST quantize it as falling
in bucket (220-1). For the wide tag quantization, too, switch implementations SHOULD keep event
counters for out-of-range low and out-of-range high occurrences during quantization. The reporting and
use of these counters is implementation-specific and outside the scope of this specification.
4.2.4.1.7 Locator Metadata (csig.lm)
Locator metadata is a 6-bit field in the compact tag and a 15-bit field in the wide tag. It identifies the
location within the network and/or attributes of the switch where the signal value in a CSIG tag was
updated. When a switch updates the signal value in a packet’s tag, it MUST also update the locator
metadata in the tag.
Locator metadata is updated by the bottleneck hop (i.e., the hop updating the signal value as part of the
CSIG-Compare-and-Update() operation). Locator metadata may provide deployment-specific
information for deployment-specific differentiation or vendor extensions (e.g., vendor-specific
enhancements to UE CC algorithms). Locator metadata may provide additional hints to improve UE
congestion management, path selection, or just provide visibility of the bottleneck hop as telemetry
data.
Informative Text:
The distinction between a last-hop bottleneck and one at any earlier point along a path is useful to
tell incast apart from “non-leaf” congestion. This distinction is important because load balancing

PAGE 611

611

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
should not attempt to change paths in an incast but should do so when congestion occurs at any
other link. Trimmed packets already use distinct DSCP code points to distinguish the incast and non-
incast cases.
Some example information that can be encoded in locator metadata is as follows:
•
Outgoing Link Capacity
o For normalized signal types like ABW/C, knowing the link capacity is helpful.
o Common link speeds can be encoded in 2 bits.
•
Outgoing Link Orientation
o Uplink, downlink, side link, penultimate hop link.
o Fabric information.
o Fat tree stages or group ID in DragonFly++ topology.
o Rail/plane ID in multi-rail or multi-plane topology.
•
Outgoing PortID/DeviceID
o Possibly only applicable to wide format: 9 bits are needed for 512-radix switches.
o TTL of packet on egress: 8 bits of information to detect the exact hop in the path.

4.2.4.1.8 Do Not Modify (csig.d)
The csig.d bit provides a Do Not Modify indication for a CSIG tag. When a switch receives a CSIG tag with
csig.d = 0, that switch MUST, according to the signal type (csig.t) specified in the tag and the signal
type’s aggregation function, perform CSIG-Compare-and-Update() on the signal value (csig.s) in that tag.
When a switch receives a CSIG tag with csig.d = 1, that switch MUST NOT modify the signal value (csig.s)
in that tag. When a CSIG tag is first initialized, its csig.d bit MUST be set to zero, to indicate that
receiving switches are permitted to update the signal value in that tag.
In a UE fabric configured to perform packet trimming and that supports CSIG, all switches MUST support
the following base case behavior: When a CSIG-tagged packet arrives at a heavily congested queue, and
the receiving switch trims the packet, that switch MUST set the CSIG tag’s csig.d bit, and SHOULD make
no further modifications to the CSIG tag. Some deployments MAY overwrite the CSIG tag’s signal value
(csig.s) with signal information from the switch where trimming occurs; this policy may benefit
congestion control at endpoints. Those use cases and their configuration are outside the scope of this
specification.
A CSIG-capable switch may support configurations in which it does not set the csig.d bit when trimming
CSIG-tagged packets. Those use cases and their configuration are outside the scope of this specification.
Moreover, all UE-compliant switches that support CSIG MUST support the base case behavior of setting
the csig.d bit in the CSIG tag on any packet they trim.
The rationale for this base case behavior of setting the csig.d bit in CSIG tags on trimmed packets is that
once a packet has been trimmed, it traverses high-priority queues, whose measured signal values may
not be representative of the congestion state at the lower-priority queues traversed by untrimmed

PAGE 612

612

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
packets. Rather than potentially overwrite the CSIG tag with an unrepresentative signal from the higher-
priority queues at subsequent switches along the path, this approach preserves the signal value in the
tag prior to the trimming of the packet, which reflects the representative congestion state of lower-
priority queues along the path prior to trimming.
Some deployments MAY set the csig.d bit under other circumstances than at packet trim time to
prevent a CSIG tag from being updated by specific switches in the fabric. Those use cases and their
configuration are outside the scope of this specification.
4.2.4.1.9 Reserved (csig.r)
The csig.r bits SHALL be set to 0 by the FEP that initializes and inserts a CSIG tag on a packet for
transmission (see 4.2.5.2).  The csig.r bits are ignored upon receipt.
4.2.5
Functionality Within the CSIG Domain
The CSIG domain is defined as the set of UE fabric elements that participate in CSIG tag processing. The
following sections describe the functionality implemented at devices within the CSIG domain.
4.2.5.1
Capability Discovery
UE 1.1 Link Negotiation (Section 5.3) provides support for negotiating CSIG capability over each link
using the UE Link Negotiations Options Organization Specific LLDP TLV. End-to-end CSIG configuration is
done through other local or system-wide management capabilities such as the UE Switch Abstraction
Interface (SAI) and the UE RedFish interfaces. The LLDP capabilities provided allow the ports of a link to
indicate if they are capable of processing only compact CSIG tags, capable of processing both compact
and wide CSIG tags, or not capable of processing CSIG tags.
A host or switch that is CSIG-capable MUST support the compact tag and the base profile. The host or
switch MAY additionally support wide tags and MAY additionally support the extended profile. For a
switch to be capable of processing CSIG tags at a port it MUST be able to forward the CSIG tag
information through the switch along with the data packet to any other switch port and update the CSIG
tag at the egress port. In addition, a host or switch that is CSIG-capable MUST be able to strip the CSIG
tag formats it supports.
4.2.5.1.1 CSIG LLDP Transmit and Receive States
When a device that supports CSIG determines that a peer device on a link does not support CSIG, that
device performs the CSIG-Strip-and-Forward() function (see Section 4.2.5.4) when forwarding CSIG-
tagged packets on that link. When a device supports compact CSIG tags but the peer does not, it MUST
strip the compact CSIG tag from the packet before transmitting it on the link, irrespective of the csig.d
bit’s value. When the device supports wide CSIG tags but the peer does not, it will strip the wide CSIG
tag from the packet before transmitting it on the link, irrespective of the csig.d bit’s value.
The local and remote LLDP database values of the csig-capable object are used in conjunction with the
presence or absence of the csig-capable object and with the local management configuration settings to
determine the forwarding of CSIG tags at the port. Table 4-7 describes how transmission and reception
of CSIG-tagged packets are processed at a port controlled using LLDP.

operations described in Table 4-7. A system MAY provide capabilities to override the LLDP configuration
for CSIG on a port or switch; however, if the UE Link Option LLDP TLV csig-capable object is supported it
MUST still be set consistent with the system configuration (i.e., if CSIG is disabled by a local system
configuration then csig-capable is set to CSIG-NO even if the switch is capable of processing CSIG tags).

4.2.5.2
Tag Initialization
CSIG tag initialization occurs when a UE FEP inserts a CSIG tag (compact or wide) into a packet. The FEP’s
policy governs generation of CSIG tags in packets.
Informative Text:
UE fabric switches do not insert CSIG tags in packets that do not already carry them; thus, they also
do not initialize CSIG tags.

Depending on the design and implementation of the CC algorithm and telemetry software in use at the
FEP, the FEP’s policy may:
•
Insert CSIG tags in all of an application’s packets (i.e., CSIG does not generate additional packets and
gathers telemetry in a pre-existing application’s packet stream).
•
Insert CSIG tags in 1 in N of an application’s packets (i.e., CSIG does not generate additional packets
and gathers telemetry in a pre-existing application’s packet stream).
•
Insert CSIG tags in probe packets. A telemetry application generates probe packets for the express
purpose of signal collection from UE fabric elements.
A FEP that inserts a tag in a packet MUST also initialize that CSIG tag’s csig.t (type) and csig.s (signal)
values (as specified in Table 4-8), and it MUST set the csig.d and csig.r (reserved) bit(s) to zero.

4.2.5.3
Tag Transit
UE fabric switch elements perform the CSIG transit function.
The transit function entails:
•
When the received CSIG tag’s csig.d bit is set to zero:
o Perform CSIG-Compare-and-Update() with the received CSIG tag in accordance with the
signal type csig.t
•
When the received CSIG tag’s csig.d bit is set to one:
o Do not update the CSIG tag; leave it unchanged when forwarding the packet. (See Section
4.2.4.1.8 for the full discussion of the csig.d bit and trimmed packets.)
Example CSIG-Compare-and-Update() sequence:
Compare-and-Update(pkt.csig.signal, pkt.csig.lm)
if (pkt.csig->t == “min-ABW[/C]”) {
  if (local_abw[/c] at packet egress port < pkt.csig.signal) {
    pkt.csig->signal = local_abw[/c] at packet egress port;
    pkt.csig->lm = local_lm;
  }
}
if (pkt.csig->t == “max-Delay”) {
  if (local_delay > pkt.csig.signal) {
    pkt.csig->signal = local_delay;
    pkt.csig->lm = local_lm;
  }
}

Note that in the pseudocode above, local values are quantized so that they are comparable to the
quantized values in the received CSIG tag.
4.2.5.4
Strip and Forward
The CSIG-Strip-and-Forward() function at a switch strips the CSIG tag from a packet and forwards the
packet without the tag. When a switch learns through LLDP that a peer switch on some link cannot
process CSIG tags, that switch MUST invoke CSIG-Strip-and-Forward() on CSIG-tagged packets before
forwarding them on that link to ensure that these packets are not dropped by the non-CSIG-capable
receiving peer. This action is performed regardless of the value of the packet’s CSIG tag’s csig.d bit.
4.2.5.5
Tag Termination
The destination FEP consumes received CSIG tags by performing the termination (Term) function,
thereby ending the forward path of the CSIG domain.

PAGE 616

616

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The CSIG-Term() function does the following:
•
Extracts the information carried in the CSIG tag (csig.t, csig.s , csig.lm, csig.d bit)
•
For a packet arriving on a transport flow using receiver-based congestion control, presents the
extracted CSIG tag information to the receiving FEP’s transport layer (for onward delivery to the
CC algorithm and/or receiver-based application)
•
For a packet arriving on a transport flow using sender-based congestion control, presents the
extracted CSIG tag information to the CSIG-Reflect() function in the receiving FEP’s transport
layer, to allow return of the CSIG tag information to the flow’s sending FEP
•
Strips the CSIG tag from the incoming packet

See Section 4.2.5.5.1 for a description of the CSIG-Reflect() function.
4.2.5.5.1 Reflection
When a CSIG-tagged packet from a source FEP arrives at a destination FEP that is CSIG-enabled, the
CSIG-Term() function at the destination FEP extracts the CSIG tag information and passes it to the
transport layer. If the transport layer is using a sender-based CC algorithm (such as NSCC), or other
sender-based functions (such as multi-path load balancing) that need the information in the CSIG tag,
the CSIG-Reflect() function at the transport layer MUST be enabled. The CSIG-Reflect() function
populates the CSIG Reflection Header with information extracted by the CSIG-Term() function. The CSIG
Reflection Header is returned to the source via an ACK or NACK packet generated by the transport layer.
This enables the source FEP to receive feedback on path conditions indicated by the CSIG tag received at
the destination. Section 3.6.9.4 describes the format of the CSIG Reflection Header as well as the
pds.ack_ccx_state and pds.nack_ccx_state formats used for CSIG reflection.
Implementation of the CSIG-Reflect() function is REQUIRED in a CSIG-capable FEP.
Figure 4-7 shows the logical interactions among the CSIG-Term(), CMS, PDS, and CSIG-Reflect() functions.
The detailed implementation of the CSIG-Reflect() function depends upon the congestion control
algorithm in use. Detailed procedures for constructing the CSIG Reflection Header in the ACK_CCX and
NACK_CCX fields, setting other transport header fields, and their use in particular congestion control
algorithms (e.g., NSCC and RCCC) are specified in 3.6.9.4.
4.2.6
CSIG Tag Layout
The CSIG tag lies within an Ethernet frame’s layer 2 headers. An EtherType unique to the deployment
(4.2.4.1.1) identifies a CSIG-tagged frame.
When layer 2 encapsulation (e.g., IEEE Std 802.1ad or stacked tags) is not in use on a frame, the CSIG tag
is always placed as the last tag in the layer 2 header. Tunneling of CSIG-tagged packets at layer 2, layer 3,
or above is out of scope of this specification.

summarizes the signals for these profiles.

4.2.8
CSIG Traffic Rate Measurement Interval
The CSIG ABW and ABW/C signal types involve the measurement of a traffic rate. Such a measurement
is taken over some time interval. Because congestion control algorithms at end systems typically
consume congestion signals measured at path-RTT granularity, CSIG-capable devices SHOULD choose an
interval for traffic-rate measurement that is no longer than the unloaded RTT for the shortest-
propagation-delay path within the fabric.
Comparisons of traffic rates measured at distinct switches and carried in CSIG tags are valid when
switches along a CSIG-tagged packet’s path use the same measurement interval. Toward ensuring that
all switches along a path support at least one common measurement interval, a CSIG-capable switch
SHOULD support a measurement time interval t of 102.4 µs and default to this value at boot. Further, a
CSIG-capable switch SHOULD support as many values as an implementation permits of the
measurement time interval t drawn from the range of values [128 ns, 1024 ms] with an increment of
128 ns. A switch SHOULD support the same measurement intervals for both the ABW and ABW/C signal
types and MUST configure the same measurement intervals across all switches in the fabric.
A switch constrained by its arithmetic capabilities can choose to approximate the time interval. In such
cases the time interval MUST be within the bounds of loss of precision during quantization.
Implementation Note:
For signals that measure a traffic rate (e.g., ABW and ABW/C), implementors should take note of the
interaction between the spacing in time of CSIG-tagged packets within a flow and the time interval
over which a device measures a traffic rate. For CSIG-tagged packets within a flow to obtain
representative traffic rate measurements that cover traffic dynamics over time, it is essential they
arrive at a device at least once per the measurement interval in use by that device. If the gap between
successive CSIG-tagged packet arrivals at the device is significantly longer than the device’s traffic rate
measurement interval, the signal values written by that device into passing CSIG-tagged packets will
not cover traffic volumes measured during such gaps. It is not generally possible to choose a traffic
rate measurement interval at devices to ensure CSIG-tagged packets will arrive often enough to avoid

PAGE 621

621

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
such gaps; if an application-limited flow sending CSIG-tagged packets from an end host goes idle on a
long-lived transport connection for some significant period, such a gap may occur.
End hosts may also perform averaging over multiple CSIG signal values received in multiple packets
over the course of an RTT or longer.

4.2.9
CSIG Signals
This section describes each signal, the algorithm for any associated computation, boundary conditions,
and the signal’s applicability in example use cases.
In the text that follows, we name each signal according to signal type and the comparison function—
min() or max()—used in CSIG-Compare-and-Update() operations on tags containing that signal.
4.2.9.1
min(ABW)
When a source FEP sends a packet with a CSIG tag for signal type min(ABW), and that packet traverses a
path through the UE fabric, that packet’s CSIG tag records the minimum absolute available bandwidth
along the path: among all switches along that packet’s path, the minimum quantized absolute available
bandwidth in bytes per second (Bps) at any output physical port traversed by that packet. Both the
unquantized and quantized absolute available bandwidth values are represented as integers.
4.2.9.1.1 Available Bandwidth Computation
The ABW signal uses a simple, time window-based computation to measure traffic rate and, thus,
available bandwidth. Given the following definitions:

All network devices in a CSIG domain SHOULD be configured with the same value for t and the same

4.2.9.1.2 Load Accounting
UE-compliant switches MUST support a mode of operation in which they exclude MAC-generated
frames in per-port transmit load accounting. min(ABW) measurements are intended to include only data
frames subject to congestion control by an originating FEP. Other MAC-generated frames (e.g., PAUSE,
LLR, CBFC, and PFC frames) SHOULD NOT be included in per-port transmit load accounting. Switches
MAY support other variations of transmit load accounting outside the scope of this specification.
4.2.9.1.3 UET Congestion Control Use Cases
A potential use case for the min(ABW) signal in UE congestion control concerns improving the
effectiveness of multi-path load balancing. Both the NSCC and RCCC congestion control algorithms
incorporate multi-path load balancing, whereby a sending FEP selects and writes an entropy value (EV)
in each packet it sends, and switches include this EV in the input to the hash functions they use for
ECMP path selection. Distinct flows may obliviously select EVs that direct their traffic to collide at the
same output port of a switch. When other uncongested paths are available, such flow collisions cause
otherwise avoidable congestion at that port’s queue.
Current proposals for multi-path load balancing in UET, such as REPS, use the presence or absence of
ECN marks on returning transport ACKs as an indication of whether a packet encountered congestion
from a flow collision when sent with a particular EV. By efficiently informing sending FEPs of the
minimum available bandwidth along a packet’s path, the min(ABW) CSIG signal may allow sending FEPs
to perform a finer-grained comparison of the merits of the paths selected by distinct EVs, such that a
sending FEP may be able not only to avoid EVs that have experienced congestion, but also to select an
EV preferentially for a path that offers comparatively more available bandwidth than other EVs’ paths.
4.2.9.2
min(ABW/C)
The min(ABW/C) signal is similar to the min(ABW) signal, but its signal value is normalized by the output
port capacity C in bytes per second. Both the unquantized and quantized normalized available
bandwidth values are represented as integers.
In fabrics with heterogeneous port speeds, comparison of absolute available bandwidths measured at
ports of different speeds does not reliably reveal which port is operating at a greater fraction of its
capacity. Normalizing by capacity reliably identifies the port operating at the greatest fraction of its
capacity, even when comparing across ports of different speeds.
4.2.9.2.1 Available Bandwidth Computation
The min(ABW/C) signal uses a simple, time window-based computation of normalized available
bandwidth, represented as an integer value between 0 and 100.

4.2.9.2.2 Load Accounting
Outbound traffic measurements performed for the min(ABW/C) signal are subject to the same
constraints as those applied to measurements for the min(ABW) signal, as described in Section 4.2.9.1.2.
4.2.9.2.3 UET Congestion Control Use Cases
A central problem in congestion control is prompt allocation of newly spare capacity on a link to flows
that can use it. For example, when a flow releases its share of a bottleneck link, it is desirable for other
flows that share the same bottleneck to rapidly claim the newly freed capacity. In this situation, a sender
faces a trade-off. It can increase its rate slowly and conservatively by probing, which risks leaving
capacity unused for multiple RTTs and lengthening flow completion time. Alternatively, it can increase
its rate aggressively, and risk overshooting the spare capacity, which incurs congestive delay and packet
losses.
NSCC incorporates a fast_increase() mechanism that reclaims spare capacity aggressively when path
queueing delay is modest and many ACKs have returned in the recent past without an ECN mark, both of
which indicate that a path is lightly loaded. While fast_increase() successfully helps flows reclaim spare
capacity rapidly, it is heuristic in nature in the sense that it is oblivious to the explicit measure of spare
capacity at a bottleneck on a path: it increases a sender’s congestion window a constant two MTUs per
returning ACK.

PAGE 624

624

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
The min(ABW/C) signal provides the NSCC sender with a direct, quantitative measure of the spare
capacity at a path’s bottleneck. This information allows NSCC to better match the increase in a flow’s
sending rate to spare capacity, and thus avoid undershoots and overshoots, both of which can lengthen
flow completion times. Because the min(ABW/C) signal is normalized by an output port’s line rate, it
correctly relatively ranks the fractional spare capacities of output ports along a path, even when they
run at heterogeneous port speeds.
4.2.9.3
max(Delay)
When a source FEP sends a packet with a CSIG tag for signal type max(Delay), and that packet traverses
a path through the UE fabric, that packet’s CSIG tag records, among all switches along the packet’s path,
the maximum service delay in nanoseconds incurred by the packet at any one switch. Both the
unquantized and quantized delay values are represented as integers.
As each switch computes its own intra-switch delay using only switch-local timestamps, there is no need
for clock synchronization across switches in support of these measurements.
4.2.9.3.1 Per-Hop Delay Measurement Method
In a CSIG-capable fabric, at each hop along a path, the switch pipeline measures per-packet delay.
The queueing delay D experienced by a packet is given by:
𝐷= 𝑡2 − 𝑡1
where t2 is the local timestamp in nanoseconds when the start-of-packet (SOP) signal is sent by the
output port’s MAC, and t1 is the local timestamp in nanoseconds when the SOP signal is received from
the input port’s MAC.
4.2.9.3.2 Timestamping Points in Switch Pipeline
Figure 4-10 shows the switch pipeline and the two points at which a switch SHOULD timestamp a
packet’s arrival and departure. The aim is for this delay measurement to capture the queueing delay
experienced by the packet. IP refers to ingress pipeline processing, and EP refers to egress pipeline
processing in a switch.
Measuring the interval between the start of the ingress pipeline and the end of the egress pipeline
offers two principal advantages:
•
It’s straightforward to perform CSIG-Compare-and-Update() on the packet in these stages.

Figure 4-10 - Timestamping Points in Switch Pipeline

PAGE 625

625

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
Timestamping in these stages includes only queueing and pipeline delays.
4.2.9.3.3 Point in Packet for Timestamping
SOP indicates the start-of-packet event at a switch port. A UE CSIG-capable switch MUST measure the
delay experienced by a packet by timestamping the packet at the SOP event at the ingress port and at
the SOP at the egress port, then taking the difference between the latter timestamp and the former
one. This approach does not include any extraneous delay proportional to a packet’s length in the
measurement and is compatible with cut-through switch fabrics. A switch MAY subtract a fixed value
from this measurement to account for the switch’s uncongested forwarding delay.
4.2.9.3.4 UET Congestion Control Use Cases
The max(Delay) signal is a trailing indicator of congestion: a packet must traverse a switch’s queue
before a measurement of the delay incurred at that queue can be calculated. The value of this signal as
an input to delay-based congestion control algorithms, such as NSCC, stems from its more targeted
measurement of congestion than is possible with total end-to-end path delay. max(Delay) reveals the
queueing delay experienced by a packet at a path’s single most constrained bottleneck, whereas whole-
path delay measurements, such as those used as input by NSCC, sum the queueing delays from all
congested queues along a packet’s path.
The more targeted congestion measurements enabled by max(Delay) can materially improve the
bandwidth fairness of delay-based congestion control protocols. Previously published work [1]
demonstrates that when two flows traverse the same congested queue, if one of the two flows
encounters no other congested queues along its path and the other flow encounters one or more
additional congested queues along its path, delay-based congestion control schemes that use whole-
path delay measurements exhibit bandwidth unfairness between the two flows. Such congestion control
schemes reduce a flow’s sending rate in proportion to the amount that the flow’s total path delay
exceeds a target path delay.
Because the flow traversing multiple congested queues experiences greater total path delay, even
though only a single queue along a path can be the most constrained bottleneck for any flow, its sending
rate will be reduced proportionally more than that of the flow traversing only one congested queue.
Poseidon, a delay-based congestion control algorithm that uses CSIG max(Delay)-like feedback [1] ,
improves fairness for such flow pairs by enabling the control loops for each of the two flows to respond
to congestion only at that flow’s single true bottleneck (most congested) queue, such that the flow that
traverses multiple congested queues is not disproportionately penalized.
The max(Delay) signal should offer similar bandwidth fairness improvements to NSCC congestion
control. Exploratory simulations of a version of NSCC modified to replace whole-path delay signals with
CSIG max(Delay) signals demonstrate material bandwidth fairness improvements over baseline NSCC in
scenarios in which multiple flows traverse a shared congested queue, while distinct flows among them
traverse varying numbers of congested queues.

PAGE 626

626

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
4.2.9.4
max(nQD)
When a source FEP sends a packet with a CSIG tag for signal type max(nQD), and that packet traverses a
path through the UE fabric, that packet’s CSIG tag will record the maximum normalized queue depth at
packet dequeue encountered along the path: among all switches along that packet’s path, the maximum
queue depth (in bytes) normalized by the output port’s speed (in bytes per second) at any one switch.
Both the unquantized and quantized normalized queue depth values are represented as integer values
in nanoseconds; note that queue depth in bytes normalized by port speed in bytes per second yields a
unit of time.
In deployments with heterogeneous output port speeds, absolute queue depths at queues for output
ports of different speeds are not directly comparable as indicators of the extent of congestion. For
example, a shorter absolute queue depth in front of a slower link might take longer to drain than a
longer absolute queue depth in front of a faster link. In such a case, a shorter absolute queue depth
might indicate more severe congestion than a longer absolute queue depth. For this reason, to render
queue depths across potentially heterogeneous port speeds comparable, the max(nQD) signal
normalizes queue depth by output port speed.
max(nQD) is a leading indicator of congestion and corresponds to “expected delay” rather than
“experienced delay”: Queue depth is measured instantaneously at the point when a CSIG-tagged packet
is dequeued for onward forwarding. In this sense, this signal is analogous to ECN marks, but with a
multi-bit indication of the extent of queueing, as opposed to ECN’s single-bit, thresholded queue depth
indication.
Informative Text:
While normalizing by output port speed addresses heterogeneous port speeds, other considerations
may arise in some deployments that make comparison of nQD values across switches problematic.
For example, in a deployment that uses multiple traffic classes of different priorities, if CSIG-nQD-
tagged packets travel in a traffic class at any priority other than the top priority, the drain rate for
those packets from that traffic class’s queue will vary over time, depending on the time-varying load
in any higher-priority traffic class(es). As such, the correctness of the max(nQD) signal’s value—
accumulated along a path as an indicator of the point of greatest congestion along that path—relies
on the absence of unpredictable, time-varying load in traffic classes of higher priority than the traffic
class in which a CSIG-nQD-tagged packet travels.

4.2.9.4.1 Normalized Queue Depth Computation
A switch computes the local nQD value by normalizing the instantaneous queue depth at the time of
dequeue by a base port speed.
// iQD: the instantaneous queue depth (in bytes) at the time of dequeue
// PortSpeed: the current port’s speed
// BasePortSpeed: the slowest port speed in the network
PortSpeedRatio = PortSpeed / BasePortSpeed
PortSpeedRatioLog2 = log2(PortSpeedRatio)

PAGE 627

627

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
if (PortSpeedRatio_is_power_of_2)

Adjusted_iQD = iQD >> PortSpeedRatioLog2
else
      Adjusted_iQD = iQD / PortSpeedRatio
Local_CSIG_nQD = Quantization (Adjusted_iQD)
Update CSIG(nQD) Tag when Local_CSIG_nQD is greater than the current “Signal
Value”

When all ports in a fabric run at the same speed, PortSpeedRatio is effectively 1, and
PortSpeedLog2Ratio is 0.
In UE deployments with heterogeneous output port speeds, the BasePortSpeed can be set to 100 Gbps.
Relative to that base value, for port speeds of 100/200/400/800/1600/3200 Gbps, we obtain
PortSpeedRatioLog2 values of 0/1/2/3/4/5 respectively.
This simple shift logic does not suffice for future non-power-of-2 speeds in a network with
heterogeneous port speeds. Consider a 300 Gbps port speed in a network with heterogeneous port
speeds as an example: division by 3 logic would be required with a BasePortSpeed of 100 Gbps.
Refer to sections 4.2.4.1.4 and 4.2.4.1.6 for the CSIG-Quantization() algorithms for the compact and
wide CSIG tag formats, respectively.

4.2.10 CSIG Deployment Considerations
As specified in Section 4.2.4, two CSIG tag formats are defined: a compact (4-byte) format and a wide (8-
byte) format. A global configuration setting for the entire UE fabric and set of FEPs indicates whether
the preferred tag format for the UE CSIG domain is the compact format or the wide format. All FEPs
SHOULD use this global configuration setting to determine whether to insert a compact- or wide-format
CSIG tag in sent packets to collect congestion information from the UE fabric, such that there will not be
a mix of compact and wide CSIG-capable paths in the same UE CSIG domain. In some cases, operators
may deploy a mix of CSIG-capable and non-CSIG-capable switches in the same UE fabric. A global
configuration setting for the entire UE fabric and set of FEPs will indicate whether CSIG is enabled for
the entire fabric or disabled for the entire fabric. This setting SHOULD be enabled only when all switches
in the UE fabric support CSIG, such that the fabric will not mix paths that support CSIG feedback-guided
congestion control and paths that do not support CSIG-feedback-guided congestion control.

Informative Text:
nQD may be useful as a replacement for ECN, as nQD logically is a multi-bit ECN signal. nQD may be
usable as a load balancing signal, a congestion control signal, and a telemetry signal.
Use of the nQD signal type in deployments with application traffic in multiple traffic classes of
different priorities is outside the scope of this specification. Future versions of this specification may
address the use of the nQD signal in such deployments.

PAGE 628

628

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

Informative Text:
In some cases, such as in multi-tenancy, when an operator deploys a mix of switches in the UE fabric,
some of which support only the compact tag format and some of which support both the compact
and wide tag formats, some applications MAY use CSIG with wide tags on those paths where switches
support them and others MAY use compact tags. In these cases, those flows using wide tags benefit
from the greater precision and/or signal type variety of wide tags on paths where they are available.
Such behavior is outside the scope of this specification, as are the mechanisms and policies FEPs use
to configure the choice of compact or wide tags in sent traffic. Whether a congestion control scheme
works correctly when CSIG-compact-tagged flows and CSIG-wide-tagged flows share a bottleneck
depends on the specifics of the congestion control scheme.
In some cases, when an operator deploys a mix of switches in the UE fabric, some of which support
CSIG and some of which do not, the operator MAY wish to use CSIG as feedback in congestion control
on those paths that support CSIG, while CSIG will not be used on those paths that do not support
CSIG. Such behavior is outside the scope of this specification. This specification contemplates only the
scenarios in which congestion control for all flows uses CSIG feedback and in which congestion control
for no flows uses CSIG feedback. Whether a congestion control scheme works correctly when CSIG-
feedback-enabled flows and non-CSIG-feedback-enabled flows share a bottleneck depends on the
specific details of the congestion control scheme.

4.2.10.1 Deployment of New Signal Types
New CSIG signal types may be introduced in the future. When a new signal type is introduced in a
deployment, it is recommended that use of that signal type be enabled only after all switches and FEPs
support that signal type, as indicated in global configuration state. When support for a new signal type is
heterogeneous across FEPs and switches in a deployment, how FEPs determine when to use the new
signal type is outside the scope of this specification.

Figure 4-11 - CSIG Domain

PAGE 629

629

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Whether a switch supports processing of a new signal type is NOT discoverable through LLDP. Such
discovery is not necessary, as a switch receiving a packet with a CSIG tag for an unsupported signal type
can still parse and forward the packet correctly. Instead, the central management entity is responsible
for configuring switches that receive a packet with a CSIG tag for an unsupported signal type to either 1)
CSIG-Strip-and-Forward() the packet or 2) CSIG-Forward() the packet while preserving the CSIG tag
unchanged. A deployment will specify which one of a few policies to follow when a switch receives a tag
for a signal type it does not implement (e.g., Forward() without updating the tag or CSIG-Strip-and-
Forward()).

5 UE Link Layer
The Link Layer Working Group is responsible for defining UE specifications that operate at and support
the link layer. These optional-to-implement specifications enhance performance and reliability of the
link layer while also simplifying configuration. The features defined by the UE link layer specifications
can operate with, and in some cases work as an alternative to, existing Ethernet link functionality.
The following sections describe the UE link layer specifications in detail:
1. Section 5.1 Link layer retry (LLR), which reduces the impact on latency when a packet is lost due
to imperfect links. LLR requires only a single-link round-trip time to determine loss and restart
the flow of packets.
2. Section 5.2 Credit-based flow control (CBFC) is an alternative mechanism to priority-based flow
control (PFC) flow control. Rather than sending PFC indications when a receive buffer is
approaching full, a CBFC receiver periodically sends buffer space updates (credits) to its link
partner. This allows the partner to preferentially send traffic on traffic classes with available
buffer space.
3. Section 5.3 Link negotiation allows UE devices supporting optional UE link layer features to
automatically determine if the link partner is capable of operating with the same mutually
supported UE link layer features. Link negotiation defines procedures and managed objects that
operate on top of existing IEEE Std 802.1AB (LLDP) implementations that are widely deployed.



PAGE 631

631

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.1 Link Layer Retry (LLR)
The impact of delay on efficiency becomes more significant as network link speeds, utilization, and scale
increase. Latency-sensitive workloads are negatively impacted by the delays created from the traditional
end-to-end approach of retransmitting lost packets. Local error handling at the link layer has proven
valuable in scale-out HPC networks, such as those used in exascale systems. The UE specification
provides a link layer retry (LLR) capability for Ethernet.
The LLR mechanism is frame-based. Each frame passed to the transmit LLR from the MAC client is
assessed for eligibility for LLR. If the MAC client does not desire LLR for the frame, or if it is otherwise
classified as LLR-ineligible, then the frame is sent as a standard Ethernet frame. If the frame is LLR-
eligible, then the LLR TX assigns a sequence number and stores the frame in a replay buffer for possible
retransmission if the link partner does not receive the frame.
The sequence number for each LLR-eligible frame passed from the LLR to the MAC is placed into the
preamble prepended by the MAC. The link partner sends acknowledgements (LLR_ACKs) for LLR-eligible
frames that are successfully received, and these LLR_ACKs are used to free space in the replay buffer.
Negative acknowledgements (LLR_NACKs) are used to signal when a missing LLR-eligible frame is
detected (due to receipt of a subsequent LLR-eligible frame). Timeouts are used to guarantee that LLR-
eligible frames will be replayed if an LLR_NACK is lost or if a replay is corrupted and there is no LLR_ACK
to indicate progress.

The receive MAC delivers LLR-eligible frames and LLR-ineligible frames to the LLR layer. For each LLR-
eligible frame, the MAC relays the sequence number of the LLR-eligible frame extracted from the
preamble. The LLR checks that the sequence number of the LLR-eligible frame is the next expected
sequence number. The LLR discards LLR-eligible frames that are not expected and returns an LLR_NACK
to the link partner to indicate that a frame has been lost.
During normal operation, the LLR receiver periodically sends LLR_ACKs that acknowledge the most
recent successfully received frame. When an out-of-sequence frame is received, a single LLR_NACK is
sent to indicate the error. No further LLR_ACKs or LLR_NACKs are sent until the frame with the expected
sequence number is successfully received.
LLR provides lossless link operation for data from the Ethernet LLC/MAC client layer. In the standard
IEEE layering model, LLR is located between the LLC/MAC client layer and MAC control layer. LLR is
above the MAC control layer because the sending of pause frames from the MAC control layer is not
blocked by LLR while it is performing a replay operation. However, it should be noted that the reception
of pause frames does not stop the replay of previously sent data frames by LLR and acts only on new
data frames (LLR-ineligible or LLR-eligible) from the LLC/MAC client layer. In this respect, showing the
LLR above the MAC control layer is slightly misleading, and care should be taken when implementing the
pause mechanism. Priority-based flow control (PFC) frames interact with LLR in the same way as pause
frames.
The correct MAC control pause behavior is achieved by bypassing the MAC control request and
information interfaces around the LLR. Requests to send pause frames are made to the MAC control

layer directly from the LLC/MAC client and are made irrespective of the LLR’s current state. Similarly,

Because received pause frames stop only new MAC client data being passed to the LLR and do not stop
LLR replay data, it is important that the maximum amount of data held in the replay buffer not be much
greater than the bandwidth-delay product for the link. If the LLR replay buffer were to contain
significantly more data than the bandwidth-delay product, then pause would not operate as expected. A
configuration is provided in the LLR to limit the maximum amount of data held in the replay buffer.
Informative Text:
The process for buffer sizing, accounting for the link bandwidth-delay product, is outside the scope of
this specification and should be performed by the implementer.

5.1.1
Frame structure
The UE LLR specification introduces a new modified frame preamble, usable with both IPv4 and IPv6
addressing to support link layer retry (LLR). When UE features such as LLR are not in use, UE link frames
are indistinguishable from standard IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frames.
All frames MUST begin with the 8-byte UE link frame preamble defined in Section 5.1.1.1.

placed in bytes 1-3, using a 20-bit sequence number. With minimum 64-byte frames at 800 Gbit/sec, this
allows for a round-trip time of over 500 µs. The longest RTT is expected to be much less than 5 µsec, but
this field width allows for link speed increases in the future.

5.1.3
LLR Operation
The LLR has two modes of operation: OFF and ON. The OFF mode of operation disables LLR functionality
and removes its effects from the IEEE layering model so that a port behaves as an IEEE 802.3 standard
port. The ON mode of operation enables the LLR mechanism and provides lossless link-level behavior for
LLR-eligible frames, while providing IEEE 802.3 standard behavior for LLR-ineligible frames.
When the LLR mode is OFF, all frames are passed through the TX LLR from the MAC client to the MAC
control layer and are not stored in the replay buffer or assigned a sequence number. When the LLR
mode is OFF, all frames are passed through the RX LLR from the MAC control layer to the MAC client
layer without any frames being filtered.
When the LLR mode is ON, the LLR mechanism is active. All LLR-ineligible frames are passed through the
TX LLR from the MAC client to the MAC control layer and are not stored in the replay buffer or assigned
a sequence number, while all LLR-eligible frames are handled as described in the following sections.
When the LLR mode is ON, unexpected (sequence number missed or sequence number duplicated) LLR-
eligible frames are filtered by the RX LLR, while expected LLR-eligible frames and LLR-ineligible frames
(not terminated by the MAC control layer) are passed through the RX LLR to the MAC client layer
without being filtered.

PAGE 636

636

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.1.3.1.1 Control Ordered Set
The LLR uses special Control Ordered Sets (CtlOS) to send control messages to the link partner when it is
in the ON mode. The PCS periodically inserts CtlOS into the data stream in a manner that is oblivious to
the data frames being sent (i.e., CtlOS can be sent pre-emptively). This limits the maximum latency for
sending control messages to the link partner and provides a guaranteed bandwidth for those control
messages.
Note that support for these CtlOS must be present in the MAC and in the PCS and RS of the physical
layer. This includes supporting the additional Control Ordered Sets described in Table 5-7, with indicated
data fields. That data needs to be communicated from/to the LLR layer. Lastly, the PCS must support the
existence of CtlOS in the block stream, including during frame data. See the UE PHY specification for
additional details.
There are four types of CtlOS that the LLR needs to send and receive:
Table 5-7 - LLR Control Ordered Sets
CtlOS Type
Description
LLR_ACK
LLR frame acknowledgement.
LLR_NACK
LLR frame negative acknowledgement.
LLR_INIT
Sent to initialize the next_rx_seq state in the link partner.
LLR_INIT_ECHO
Sent to indicate that an LLR_INIT CtlOS has been received and processed and that
the station is ready to receive LLR frames.

In addition to the standard 802.3-defined Sequence ordered sets, the UE LLR specification defines a
Control Ordered Set (CtlOS) for purposes of LLR messaging. The corresponding 64B/66B block formats
are shown in Table 5-8—which matches the format of Figure 82-5 - 64B/66B block formats in IEEE Std

0x6. Octets D1 through D3 and D5 through D7; the O code; and the upper four bits of octet D4 are all

PAGE 637

637

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
transmitted from least-significant bit to most-significant bit. For example, an LLR_ACK with
ack_nack_seq[19:0]=0x12345 would result in the following CtlOS being transmitted:
 10_11010010_10000000_01001000_00101100_01101010_00000000_00000000_00000000.
For the LLR signaling CtlOS, D1 is set to the CtlOS message type. Four different message types are
supported and are identified by the value of D1: LLR_ACK, LLR_NACK, LLR_INIT, and LLR_INIT_ECHO (see
Section 5.1.9 for more detail on the purpose of these messages). The 20-bit message sequence number
is carried in D2 (sequence number bits <19:12>), D3 (sequence number bits <11:4>), and D4[7:4]
(sequence number bits <3:0>). In addition, the LLR_INIT and LLR_INIT_ECHO types carry init data bits
<15:8> in D5 and bits <7:0> in D6. For example, an LLR_INIT with init_seq[19:0]=0x8A72C and
init_data[15:0]=0x4DE1 would result in the following CtlOS being transmitted:
10_11010010_11000000_01010001_01001110_01100011_10110010_10000111_00000000.

LLR_ACK/LLR_NACK Control Ordered Set should be transmitted periodically (according to
ctlos_target_spacing) to ensure an adequate frequency of communication between stations, with the
appropriate sequence number corresponding to the most recently processed received frame.
Implementations may deviate (for any given interval between successive Control Ordered Set) from the
target spacing, but the LLR_TX MUST transmit the CtlOS LLR_ACK / LLR_NACK at a rate between a
maximum rate of once every 400 bytes and a minimum rate of once every 17296 bytes16 (unless the
ACK/NACK transmit state machine is in the NACK_SENT state). To mitigate the impact on per-frame
switch latency, a CtlOS SHALL NOT be inserted among the first 256 bytes of a frame. Similarly, two CtlOS
within the same frame MUST be spaced apart by at least 2 KB of data so that underrun can be managed
on cut-through switches.
5.1.4
LLR configuration
The LLR REQUIRES certain configuration registers to be accessible to management software for the
purposes of configuring and controlling its operation. The llr_mode_local and llr_mode_remote are
enabled from the link negotiation process. The llr_mode_local is set when negotiation determines that
both ends of a link support LLR. The llr_mode_remote is set when negotiation receives indication from
the remote end of the link that its llr_mode_local has been set to ON.

sent.
Values: OFF, ON

impact of implementation factors that can delay the specific point at which CtlOS is inserted into the stream, such
as insertion of a CtlOS from another function as well as avoiding a CtlOS within the first 256 bytes of a frame.
