Even if the local port has set the LLR-E flag, indicating the local port is set to use LLR, the local port SHALL
NOT begin using LLR until the remote link partner indicates it has enabled LLR by setting its LLR-E flag to
TRUE(3). Both link partners SHALL enable LLR before the LLR feature is operational.
5.3.2.1.6.2 IPGR
If the 1-bit IPGR-C is set TRUE(1), the sending port is capable of sending and enabled for receiving
reduced idle bytes (see 5.5). A port SHALL NOT transmit reduced idles unless it sees the IPGR-C flag
TRUE(1) in the remote LLDP database. If a port sees the remote port is capable of receiving a reduced
number of idle bytes indicated by the IPGR-C flag being TRUE(1) in the remote LLDP database, the port
seeing the remote IPGR-C flag TRUE(1) SHALL enable idle reduction on transmission if it is capable. If the
LLDP Options TLV is NULL or is version 0, the link ends SHALL behave the same as if IPGR-C is set
FALSE(0).
5.3.2.1.6.3 CSIG
The 2-bit CSIG-C flag can take one of three values (see Table 5-3). If CSIG-C is set to 0, the port cannot
participate in CSIG. If CSIG-C=0 or if the LLDP Options TLV is NULL or if the LLDP Options TLV is version 0,
then there isn’t any forwarding behavior defined for CSIG. If CSIG-C=1, the port can forward and update
only compact CSIG tags. If CSIG-C=2, the port can forward and update both compact and wide CSIG tags.
The link negotiation supports only CSIG wide tags in combination with CSIG compact tags, as support for
CSIG compact tags is mandatory for all implementations (see Section 4.2).
Table 5-34 - UE Link Negotiation Options TLV CSIG-C Field Options
CSIG-C Value
UE Link CSIG capability
0
The port cannot participate in CSIG (default value).
1
The port can participate in CSIG compact-tag updates only.
2
The port can participate in both CSIG compact and CSIG wide-tag updates.
3
Reserved

If the LLDP advertisement from one or both link partners is CSIG-C=0, then the link end is not capable of
processing CSIG tags (though it might forward them); therefore, the link is not capable of forwarding
packets with CSIG tags. If one link end is CSIG capable (CSIG-C=1 or CSIG-C=2) while the other is not
(CSIG-C=0), then the link end that is CSIG capable SHALL NOT transmit packets with CSIG tags. If the LLDP
Options TLV is NULL or is Version 0, the link end SHALL behave the same as if CSIG-C=0.
If the LLDP advertisements from one link partner is CSIG-C=1 and the other link partner advertises CSIG-
C=1 or CSIG-C=2, then the CSIG-C=1 link end is capable of processing and forwarding only compact CSIG
tags; therefore, the link is capable of forwarding only packets with compact CSIG tags. In this case both

PAGE 691

691

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
ends of the link SHALL NOT send any wide CSIG tags and SHALL log an error if any wide CSIG tags are
received.
If the LLDP advertisements from both link partners have CSIG-C=2, then both ends of the link are able to
process and forward packets with compact and wide CSIG tags; therefore, the link is capable of
forwarding both compact and wide CSIG tags.
5.3.2.1.6.4 UFH
The 2-bit UFH-C field can take one of four values (see Table 5-4). If UFH-C is set to 0, the port cannot
participate in forwarding the unified fabric header (UFH). If UFH-C=0 or if the LLDP Options TLV is NULL
or if the LLDP Options TLV is version 0, then the port isn’t capable of forwarding UFH encoded packets. If
UFH-C=1, the port can forward only UFH_32-encoded packets. If UFH-C=2, the port can forward only
UFH_16-encoded packets. If UFH-C=3, the port can forward both UFH_32- and UFH_16-encoded
packets.
A port SHALL discard all UFH-encoded frames before transmitting them onto the link until it has both the
local and remote Options TLV. Once a port sees both the local and remote UFH-C values along with the
UFH configuration parameters, it SHALL choose an operating mode that is common to both ports, if one
exists; set the local UFH-S to reflect that operational state by setting the UFH-S to the appropriate value
from table 5-4; and stop discarding the UFH encoded packets that conform to the chosen operational
mode. If there is no common operating mode, UFH-S=0 SHALL be set in the local database and
transmitted to the link partner. For an operating mode to be valid, the link partners MUST be using the
same number of bits, as indicated by the UFH_32 and UFH_16 configuration fields, and be running the
same UFH version, indicated by the V32 and V16 bits.
Table 5-35 - UE Link Negotiation Options TLV UFH-C and UFH-S Field Options
UFH-C or UFH-S Value
UE Link UFH capability or status
0
The port cannot participate in UFH (default value).
1
The port can participate in UFH_32 forwarding.
2
The port can participate in UFH_16 forwarding.
3
The port can participate in both UFH_32 and UFH_16 forwarding.

The UFH_32 parameter indicates how many address bits are used for addressing in the UFH_32
encoding. The range of the UFH_32 parameter is 4 to 32 bits where 32 is represented by UFH_32=0. The
UFH_16 parameter indicates how many address bits are used for addressing in the UFH_16 encoding.
The range for the UFH_16 parameter is 4 to 16 bits where 16 is represented by UFH_16=0. The V32 and
V16 parameters indicate the version of the UFH_32 and UFH_16 encoding respectively. The first version
is indicated by a 0 in the V32 or V16 fields, while a future version is indicated by a 1 in the V32 or V16
field.
If the LLDP advertisements from both link partners have the same UFH capabilities, indicated by the
value of UFH-C, then both ends of the link are able to forward packets with the indicated UFH encoding.
In addition to having matching encodings for the link to exchange packets, the link partners SHALL also

PAGE 692

692

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
have matching versions and matching address bit lengths as specified by the V32, UFH_32, V16, and
UFH_16 UFH configuration parameters. For UFH_32 encoding, the V32 and UFH_32 parameters SHALL
match. For UFH_16 encoding, the V16 and UFH_16 parameters SHALL match. If both link partners
support both UFH_32 and UFH_16 encoding, both encodings SHALL be used only if the V32, UFH_32,
V16, and UFH_16 parameters match. If both link partners support UFH_32 and UFH_16 encoding, but if
one of the parameter sets—V32/UFH_32 or V16/UFH_16—does not match. then the link SHALL forward
only packets that are encoded with the matching parameter set.
If the LLDP advertisements from both link partners have different UFH capabilities, indicated by the
value of the UFH-C, the operation SHALL be limited to the packet encoding supported by both ends of
the link. The link partners SHALL NOT transmit UFH encoded packets onto the link that are not part of
the packet encoding supported by both link partners. If the LLDP advertisement from both link partners
have different UFH capabilities without any common encoding, then the ports SHALL NOT transmit
packets with UFH encoding on the link.
Each port sets the UFH-S flag in its local database to a value from Table 5-4 that matches its operational
state.
The 2-bit RR32 and RR16 fields of the LLDP TLV SHALL be transmitted as zero and ignored on receipt.
5.3.2.1.6.5 RESV1
A 1-bit reserved field that SHALL be transmitted as 0 and ignored on receive.
5.3.2.1.6.6 RESV2
A 4-bit reserved field that SHALL be transmitted as 0 and ignored on receive.
5.3.2.1.6.7 RESV3
A 1-bit reserved field that SHALL be transmitted as 0 and ignored on receive.
5.3.2.2
UE Link Negotiation CBFC TLV (CBFC TLV)
The UE Link Negotiation CBFC TLV is exchanged via LLDP and conforms to the LLDP TLV specification [1]
for organizationally specific TLVs. The UE Link Negotiation CBFC TLV is also called the CBFC TLV within
this specification.
The CBFC TLV provides the capabilities to:
•
Determine if CBFC is supported by the presence or absence of the CBFC TLV in both the local
and remote LLDP databases.
•
Exchange the receiver buffer parameters including the buffer size (cell size), per-packet
overhead, and total credits (each of cell size) assigned to CBFC.
•
Negotiate the sender credit size and packet overhead.
•
Identify each CBFC virtual channel (VC) the receiver wants to support, along with the VC
identifier, state, queue, and packet stream selector, and optionally the per-VC credit limit.
•
Allow the sender to indicate to the receiver when the sender is ready to start sending to the
wanted VC(s).

PAGE 693

693

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
Allow the receiver to indicate to the sender when the receiver is ready to begin operation of the
wanted VC(s).
•
Allow the receiver to modify the credit limit on each VC independently.
•
Allow the receiver to stop CBFC on each VC and to re-activate each VC independently.
The CBFC clause provides a complete explanation of how the CBFC TLV exchange is used to configure
CBFC service on a link. The CBFC TLV contains all the parameters required to initialize CBFC for each
virtual channel. Configuration of VCs is performed independently for each direction on the link. The
initialization begins when the receiver sets R_VC_WANT = TRUE(1) for the VC(s) desiring CBFC service.
The sender seeing R_VC_WANT = TRUE in its remote database from the remote link partner configures
the requested VC(s), then acknowledges the configuration by setting S_VC_RTS = TRUE(1) for the
requested VC(s) in its local database. The receiver seeing S_VC_RTS = TRUE for its requested VC(s) in its
remote database from its remote link partner configures itself based on the parameters provided by the
sender, then indicates it is ready to receive by setting R_VC_RTR = TRUE(1) for the VC(s) in its local
database. From this point onward the sender uses CBFC for transmissions on the configured VCs. The
sender SHALL NOT set S_VC_RTS = TRUE for a VC unless the remote receiver has set R_VC_WANT =
TRUE for the VC. The receiver SHALL NOT set R_VC_RTR = TRUE for a VC unless the remote sender has
set S_VC_RTS = TRUE for the VC. The sender SHALL NOT use CBFC for a VC unless the remote receiver
has set R_VC_RTR = TRUE for the VC.

5.3.2.2.1 TLV Type
The 7-bit IEEE-assigned TLV type 127 indicating this TLV is encoded using an organizationally specific
identifier format and subtype [1] .
5.3.2.2.2 TLV Information String Length
The 9-bit TLV information string length indicates the number of bytes following the information string
length field. The CBFC TLV string length depends on the number of receive VCs desired. For 0 <= n <= 32

PAGE 695

695

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
where n is the number of receive VCs listed by this port, the string length is n*6+20. The maximum CBFC
TLV information string length is 212 bytes. The maximum total TLV length is 214 bytes.
5.3.2.2.3 Company ID (CID)
The 24-bit UEC Company ID (CID) used to identify UE TLVs is FA-7A-CB.
5.3.2.2.4 Subtype
The 5-bit subtype value 1 identifies the CBFC TLV. The UE subtype and version fields together occupy the
1-byte field specified by IEEE Std 802.1AB-2016 subclause 8.6.1 for the organizationally defined subtype.
The subtype value 0x1F is reserved for extending the UE TLV subtype field.
5.3.2.2.5 Version
The 3-bit version used to identify the initial version of the CBFC TLV is 0. Future versions of the TLV
SHALL be backward-compatible with version 0. They can extend the length of the TLV to add additional
information and definitions for reserved fields. Older versions ignore any updated reserved fields, code
points, or TLV length extensions.
5.3.2.2.6 Error_Code
The 4-bit Error_Code is used by the CBFC sender to indicate error conditions to the remote CBFC
receiver. If no error is detected the Error_Code = 0. The error codes are:
Table 5-36 - UE Link Negotiation CBFC Error Codes
Value
CBFC Sender Meaning
0x0
No error.
0x1
CBFC sender is unable to support the receiver cell size.
0x2
CBFC sender is unable to support a requested VC.
0x3
CBFC sender is unable to support the credit pool size.
0x4
CBFC sender is unable to support a requested VC credit limit.
0x5
CBFC sender and CBFC receiver packet identification do not match.
0x6
Other error condition.
0x7-0xF
Reserved for future UE specification.

5.3.2.2.7 S_CreditSize
The 12-bit S_CreditSize field identifies the number of bytes in a single credit at the sending port. When
S_CreditSize = 0, the CBFC sender has not yet set its credit size. A CBFC sending port waits to see the
CBFC receiver cell size, R_CellSize, in the remote LLDP database before selecting its credit size. The
S_CreditSize SHALL be valid when any of the S_VC_RTS[x] flags are TRUE. While any S_VC_RTS[x] flag is
TRUE, the S_CreditSize SHALL NOT change.
5.3.2.2.8 S_PacketOverhead
The 8-bit S_PacketOverhead field identifies the number of overhead bytes per packet at the sending
port. The S_PacketOverhead SHALL be valid when any of the S_VC_RTS[x] flags are TRUE. While any
S_VC_RTS[x] flag is TRUE, the S_PacketOverhead SHALL NOT change.

PAGE 696

696

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.3.2.2.9 S_VC_RTS
The 32-bit S_VC_RTS field contains 32 ready-to-send flags, one for each of the 32 possible VCs. The
S_VC_RTS flag in bit position 0 indicates the VC0 CBFC sender state. When the S_VC_RTS flag is TRUE(1),
the sender is ready to send but SHALL wait to begin until the receiver sets R_VC_RTR=TRUE.
5.3.2.2.10 R_VCnLength
The 4-bit R_VCnLength field specifies the length of each element of the per-VC fields R_VCn. For version
0 the length is 6 bytes. Future versions can increase the length. Version 0 SHALL skip over any bytes
beyond 6 when reading the R_VCn fields.
5.3.2.2.11 R_CellSize
The 12-bit R_CellSize field identifies the number of bytes in a single credit at the receiving port.
5.3.2.2.12 R_PacketOverhead
The 8-bit R_PacketOverhead field identifies the number of overhead bytes at the receiving port.
5.3.2.2.13 R_TotalCredits
The 24-bit R_TotalCredits field identifies the total number of credits, of credit size, available for all VCs
at the receiver.
5.3.2.2.14 R_NumVCs
The 6-bit R_NumVCs field indicates the number of receiver VC configuration subfields (R_VCn) following
in this TLV.
5.3.2.2.15 R_VCn
R_VCn represents R_NumVCs fields, one for each VC the receiver at this port wants to activate or
catalog. Each R_VCn field contains parameters for configuring CBFC for this VC as listed in the following
subclauses.
5.3.2.2.15.1 R_VC_Want
The 1-bit R_VC_Want field indicates if the receiver wants CBFC lossless service for this VC. If TRUE(1),
this port wants CBFC lossless receiver service for this VC on this port. If FALSE(0) this VC is best effort. If
R_VC_Want transitions to FALSE(0), the sender SHALL stop using CBFC credits to qualify transmission of
packets on this VC, set the corresponding S_VC_RTS flag to FALSE(0), and return to best-effort
forwarding.
5.3.2.2.15.2 R_VC_RTR
If the 1-bit R_VC_RTR field is TRUE, this VC receiver is ready. The R_VC_RTR field SHALL NOT be set
TRUE(1) until after a corresponding S_VC_RTS is set TRUE by the remote link partner. If R_VC_RTR
transitions to FALSE(0), the sender SHALL stop using CBFC credits to qualify transmission of packets on
this VC.
5.3.2.2.15.3 R_VcID
The 5-bit R_VcID field indicates the receive VC number configured by the parameters in R_VCn. VC
numbers range from 0 to 31. Implementations are not required to support all 32 possible VCs.

PAGE 697

697

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.3.2.2.15.4 R_PktID_Sel
The 4-bit R_PktID_Sel field indicates the type of identifier for the VC.  Table 5-37 shows the possible
R_PktID_Sel options. This is an optional service that provides assurance that both the CBFC sender and
receiver are configured to count credits on the same packets. If the link partners do not agree on the
packets that belong to each VC, then the credit counts will be incorrect and the link can lose packets
even with CBFC.
Table 5-37 - UE Link Negotiation CBFC TLV R_PktID_Sel Field Options
Value
Meaning
0x0
Disable packet to VC identification matching.
0x1
The R_PcpDei contains a 4-bit PCP/DEI value used by this VC. The R_MaskPcpDei
parameter identifies which R_PcpDei bits are valid.
0x2
The R_DSCP contains a 6-bit DSCP value used to identify this VC. The
R_MaskDSCP parameter identifies which DSCP bits are valid.
0x3
The R_Handle contains a 12-bit stream handle identifying this VC. The handle
identifies a stream handle such as specified in IEEE Std 802.1CBdb-2021 clause 6
[10] .
0x4-0xF
Reserved for future specification by UE.

5.3.2.2.15.5 R_PktID
The R_PktID contains one of three sets of fields that are used to identify the packets to VC mapping. The
type of field is determined by the R_PktID_Sel parameter. The R_PktID information is provided by the
receiver for each receiver VC and can be used by the sender in one of three ways depending on the local
configuration of the sender’s CBFC management agent. The sender MAY:
1) Ignore the packet to VC mapping.
2) Compare the mapping to its own sending VC configuration to verify agreement.
3) Dynamically install the mapping for its sending VC.
If the receiver elects to disable packet-to-VC mapping identification by setting R_PktID_Sel = 0, then the
sender cannot use dynamic packet identification. In the event the receiver disables packet identification
while the sender is configured for dynamic mapping, then the sender disables the VC and reports an
error.
5.3.2.2.15.6 R_MaskPcpDei
Selected if R_PktID_Sel = 1. The 4-bit R_MaskPcpDei field identifies the bits of the L2 PCP/DEI fields that
are valid for identifying this VC. The DEI bit is the least significant bit of the R_MaskPcpDei field.
5.3.2.2.15.7 R_PcpDei
Selected if R_PktID_Sel = 1. The 4-bit R_PcpDei field contains the L2 packet PCP/DEI value after the
R_MaskPcpDei mask is applied identifying this VC. The DEI bit is the least significant bit of the R_PcpDei
field. The set of packets that are members of the VC are those where (PcpDei & R_MaskPcpDei) ==
R_PcpDei is TRUE.
5.3.2.2.15.8 R_MaskDSCP

PAGE 698

698

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Selected if R_PktID_Sel = 2. The 6-bit R_MaskDSCP field identifies the bits of the L3 DSCP field that are
valid for identifying this VC.
5.3.2.2.15.9 R_DSCP
Selected if R_PktID_Sel = 2. The 6-bit R_DSCP field contains the L3 packet DSCP value after the
R_MaskDSCP mask is applied identifying this VC. The set of packets that are members of the VC are
those where (DSCP & R_MaskDSCP) == R_DSCP is TRUE.
5.3.2.2.15.10
R_Handle
Selected if R_PktID_Sel = 3. The 12-bit R_Handle is an opaque handle that can be used as an identifier
for a packet match method. The R_Handle is intended to cover complex packet match cases that can’t
be expressed by a simple mask and match of the PCP, DEI, and DSCP bits. The use of R_Handle requires
pre-arranged values by network management on each side of the link. These pre-arranged R_Handle
lists MUST match on both sides of the link. In some cases, a standard packet match method can be used,
such as stream identification as defined in IEEE Std 802.1CB-2017 [12] and IEEE Std 802.1CBdb-2021
clause 6 [10] . In other cases, the methods can be proprietary. There is no requirement to support any
particular packet match method or identifier list.
5.3.2.2.15.11
R_VC_CreditLimit
The 24-bit R_VC_CreditLimit field identifies the credits available for this VC receiver. A receiver SHALL
NOT set both R_VC_CreditLimit and R_TotalCredits to non-zero values. CBFC operates with either
R_VC_CreditLimit or R_TotalCredits, but not both.
5.3.2.2.15.12
Resv
All reserved fields are sent as 0 and ignored on receive.

This clause specifies the YANG modules that provide control and status monitoring of UE link options.

modeling language as specified in [3] . The YANG framework applies hierarchy by using a uniform
resource name (URN) [8] , a private uniform resource identifier (URI), and the YANG objects that form a
hierarchy.
The YANG structure that incorporates the UE link YANG modules is represented by Figure 5-21. In this
diagram, white boxes are defined by the IETF, gray boxes are defined by the IEEE, and hashed boxes are
defined by the UE. As shown in the diagram, the UE link YANG augments IEEE LLDP management [2] .

5.3.3.2
Security Considerations for UE LLDP Extension YANG Modules
The YANG modules defined in this clause are designed to be accessed via a network configuration
protocol, e.g., NETCONF protocol [5] . In the case of NETCONF, the lowest NETCONF layer is the secure
transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH [6] . The NETCONF access

PAGE 702

702

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
control model [7]  provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF users to a preconfigured
subset of all available NETCONF protocol operations and content.
It is the responsibility of a system’s implementor and administrator to ensure that the protocol entities
in the system that support NETCONF, and any other remote configuration protocols that make use of
these YANG modules, are properly configured to allow access only to those principals (users) that have
legitimate rights to read or write data nodes. This standard does not specify how the credentials of
those users are to be stored or validated.
Several management objects defined in the uec-link-neg-options-tlv and uec-link-
neg-cbfc-tlv YANG modules are configurable (i.e., read-write) and/or operational (i.e., read-only).
Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. A network
configuration protocol such as NETCONF can support protocol operations that can edit or delete YANG
module configuration data (e.g., edit-config, delete-config, copy-config). If this is done in a non-secure
environment without proper protection, it is possible to result in negative effects on the network
operation.
5.3.3.3
Schema for UE LLDP Extension YANG Modules
A simplified graphical representation of the data model is used in this document. The meaning of the
symbols in these diagrams is as follows:
•
Brackets “ ” and “ ” enclose list keys.
•
Abbreviations before data node names: “rw” means configuration (read-write), and “ro” means
state data (read-only).
•
Symbols after data node names: “?” means an optional node, “ ” means a presence container,
and “*” denotes a list and leaf-list.
•
Parentheses enclose choice and case nodes, and case nodes are also marked with a colon (“:”).
•
Ellipsis (“...”) stands for contents of subtrees that are not shown.

5.4 Optimized Headers and Packet Rate Improvement
The standard layering of Ethernet and IPv4/v6 headers emphasizes flexibility for heterogenous inter-
networking environments. Protocol content is separated across multiple functional layers, and features
such as packet fragmentation enable interconnectivity between heterogenous networks. This flexibility
comes at the cost of larger packet overheads.
Many HPC and AI applications generate a significant volume of small messages where the payload is
small relative to packet headers. Examples include applications accessing partitioned memory over
single-hop or multi-hop fabrics. For efficient bandwidth utilization and high goodput, it is desirable that
the interconnect overhead also be small.
Special-purpose network fabrics optimize for this requirement by making assumptions about a
homogenous environment, reducing flexibility, simplifying the information carried with a packet, and
improving encoding over a link by reducing inter-packet gaps. Such techniques can also be applied to an
Ethernet-based high-performance interconnect to improve bandwidth efficiency and packet rates.
The current Ethernet and IPv4/v6 header stacks are deeply entrenched, with a rich and diverse
ecosystem of tools and silicon built around them. Completely redefining the headers is not practical.
Instead, an approach that superimposes information on existing headers is more likely to find
acceptance, especially if it enables coexistence with standard Ethernet silicon, tools, and operational
practices.
This specification defines an optimized header format called the Unified Forwarding Header (UFH) to
supplement the common combination of Ethernet MAC and IP headers. The optimization involves:
•
Removing redundancies across the MAC and IP headers.
•
Eliminating header fields generally not required in a homogenous, well-controlled fabric.
•
Retaining features that allow UFH and standard Ethernet + IP frames to coexist on a link.
•
Retaining features that enable extensibility, a key advantage of Ethernet.
UFH is intended for applications in well-contained network domains and is not intended to be a generic
replacement for the Ethernet + IP stack. The UFH format defines two variations to match the slightly
divergent needs of scale-up and scale-out fabrics. See Section 5.4.4.
This specification does not define any new control protocols. Coexistence of UFH and standard Ethernet
frames on a link enables the use of standard Ethernet and IP protocols such as LLDP, ICMP, or DHCP to
bootstrap and manage endpoints in a network.
5.4.1
Requirements and Considerations
The UFH definition aligns with the following requirements and considerations:
•
UFH frames MUST coexist with standard Ethernet frames on a link. This is essential to leveraging
the benefits of the Ethernet ecosystem and in accelerating UFH adoption. This implies no
changes below the Ethernet MAC layer.

PAGE 717

717

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
UFH usage is optional, and an initiator SHOULD use it only for data flows that benefit from
improved wire efficiency and throughput. Applications that do not benefit from an optimized
header can continue to use standard Ethernet and IP formats. (e.g., LLDP, ARP, DHCP)
•
Ethernet enables feature extensibility by stacking tags such as VLAN, MACSEC, and CSIG. The
UFH definition MUST support header stacking.
•
UFH MUST be compatible with LLR (link level retry) and CBFC (credit-based flow control) but not
depend on them.
•
UFH addressing MUST support scale-out fabrics with at least 256 k endpoints with a stretch goal
of 1 M+ endpoints.
•
UFH source and destination address fields should not assume a specific address family even if IP
addressing is likely to be the de facto standard. Deployments should have the freedom to map
different address namespaces to UFH address fields, such as IB LIDs or device IDs, to enable
migration of different solutions to Ethernet using UFH.
•
The UFH definition SHOULD support stateless translation to standard Ethernet + IP headers,
when addresses are interpreted as IPv4 or IPv6. Network elements such as gateway switches
MAY optionally enable such a capability.
The following are non-goals:
•
Ethernet limits minimum frame size to 64 B. UFH does not modify this limit.
•
Ethernet IPG and preamble reduction are outside the scope of the UFH specification.
•
Extending existing control protocols such as DHCP or ARP to add UFH awareness is not in scope.
•
It is expected that while many existing Ethernet switches will have the flexibility to forward UFH
packets, compatibility with standard 802.1 Ethernet bridges is not a goal.
5.4.2
Header Optimization Approach
Large-scale Ethernet fabrics are commonly designed as IPv4/v6 routed topologies. The Ethernet MAC
has link-local significance, and the DA and SA fields are swapped at each hop. This creates an addressing
redundancy that can be removed by collapsing to one address space. A review of the IPv4 and IPv6
headers suggests other optimization possibilities. Fragmentation can be avoided in homogenous fabrics
and length, and header checksum fields can be removed by relying on link capabilities such as Forward
Error Correction (FEC), link level retry (LLR), or end-to-end transport checksums such as an ICRC.
 summarizes optimizations for single- and multi-hop fabrics.

5.4.3
UFH Definition
The UFH is defined as an overlay on the 12-byte Ethernet MAC header with special encodings in the
MAC DA and MAC SA fields. Fields identified as essential to UFH are overlaid on this 12-byte base
header, and UFH defines two sub-variants to cover different needs. The Ethernet rule of inserting an
EtherType field at offset 12 from the start of frame is followed to maintain backward compatibility and
to allow UFH and standard Ethernet + IP frames to coexist on a link. This EtherType identifies the next
header in the stack and is not essential for UFH itself.
The IEEE Std 802-2024 specification [2] defines a Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) to support
allocation of local addresses. This specification reserves 4 bits in the MAC address for identification,

Figure 5-24 - UFH Header Overlay












PAGE 719

719

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
identified as ZYXM in Figure 5-25. The X and M bits are the well-known local address and multicast bits
in the MAC header; the ZY bits are new per SLAP. To identify UFH:
•
The Z and Y bits are set to 00 indicating an Administratively Assigned Identifier (AAI)18.
•
The X bit is set to 1 indicating local assignment.
•
The M bit is retained to indicate a multicast frame.
This UFH specification further defines the upper 4 bits of the DA for additional UFH specific flags.
•
The V bit identifies UFH version, with V = 0 indicating the current version.
•
The W bit is interpreted in the context of V = 0.
o W = 0 -> Normal format with broad applicability (32-bit address container, hop-limit).
o W = 1 -> Compressed format for efficiency (16-bit address container).
•
The RR bits are reserved and currently set to 00.
Per this spec, a transmitter generating a UFH frame MUST set V to 0, and a receiver must verify the V
and W bits to process the frame. V = 1 is available for a future version.
UFH uses the IEEE SLAP AAI encoding as it gives the administrator of a local domain the freedom to
define the address structure and reclaim 44 bits from the DA and 44 bits from the SA. The intent behind
the Extended Local Identifier (ELI) and Standard Assigned Identifier (SAI) encodings is to share local
address space across companies or standards, and the bits used to encode this (CID for ELI, undefined
for SAI) will result in fewer available bits and lower efficiency.
The IEEE Std 802-2024 specification does not define a mechanism for different applications to
simultaneously use AAI-encoded addresses within a network. This need is not anticipated, but if
required, it is possible to use the RR bits for disambiguation.
UFH should be viewed as a distinct header format with its own address space and forwarding semantics
as described later in Section 5.4.6. Network devices identify it by matching the flags byte.



18 Alternative encodings are possible if approved by the IEEE.

5.4.4
UFH Variants
UFH defines two variants to address the opposing needs of efficiency and broad capability: UFH_32 and
UFH_16. As shown in Figure 5-26, UFH_32 reserves 32 bits for addresses, 8 bits for a traffic class, and
4 bits for a hop-limit, making it better suited for multi-hop topologies. UFH_16 reserves 16 bits for
addresses and 8 bits for a traffic class, making it better suited for single-hop topologies.
The traffic class field is in the same location in both formats. This covers 6 bits for a DSCP codepoint and
2 bits for the ECN field aligned with IPv4/IPv6 usage and format. The same encodings and namespace
SHOULD be retained to enable stateless translation between UFH and IP and to simplify processing in
switches.
The UFH_32 format has 8 bits of opaque space while the UFH_16 format has 44 bits. These “opaque”
bits can be overlaid with any end-to-end data, and switches MUST ignore them when forwarding
packets.

5.4.5
UFH and Header Stacking
UFH retains the use of the EtherType field to identify the next header in the header stack and extend the
information carried with a packet. For example, VLAN tags can be used to partition a network domain
for multi-tenancy, MACSEC tags can add link security, and CSIG tags can carry telemetry for congestion
control or diagnostics. Figure 5-27 shows different tag stacking examples.
The ordering of tags in the header stack MUST follow Ethernet ordering rules. For example, a VLAN tag if
present MUST be the first tag on a frame at offset 12.
Because UFH subsumes the traditional network layer, there is no additional IP header, and tags are
followed by an L4 transport header. UFH is designed to be used with UDP, UET, and future transports.
New EtherType encodings are required to identify them.

Figure 5-27 - UFH Coexistence and Extensibility

PAGE 723

723

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.4.6
UFH Termination and Forwarding
UFH packets appear as legal L2 frames on the wire but cannot be forwarded by standard Ethernet
bridges as defined in IEEE 802.1. A UFH-capable switch needs to mask out non-address portions of the
DA and SA when implementing forwarding behaviors and support additional capabilities defined by the
UFH header. A conceptual view of a UFH endpoint and switch is shown in Figure 5-28.
The MAC layer at an endpoint identifies received UFH packets and forwards them to an upper layer
through a “MAC Service Access Point.” The upper layer validates and terminates UFH packets addressed
to the endpoint and passes them to the transport protocol identified in the header stack.
Packets addressed to other endpoints are directed to a UFH switch that implements UFH-specific
forwarding functions. The forwarding function looks up the UFH destination address to identify an
egress interface, maps the encoded COS to a queue, and applies ECN and hop-limit updates analogous
to those applied by an IP router. The forwarding function must ignore any opaque fields and reserved
flags in the header.
UFH defines 32-bit and 16-bit address container variants to support different deployment needs. These
header variants are known as UFH_32 and UFH_16 respectively. While use of IP addresses is preferred
with the 32-bit address variant, this specification intentionally does not mandate the use of a specific
address family with either variant. The address fields are viewed as “containers” to which an
implementation can map a suitable address namespace and conform to its forwarding rules. This
flexibility is to help bespoke HPC and scale-up fabrics migrate to Ethernet.
The address namespace used by an implementation might need fewer than 32 or 16 address bits, and
the addresses must be LSB-aligned within an address container. UFH endpoints and switches MUST be
configured to ignore unused upper bits of a container when using the address for any function. For

Figure 5-28 - Conceptual Layering of UFH

example, a scale-up fabric mapping a 10-bit device ID to a 16-bit address container must place it in the
lower 10 bits, and endpoints and switches must mask out the upper 6 bits when using the address
container.
The UFH forwarding function behaves analogously to an IP router for implementations mapping a 32-bit
IPv4 or 128-bit IPv6 address to the address containers. The UFH address containers carry the lower 32
bits or 16 bits of the address, with the upper bits configured consistently with a subnet prefix at every
endpoint and switch within a UFH domain (see 5.4.11).
The UFH format retains the ability to mark a frame as multicast via the M bit, and its usage should be in
accordance with the needs of the mapped address space. If the mapped address space is IP and the
destination is a multicast or broadcast address, the M bit SHOULD be set to 1. A UFH switch can
interpret the destination is multicast using either the M bit or the IP address type.
Hop-limit processing for UFH follows the same rules as IPv6 as defined in RFC 8200. Senders initialize the
hop-limit to a non-zero value in the range 1–15. Transit switches verify the incoming hop-limit,
forwarding packets if it is greater than 1 and dropping them if it is 0 or 1 and the switch is not the
destination for the packet. Destinations (endpoints or switches) accept all hop-limits including 0. ICMP
generation on hop-limit expiry is possible if a deployment maps an IP address namespace to UFH.
The ECN field is interpreted and marked per the rules for IP packets as described in RFC 3168.
This UFH specification does not define a UFH learning function or a spanning tree analog. The source
address within a UFH packet plays no direct part in forwarding; it can be optionally used by an UFH
switch for load balancing and by upper layers to track connection partners.
5.4.7
UFH and Queue Assignment
In a routed IP network, the DSCP field serves to assign the traffic class and queue assignments. The DSCP
field in UFH is expected to serve the same purpose.
When UFH packets are used with VLANs, there is an option to use the VLAN PRI field for traffic class and
queue assignment. In such cases, network configuration will determine the preference given for either.
This is no different than usage of IP over Ethernet VLANs.
5.4.8
UFH and Packet Trimming
UFH packets dropped due to congestion may be “trimmed” and sent as drop notifications to a receiver.
The UFH DSCP code point MUST be updated in accordance with the UE Packet Trimming specification
(see Section 4.1).
5.4.9
UFH and VLANs
VLANs are commonly used to isolate endpoints in an Ethernet network, and they can serve the same
function when used in conjunction with UFH. In a multi-tenant UFH environment, tenant identification
can be encoded in VLANs and isolation enforced in the switches through either VLAN filtering or VRF
assignment.

PAGE 725

725

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.4.10 UFH and Transport Layer Checksums
Transport protocols such as TCP/IP and UDP/IP include a checksum field whose calculation covers the
payload, the transport header, and select fields from the IP header represented by a pseudo-IP header.
The pseudo-IP header includes the source and destination IP addresses, the IP protocol used to identify
the transport, and the transport length (header + payload).
This method of checksum calculation and verification remains unchanged when such transports are
carried over UFH. The initiator and receiver assume the packet is carried over IP and create a suitable
pseudo-IP header based on the source and destination UFH address containers, the IP protocol number
assigned to the transport, and the length from the transport header.
All endpoints in a UFH domain (see next section) must be configured to consistently use the IPv4 or IPv6
pseudo-header. The UFH address containers are masked and then expanded to the necessary length by
adding a suitable address prefix. The prefix can be one that is assigned to the UFH domain and can be
set to all zeros if there is no intent to use the full address for any function other than checksum
calculation.
Example
•
Suppose a UFH-_32 format contains a non-IP 24-bit address “00.aa.bb.cc”.
•
The desire is to map it to an IPv6 pseudo-header for checksum calculations.
•
Suppose the UFH domain is assigned the IPv6 prefix “XX:YY:  ”.
•
Then the generated address for checksum calculation is “XX:YY:  ::0:aa:bb:cc”.
This approach simplifies protocol migration to UFH and will additionally support stateless translation to
Ethernet + IP at gateway switches if required.
A sender MAY set the transport header checksum to zero for the special case of UDP over IPv4 and it
MUST be ignored by a receiver.
5.4.11 UFH Deployment Considerations
For simplicity of deployment, it is assumed that all endpoints and switches within a UFH domain can
support UFH and can communicate with each other using UFH on ALL network paths. UFH usage within
the domain MUST be explicitly enabled using a suitable administrative approach.
If a UFH domain is a standalone cluster with no external connectivity, a sender’s decision to use UFH will
be based primarily on the needs of an application. In more complex deployments, a UFH domain may be
a local island within a larger network. Devices and paths within the island are UFH-capable, but
destinations outside the domain are either not capable or not reachable via a UFH-capable path. A
sender’s decision to use UFH will depend on both the application and on the relative locations of the
sender and destination.
In theory, it is possible to carry UFH packets from one UFH domain to another by translating them to
Ethernet + IP at gateway switches or by encapsulating them in tunnels that support L2 payloads, such as

PAGE 726

726

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
VxLAN and SRv6. These applications are possible as a side effect of retaining the Ethernet MAC
structure, and the capability may be useful in special scenarios.
This specification does not describe any methods to ascertain if a sender can use UFH to communicate
with a destination. Methods for assigning UFH addresses to endpoints or distributing routes within a
domain are also outside the scope of this specification.

5.4.12 UFH Efficiency Calculations
Packet efficiency for different header permutations is calculated using the equation below:
𝐸=
𝑃𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑 𝑆𝑖𝑧𝑒
𝑃𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑 𝑆𝑖𝑧𝑒+ 𝐻𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑒𝑟 𝑂𝑣𝑒𝑟ℎ𝑒𝑎𝑑
The header overhead adds all L2, L3, and L4 headers, with IPG and preamble ignored for simplicity.
Opaque fields are not included in the overhead. A common transport size is assumed for all, and the
resulting efficiency numbers in tabular and chart form are as below. For small payloads and compressed
headers, the minimum Ethernet frame size is 64 B.

5.5 Idle Reduction
This standard specifies an optional feature that reduces the number of idle bytes inserted between
frames. The goal of this feature is to improve payload efficiency for small frames and increase the packet
rate.
A standard UDP Ethernet frame contains 18 bytes for the Ethernet header and CRC, 20 bytes for the IPv4
header, and 8 bytes of UDP header. With an 8-byte preamble and 12 bytes of inter-packet gap (IPG),
there are already 66 bytes of overhead before accounting for the transport header(s). Each of these
headers can potentially be reduced in size, increasing transmission efficiency for small payloads.
The idle reduction feature focuses on reducing the average of 12 idle bytes that are required by the
standard (as introduced in IEEE Std 802.3-2022 Clause 46.3.1.4). At the latest link speeds specified in
IEEE Std 802.3, frames start on an 8-byte boundary, so the number of idles bytes cannot always be
exactly 12. Instead, a deficit idle count tracks idle bytes across a stream of frames and ensures the short-
term average is at least 12 bytes. Ignoring upper-level protocols, the minimal Ethernet packet of 64
bytes requires 8 bytes of preamble and at least one byte for inter-packet gap (for the terminate block).
With the restriction of starting frames on an 8-byte boundary, the minimum number of bytes on the
wire is 80. The 12-byte average IPG requirement will cause some minimum frames to be further padded
to 88 bytes on the wire, so that the average comes to at least 12 bytes of idle between packets.
To improve this design, this specification removes the 12-byte requirement while retaining the
requirement to start frames on an 8-byte boundary. Maintaining this boundary reduces the impact of
supporting idle reduction. For minimum-sized frames, this change reduces the wire usage to 80 bytes
and eliminates the occasional need to pad to 88 bytes to achieve the target idle count. Furthermore, the
frame size can now increase by up to 7 bytes (within the terminate block) while still maintaining the 80-
byte wire usage.
5.5.1
Approach
This specification defines a reduction of the per-frame overhead, to increase the efficiency of small size
frames. In IEEE Std 802.3 high-speed links, 12 bytes of idle are required. This is an average requirement,
since idles on these links are added in blocks of eight bytes. While this is less significant for large frames,
it is significant for minimum-sized frames. This optional feature allows most of these idle bytes to be
omitted.
When this feature is supported and enabled, an average of 12 bytes of idle is no longer required. A
terminate block (with up to 7 data bytes) MUST be included and MUST be sized to ensure 8-byte
alignment. With modern network architectures, incoming link data is typically retimed to a core clock
that runs faster than the fastest legal line rate. With this structure, issues transitioning from a fast clock
to a slow clock do not immediately cause clock-domain-crossing FIFO problems. While the standard
inter-frame gap is less significant for large packets, it wastes bandwidth when there is a large fraction of
short packets.

PAGE 729

729

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
5.5.2
Rate Control
Per the standard, link speeds may deviate from nominal by +/- 50 ppm. When a fast sender sends traffic
to a slow receiver, overrun has to be considered. The standard IPG of 12 bytes allows the receiver some
slack to retime the incoming data to its slower clock by eliding some idle bytes. Rather than imposing
the idle overhead per packet, this feature requires internal flow control in the link logic to provide any
necessary compensation.
Modern high-performance Ethernet devices often have a core clock that runs faster than even the
fastest legal incoming data rate. Such a clock allows incoming data to transit through a clock domain
crossing FIFO without needing to drop any bytes. In this environment, the egress path requires flow
control; otherwise, the higher-speed core would overrun the output link.
Besides clock rate issues, forming the proper Ethernet stream on the wire requires inserting control
data, such as alignment markers. These markers are infrequent and are properly inserted in the data
stream without data loss.
5.5.3
Maximum Packet Rate
With standard idle formatting, the minimum spacing from one frame start to the next frame start
averages at least 84 bytes. Because of the 8-byte boundary requirement, the actual spacing might toggle
between 80 bytes and 88 bytes. With a 100 GB/s Ethernet link, the frame rate could average as fast as
1.19 G frames/sec. With idle reduction, the 80-byte spacing may be constantly achieved, potentially
saving an average of 4 bytes per packet. This raises the peak frame rate possible to 1.25 G frames/sec,
realizing the maximum possible benefit from idle reduction.
5.5.4
Requirements
Devices supporting the idle reduction feature SHOULD report this capability to the management
software. To ensure seamless interoperability, any link advertising support MUST be capable of receiving
and processing frames with the idle reduction defined by this feature, regardless of whether the feature
is currently enabled. The enabled capability specifically controls the transmission logic, determining
whether the MAC will actively insert reduced-width idle counts during outgoing data streams.
5.5.5
Enabling Idle Reduction
The idle reduction enhancement is optional. Cost-optimized devices might not easily support idle
reduction due to their internal architecture. Further, idle reduction on some but not all links in a
heterogeneous network could easily be a source of congestion. Consequently, management software
may elect not to enable this feature on links that support it, in order to prevent congestion in a network
that also contain links without this capability.
To accommodate these limitations, each link SHOULD advertise whether it supports this feature. Using
UE link negotiation, capable devices SHOULD advertise IPGR-C (inter-packet gap reduction “capable”).
Management software MAY determine, after interrogating each end of all links, to enable this feature.
Once enabled, links will no longer be required to ensure that the standard number of idle bytes are
transmitted.

PAGE 730

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
6 UE Physical Layer
Ultra Ethernet (UE) applications, such as AI and HPC systems, require physical layers that support a
variety of electrical and optical channels; provide low frame loss ratio, low latency, power efficiency, and
reliability at scale; and leverage existing ecosystems and standards that enable seamless
interoperability.
Informative Text:
The UE Physical Layer specification strives to maintain consistency with terminology defined by IEEE
Std 802.3. However, the 802.3 definition of the term “packet” is inconsistent with other portions of
the UE specification. When used in this Physical Layer specification, the 802.3 term “packet” is
replaced with “802.3 packet.”

6.1 UE PHY Support
UE PHYs include a subset of Ethernet PHYs with 100 Gb/s  or 200 Gb/s per lane signaling, defined in IEEE
Std 802.3™-2022 [1], IEEE Std 802.3db™ 2022 [2], IEEE Std 802.3ck™ 2022 [3], IEEE Std 802.3df™ 2024
[4], and P802.3dj [5] (henceforth referred to collectively as the Ethernet standard).
A device compliant with the UE PHY specifications SHALL conform to one of the specifications of PHY
types listed in either 6.1.1.2or 6.1.2.2.
Informative Text:
Other Ethernet PHYs may be able to support some of the UE specifications but are not considered
compliant with the UE specification.

6.2 Control ordered sets
UE control ordered sets are an OPTIONAL UE feature. A PHY that supports this feature SHALL comply
with the requirements in this section.
The control ordered set (CtlOS) is a message mechanism utilized by the UE link layer features credit-
based flow control (CBFC) and link layer retry (LLR). The general format is extensible to future link-level
features as well. It is an 8-byte message encoded as an ordered set in the 64B/66B PCS encoding with an
O code value to distinguish it from standard Ethernet sequence ordered sets.
6.2.1
Sequence ordered sets and control ordered set background
Sequence ordered sets, as defined in IEEE Std 802.3-2022 [1] clause 81, are encoded 8-byte messages
that interrupt 802.3 packet transmission with critical link fault status. Three sequence ordered sets are
defined: Local Fault, Remote Fault, and Link Interruption. Each sequence ordered set has a defined MII
format and a generic 64B/66B PCS translation, as summarized in Table 6-2. See [1], subclause 81.3.2.2,
Table 81-4 “Permissible lane encodings of RXD and RXC” and subclause 81.3.4, Table 81-5 “Sequence
ordered sets” as well as subclause 82.2.3.3, Figure 82-5 “64B/66B block format”.

The sync field (bits 0:1) and block type field (bits 2:9) are transmitted as 10_11010010, where the
leftmost bit is transmitted first19. Starting with bits 10:17, each remaining byte is transmitted, starting
with its least significant bit.
In the PCS decoder, MII D1 through D7 are taken from bits 10 to 65, while the control character (MII D0)
is decoded from the O code in bits 34:37. For an O code value 0x0, MII D0 is set to 0x9C. For an O code
value 0x6, MII D0 is set to 0x5C.
The Ethernet standard’s state-based PCS encoder and decoder discard any non-data blocks that occur
between the Start and Terminate blocks of an 802.3 packet. However, CtlOS are allowed to preempt
regular 802.3 packet transmission and can occur at any point in the sequence of MII blocks.
In order to support 802.3 packet preemption, the following requirements apply to the PCS 64B/66B
encoder and decoder:
6.2.3.1
PCS 64B/66B Decoder
For 200GBASE-R or 400GBASE-R PHYs using the PCS defined in Clause 119 of [1], 800GBASE-R PHYs using
the PCS defined in clause 172 of [4], and 1.6TBASE-R PHYs using the PCS defined in clause 175 of [5], the
PCS SHALL use the stateless 64B/66B decoder specified in subclause 119.2.5.8.2 of [5], with the
corresponding requirements from the Reed-Solomon decoder in subclause 119.2.5.3 of [5].
For 100GBASE-R PHYs, which use the PCS defined in Clause 82 of [1], the following requirements apply.
The sublayer below the 100GBASE-R PCS is either RS-FEC (as defined in Clause 91 of [1]) or RS-FEC-Int (as
defined in Clause 161 of  3 ). The term “FEC” is used to refer to either of these sublayers. The specified
behavior of the FEC includes marking of received codewords that are uncorrectable by altering the sync
headers of certain 66-bit blocks within the codewords (as specified in 91.5.3.3 of [1] and in 161.5.3.3 of
[3]). This is different from the specification of the Reed-Solomon decoder within the PCS in 119.2.5.3 of
[1], where the whole content of a received uncorrectable codeword is replaced with error blocks
(EBLOCK_R).
In a PCS implementation that is integrated with the FEC, the combined PCS+FEC can perform error
marking by setting every 66-bit block within an uncorrected codeword (when Clause 91 RS-FEC is used)
or two associated uncorrected codewords (when Clause 161 RS-FEC-Int is used) to an error block, as
done in the Clause 11  PCS. This behavior is referred to within this specification as “FEC error overwrite
marking.”
Informative Text:
The FEC error overwrite marking behavior may seem to deviate from the RS-FEC and RS-FEC-Int
specifications. However, if the interface between FEC and the PCS is not observable, then this
behavior is indistinguishable from the specified one. This is considered a valid implementation choice.

6.2.3.2
PCS 64B/66B Encoder
The following requirements apply in all supported data rates.The PCS encoder SHALL use the stateless
encoder as specified in subclause 119.2.4.1.2 of [5], rather than the state-diagram PCS encoder (defined
by Figure 82–16 or Figure 119–14 of [1]).
Informative Text:
The stateless encoder assumes that the block type sequence that the MAC generates is valid, and thus
the PCS encodes the blocks as they arrive with no further checking.
6.2.4
RS required modifications
Support of CtlOS requires several enhancements to the reconciliation sublayer (RS) specified in the
Ethernet standard.
When the MAC sublayer requests transmission of a CtlOS, the RS indicates a CtlOS on the MII,
corresponding to the RS transmission of TXD<63:0> and TXC<7:0>. Otherwise (when not a CtlOS), the RS
requests transmission of 64 data bits by the PHY as described in [1], subclause 81.1.7.1.4.
When the RS detects a valid CtlOS on the MII, corresponding to the RS reception of RXD<63:0> and
RXC<7:0>, the RS sends an indication to the MAC sublayer. Otherwise (when not a CtlOS), the RS maps
the MII signals to PLS_DATA.indication as described in [1], subclause 81.1.7.2.
6.2.4.1
MII transmit functional specifications
The transmit RS is permitted to send a CtlOS (composed of the CtlOS control character and subsequent
seven data octets) anywhere in the MII data stream, subject to the restriction that the CtlOS control
character is aligned to lane 0 on the transmit MII. See [1], subclause 81.2 for details on the MII data
stream.

PAGE 736

736

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Insertion of a CtlOS anywhere in the MII data stream SHALL NOT corrupt any 802.3 packet transfers,
regardless of whether the CtlOS interrupts 802.3 packet transmission or falls outside 802.3 packet
boundaries.
The presence of a CtlOS SHALL NOT impact the Deficit Idle Count (DIC) of the transmit RS. See [1],
subclause 81.3.1.4 for details on DIC.
6.2.4.2
MII receive functional specifications
The receive RS SHALL consider a CtlOS (composed of the CtlOS control character and subsequent seven
data octets) arriving in lane 0 on the receive MII as a permissible lane encoding (see [1], subclause
81.3.2.2, Table 81-4).
A valid receive CtlOS SHALL have no impact on the RS DATA_VALID_STATUS parameter.
For setting DATA_VALID_STATUS to DATA_VALID (see [1], subclause 81.1.7.5.3), the RS SHALL skip over
(not consider) a CtlOS immediately preceding the reception of a Start control character on lane 0. The
RXC<7:0> and RXD<63:0> preceding the CtlOS are used to determine whether DATA_VALID_STATUS is
set to DATA_VALID upon reception of a Start control character on lane 0.
Table 6-6 - RS Layer CtlOS spacing constraints
Parameter
Value (bits)
RS_CTLOS_MIN_RX_SPACING
2048

For setting DATA_VALID_STATUS to DATA_NOT_VALID (see [1], subclause 81.1.7.5.3), the RS SHALL skip
over (not consider) a single occurrence of a CtlOS (not cause DATA_VALID_STATUS to assume the value
of DATA_NOT_VALID). Occurrence of multiple CtlOS within a window of RS_CTLOS_MIN_RX_SPACING
MII data bits (see Table 6-6) is considered an error, and the RS may set DATA_VALID_STATUS to
DATA_NOT_VALID upon reception of a second (and any subsequent) CtlOS received within that window
of bits. It is also permissible for the RS to ignore (not cause DATA_VALID_STATUS to assume the value of
DATA_NOT_VALID) multiple CtlOS received within that window.
6.2.4.3
Link fault signaling
When the RS variable link_fault status indicates Local Fault or Remote Fault, the RS does not send CtlOS
on the MII. During that time (as described in [1], subclause 81.3.4), the RS sends either Remote Fault (in
response to link_fault status of Local Fault) or Idle (in response to link_fault status of Remote Fault).
When the link_fault status is set to OK, the transmit RS may send CtlOS on the MII.
6.3 FEC statistics for prediction of link quality
FEC statistics for prediction of link quality is an OPTIONAL UE feature. A PHY that supports this feature
SHALL comply with the requirements in this section.

PAGE 737

737

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Ethernet specifies the link quality in terms of frame loss ratio (FLR). FLR is defined at the MAC/PLS
service interface and is measurable in the MAC. An example of FLR requirements can be found in
subclause 167.1.1 of IEEE Std 802.3db-2022 [2] and its amendment in IEEE Std 802.3df-2024 [4].
For a 100 Gb/s Ethernet Physical Layer, the required FLR is less than 6.2e-10 (equivalent to BER of 1e-12
for a link that has no error correction and randomly occurring errors). For 200, 400, and 800 Gb/s, and
for 1.6 Tb/s Ethernet Physical Layers, the required FLR for 64-octet frames with minimum interpacket
gap is less than 6.2e-11 (equivalent to BER below 1e-13 for a link that has no error correction and
randomly occurring errors).
Informative Text:
Although not written explicitly in the IEEE Std 802.3 PHY specifications, it is generally expected that
the actual FLR in most network links is several orders of magnitude lower than the values above. This
is especially true for large networks typical of UE applications. The maximum FLR that is acceptable is
application dependent. This specification is intended to help in defining and verifying FLR
requirements. Some examples are provided in 6.3.3.

For Ethernet types supported by UE (see Section 6.1), the link is always protected by Reed-Solomon
forward error correction (RS-FEC) code, denoted RS(544,514). Three variations of RS-FEC using the
RS(544,514) code are defined in clauses 91, 119, and 161 of the Ethernet standard.
Measuring FLR is impossible in the PHY and is not always practical at the MAC. Additionally, the required
measurement times depend on link utilization level, which may be unknown. However, the FLR
requirements of Ethernet types supported by UE can be translated to an uncorrectable codeword ratio
(UCR), which is independent of traffic and measurable at the PHY level. The relationship between UCR
and FLR is described in 6.3.1.1.
The effect of UCR on application performance in a large network is easier to comprehend by converting
it to a metric in units of time, the mean time between PHY errors (MTBPE). In this context, a PHY error is
an event of an uncorrectable RS-FEC codeword, which can cause one or more consecutive MAC frames
to be discarded.
Informative Text:
MTBPE is unrelated to the mean time to false 802.3 packet acceptance (MTTFPA). In a compliant
Ethernet link, the probability of having an uncorrectable RS-FEC codeword that is not detected as
such is extremely small, and the probability of false 802.3 packet acceptance is even smaller. As a
result, the MTTFPA for a single link that meets the FLR requirements is many billions of years.

The worst-case MTBPE for a single link that meets the FLR requirements is different across Ethernet link
rates due to the different RS-FEC interleaving schemes and FLR specifications. The resulting MTBPE
values are summarized in Table 6-7. The calculation of MTBPE is based on the relationship between
performance metrics described in 6.3.1.

6.3.1
Relationship between performance metrics
6.3.1.1
Relationship between UCR and FLR
UCR can be considered a fundamental quality metric of an Ethernet link. It is a function of lower-level
metrics that are not observable and thus are beyond the scope of this specification.
Ethernet uses RS-FEC with a technique called codeword interleaving, in which traffic can be spread
across multiple codewords that are interleaved in time. The number of codewords interleaved together
is referred to as the codeword interleaving ratio (CIR) and is either 4, 2, or 1, where 1 is equivalent to no
interleaving. A higher CIR generally improves the RS-FEC’s ability to handle correlated errors and
reduces the link UCR while increasing the FLR for a given value of UCR.
Informative Text:
The reduction of UCR due to the increased CIR can be orders of magnitude. In comparison, the
increase of FLR for a given UCR is up to a factor of 4, so the net effect is beneficial.

Codeword interleaving varies between data rates and PHY types:
•
For 100 Gb/s Ethernet, 2-way interleaving (CIR=2) is defined as OPTIONAL for backplane and
copper cable PHYs (100GBASE-KR1 and 100GBASE-CR1). If this option is not selected, then
CIR=1. For all other PHY types (specifically optical PHYs), interleaving is not available (CIR=1).
•
For 200 Gb/s and 400 Gb/s Ethernet, 2-way interleaving (CIR=2) is used for PHY types using
up to 100 Gb/s signaling, and 4-way interleaving (CIR=4) is used for PHY types using 200 Gb/s
per lane signaling.
•
For 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s Ethernet, 4-way interleaving (CIR=4) is used for all PHY types.

PAGE 739

739

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
A single RS-FEC codeword has a payload of 5140 bits, corresponding to 80 PCS blocks or 640 octets (as
observed at the MII interface). A block of codewords that are interleaved together is referred to as a
codeword group (CG).
The default behavior of Ethernet RS-FEC is that an uncorrectable codeword causes all data in the CG that
this codeword is in to be marked as error by the PCS and discarded. As a result, any MAC frame fully or
partially included in a CG that includes an uncorrectable codeword will not be delivered to the MAC and
will be lost.
The Ethernet FLR requirements are stated for 64-octet frames with minimum interpacket gap (IPG),
which creates 84 octets in total per frame (including IPG and preamble). This condition (maximum
utilization with smallest frames) results in up to 8 frames per codeword (FPC), which is the maximum
possible number. Due to possible misalignment of frame and codeword boundaries, the maximum
number of frames that can be lost due to a single codeword error is 𝐶𝐼𝑅⋅𝐹𝑃𝐶+ 1.
Informative Text:
The maximum number of frames that can be lost due to a single codeword error is not necessarily
dependent on link utilization, since frames with minimum IPG can occur even with low utilization.

Table 6-8 shows the size of a CG in octets and the maximum number of frames that can be lost due to a
single uncorrectable codeword as a function of the CIR.

Error marking in the PCS may optionally be bypassed, and in that case, error detection is only
performed by the MAC using CRC. When this option is enabled, it is possible that some frames in an
uncorrectable codeword will reach the MAC without error, and the frame loss ratio will be somewhat
lower. The FLR analysis above is valid for the case where error marking is not bypassed.

6.3.1.2
Relationship between UCR and MTBPE
Unlike the relationship between UCR and FLR described in 6.3.1.1, which is dependent on many factors,
the relationship between UCR and MTBPE is simple. For each Ethernet data rate, MTBPE on a single link
is a deterministic function of the UCR on that link, which can be estimated from FEC statistics as
described in 6.3.2.
The number of codewords in a given period of time can be calculated from the period of a single
codeword (5440 bits), denoted TCW. Table 6-10 lists the value of TCW for different Ethernet rates.

Informative Text:
It is sometimes suggested that in a network comprising N Ethernet links of the same data rate, the
UCR of a single link should be multiplied by N or, equivalently, MTBPE should be divided by N.
However, this scaling assumes that all links have the same UCR. In large networks, it is often the case
that the UCR of most links is very low, but some links have much higher UCRs than the average.
Consequently, it can be expected that the MTBPE on the network depends on the UCR of good links
multiplied by N and on the UCR of a small number of the weakest links. The examples in 6.3.3
demonstrate this dependence. This provides motivation for identifying the weakest links in the
network (which can be done through the methods described in 6.3.2) and taking appropriate
measures suitable for the application, e.g., routing traffic away from such links or scheduling
replacement of parts.

6.3.2
Estimation of UCR from FEC statistics
Ethernet specifications include several RS-FEC counters that can be used to estimate the probability of
an RS-FEC codeword to be uncorrectable and thus provide an estimate of the UCR. From the UCR, the
MTBPE can be calculated by multiplication with the period of a single codeword.
The following counters are defined for Ethernet BASE-R PHY types that include RS-FEC functionality and
are mapped to MDIO registers. All registers are defined as clear-on-read and non-rollover.
Implementation of these counters and registers, and the method of accessing them, may depend on PCS
implementation.
•
FEC_uncorrected_cw_counter (see [1], subclause 45.2.3.63) is a 32-bit counter that counts once
for each codeword that contains errors that were not corrected (i.e., contains more than t
symbol errors, where t=15 for the RS(544,514) FEC).
•
FEC_corrected_cw_counter (see [1], subclause 45.2.3.62) is a 32-bit counter that counts once for
each codeword that contains errors that were corrected (i.e., contains between 1 and t symbol
errors).
•
FEC_cw_counter (see [3], subclause 45.2.1.120a) is a 48-bit counter once for each FEC
codeword received. Note that this counter is defined as optional in the Ethernet standard.

PAGE 742

742

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
FEC_codeword_error_bin_i (see [3], subclause 45.2.1.131a), where i takes a value from 1 to 15.
Each of these counters is a 32-bit counter that counts once for each codeword that contains
exactly i symbol errors. Note that these counters are defined as optional in the Ethernet
standard.
A UE PHY that supports the OPTIONAL MTBPE estimation SHALL include all of these counters and have
them accessible to software.
Reading these counters periodically can provide the probability of specific events by dividing the read
value by the total number of codewords since the previous readout, denoted Ntotal. Ntotal may be
obtained by reading FEC_cw_counter if that counter is available; alternatively, it can be estimated quite
accurately by the time since the previous reading. In this specification, it is assumed that the counters
are read regularly once per minute, and the approximate values of Ntotal for this period are provided in
Table 6-12. Other observation periods may be used instead, with calculations adjusted as appropriate.
Table 6-12 - Number of codewords received in one minute, Ntotal (approximate)

Informative Text:
The counters above are defined at the PCS decoder, and thus UCR estimates can be calculated only at
the receive side of the link. However, a high UCR could indicate issues unrelated to the receiver, such
as in the link partner’s transmitter or in the cabling.

For links in a large network, the UCR is expected to be lower than 1e-12 (and preferably much lower).
Therefore, when reading once per minute, the value of FEC_uncorrected_cw_counter should almost
always be 0. If the UCR needs to be estimated using only this counter, the calculated values of UCRest1
should be averaged over longer periods of time. Also, this estimate cannot be used proactively to
predict the MTBPE, since the estimated UCR can be calculated only after some PHY error events occur.

The uncorrelated error model is not accurate in many practical cases. Correlated errors increase the
UCR, so this estimate is biased and can predict a higher MTBPE than the true value. The effect of
correlated errors can increase the actual UCR by an unknown factor, and therefore UCRest2 should be
considered inaccurate and not be used to predict the MTBPE of a link. Despite this possible inaccuracy,
this estimate can be useful for identifying outliers in the statistics of links in a large network.

Informative Text:
Calculation of Pk and UCR as in equations 10 and 11 is susceptible to numerical errors. These
calculations can be performed by various mathematical tools that provide binomial distribution
functions. As an example, the Excel function BINOM.DIST can be used to calculate Pk using the
formula “=BINOM.DIST(544-k, 544, 1-SER, TRUE)”.

Correlated errors can create different statistics than uncorrelated errors. In this method, the effect of
correlated errors is accounted for by calculating the UCR using Pk for several values of k and taking the
worst of the results as the estimate. If the estimates obtained with different values of k do not
significantly deviate from each other, it is an indication that the errors are uncorrelated.
Informative Text:
A specific example of correlated errors results from using 1/(1+D) precoding in the PHY. Precoding
typically results in errors occurring in pairs, and thus the statistics of errors with precoding is different
than it is without precoding, because even-numbered bins represent single-error events. Inspecting
several even values of k enables detection of poor links whether precoding is used or not.

Assuming an observation period of one minute, the Ntotal values provided in Table 6-12 are between 1e9
and 1e10, and probabilities of 1e-8 and higher can be verified with a reasonable level of confidence. For
a probability of 1e-8, the values of P6, P8, and P10 can be calculated by periodically reading the set of
counters FEC_codeword_error_bin_i, calculating the cumulative counts Nk, and dividing them by Ntotal,

When the counters are read once per minute, the resolution of Pk will not be better than 1e-9, and for
some values of k, it may be estimated as 0; in that case, the corresponding UCR can be taken as the
minimum value in the table. Values of P10 corresponding to N10=1 may occur occasionally and may be

about 1e-20 when registers are read once per minute. Other values of k can be used instead, with
calculations adjusted as appropriate, to provide faster measurement or better resolution. Specifically,
if there are indications of correlated errors, higher values of k may provide better estimates.

6.3.3
Examples
6.3.3.1
MTBPE of a large network
Consider a network with N=100000 links with 400 Gb/s each, where most links have a UCR of ~1e-20 but
K=10 links are barely compliant and have a UCR of 1e-10 (where the UCR is estimated through either of
the methods described in 6.3.2).
From Table 6-11, the MTBPE of a single bad link (M1) is about 1 minute, and the MTBPE of a single good
link (M2) is about 20 thousand years. The frequency of errors in the full network is
𝐾
𝑀1 +
𝑁−𝐾
𝑀2 , and the
MTBPE is the reciprocal of this value, about 6 seconds.
It can be observed that, for the MTBPE of the network, the worst-case UCR is multiplied by K rather than
by N.
If the K=10 worst links have a UCR of 1e-16 instead (corresponding to an MTBPE of about 2 years), the
MTBPE of the full network becomes about 7 days. In this case, the MTBPE is mostly governed by the
total number of links N, and further improvement of the worst links has negligible effect.
6.3.3.2
Monitoring a network
Consider a network with N=1000 links with 800 Gb/s each. A software agent runs on each node
(endpoint or switch) and monitors the PCS FEC counters of each active link.

•
The software agent on node A can report this estimate or just that the link is not expected to
experience PHY errors.
•
Note that there is no way to tell from the FEC_corrected_cw_counter alone whether errors are
correlated and thus whether this estimate is reliable. If PHY errors occur despite this estimate, it
is likely due to correlated errors.
Another node in the network, denoted node B, also has a PCS with only the FEC_corrected_cw_counter
available. If the agent on node B reads this counter once per minute, the counter is saturated at 2 32 ≈
4.3e9. To enable estimation of the MTBPE, the agent has to read the counter more frequently to
prevent saturation. When reading the counter once per second, the average count turns out to be about
1.1e8.
•
The value of Ntotal for an observation time of one second is  .4e /60≈1.5 e8.
•
Using the method in 6.3.2.2, the CCR is 1.1e8/1.5 e8≈0.7.
•
Looking at Figure 6-1, this value of CCR corresponds to a UCR higher than 1e-13.
•
Even without applying any guard band, from Table 6-11, a UCR of 1e-13 corresponds to an
MTBPE of less than one day. Thus, node B is expected to experience frequent PHY errors.
•
The software agent can report the estimated MTBPE to a network monitoring system so that the
specific link can be handled proactively.
Another node in the network, denoted node C, has a PCS with FEC_codeword_error_bin_i counters
available. The agent on node C reads these counters once per minute to obtain N6, N8, and N10. The
average values are approximately 90000, 440, and 1, respectively, where N10 is calculated by averaging
multiple readouts (the values are mostly between 0 and 2).
•
From Table 6-12, for 800 Gb/s and 1-minute observation time, the value of Ntotal is 9.4e9, or
approximately 1e10.
•
Dividing the average counter values by 1e10, we get that P6, P8, and P10 are about 9e-6, 4.4e-8,
and 1e-10, respectively.
•
Looking at Figure 6-2, these values of P6, P8, and P10 correspond to UCR values of approximately
1.1e-19, 2.0e-19, and 1.7e-19, respectively. Taking the maximum of the three values, the UCR is
estimated as 2e-19. Since the values are close, the estimate can be considered accurate.

PAGE 749

749

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
•
From 6.3.1.2, the MTBPE can be estimated as 6.4e-9/2e-19=3.2e10 seconds, or about 1000
years. Thus, node C is not expected to experience frequent PHY errors.
•
The software agent can report the estimated MTBPE to a network monitoring system that
aggregates information from all ports on the network. If all 1000 nodes in the network report
similar MTBPE estimates, the full network is expected to have a PHY error once a year.
6.3.3.3
Planning a large-scale network with reliability requirements
Consider a plan to build a network with 1 million links of 100 Gb/s each. Two options for reliability
requirements are considered:
•
Option A targets minimization of retransmissions due to PHY errors, with a requirement that the
network-wide MTBPE is less than once per day.
•
Option B assumes that occasional retransmissions are acceptable and allows a network-wide
MTBPE up to once per minute.
Assuming that all links have the same performance, the minimum MTBPE on each link has to be at least
1 million days (8.6e10 seconds) for option A or 1 million minutes (6e7 seconds) for option B.
At 100 Gb/s, the codeword period is 51.2 ns (see 6.3.1.2), so these requirements can be translated to a
maximum UCR of approximately 6e-19 for option A or approximately 8.5e-16 for option B.
Assuming that all nodes have observable FEC_codeword_error_bin_i counters, the estimation method
in 6.3.2.3 can be used. Using the approximate log-linear relationships shown in Figure 6-2, the maximum
allowed values of P6, P8, and P10 are approximately 1.6e-5, 7.5e-8, and 2.1e-10, respectively, for option A
or 2.1e-4, 2.5e-6, and 1.8e-8, respectively, for option B.
From Table 6-12, at 100 Gb/s, Ntotal is approximately 1.2e9 per minute. To verify the UCR requirements,
network agents on each node can read the FEC_codeword_error_bin_i counters once per minute. With
this observation period, the values of N6, N8, and N10 corresponding to the maximum UCR are
approximately 19 800, 90, and 0.26, respectively, for option A or approximately 257000, 2990, and 22,
respectively, for option B.
With either option A or option B, if the counters exceed the maximum values on any of the nodes, that
node might fail the per-node UCR requirement, and the link associated with it can be considered a weak
link. However, the overall network performance can still be acceptable if other links are better than the
requirement and compensate for the weak link. It is therefore preferable that a software agent on each
node reports the MTBPE to a network monitoring system that aggregates information from all ports on
the network to assess the network-wide MTBPE. If the network-wide MTBPE is shorter than the
reliability requirement, the weak links should be identified and handled.
6.4 Recommendations
To meet the requirements of AI and HPC environments and enable efficient and scalable
communication, special attention is needed in the following areas of PHY and channel design.

PAGE 750

750

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
6.4.1
Low error rate
To improve performance and efficiency of communication in UE networks and applications using them,
it is RECOMMENDED to minimize the error rate through optimized PHY and channel design and close
monitoring of the network.
Ethernet links with higher-than-minimum MTBPE (i.e., on the order of hundreds of years) could reduce
802.3 packet retry and improve the link bandwidth efficiency and overall network performance. It is
RECOMMENDED that network management uses MTBPE estimates collected from multiple links, if
available, to configure the network for improved application performance.
Informative Text:
The choice of network configuration methods depends on the application. Network configuration can
include settings above the physical layer, such as changing routing tables to avoid usage of poor links
or enablement of reliability features (such as LLR) for specific links.

6.4.2
Low power
Power consumption is usually one of the limiting factors for scaling AI and HPC systems. It is
RECOMMENDED to have a power-optimized PHY that supports a wide range of channel conditions, with
configurable power tailored to each usage case.
Emerging technologies such as linear optics and co-packaged optics can also potentially reduce the
power of the link.
6.4.3
Low latency
Latency plays a critical role in the performance of AI and HPC systems, and the PHY latency can be an
important factor in the overall latency. It is RECOMMENDED to optimize both average and tail latencies
for robust and high-performance networks.
Average latency: Examples of PHY technologies under development that would potentially be beneficial
to average latency include: low-latency FEC error correction solutions; reducing lane-to-lane skew, as
the link latency is dictated by the slowest lane; and new electro-optical integration (e.g., optical direct
drive).
Tail latency: Reducing PHY error rate, as discussed in Section 6.4.1, and the resulting 802.3 packet
retransmit through link or end-to-end mechanisms, can significantly reduce tail latency. This is especially
important for AI and HPC with scalable applications relying on global synchronization.
