7 UE Management
“Ultra Ethernet, Ultra Ethernet Consortium, and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium logo are the
unregistered trademarks of Ultra Ethernet Consortium in the United States and other countries. Other
brands, names, or logos contained herein are the property of their respective owners.
7.1 UE Management Scope
The UE specification covers the layers between the UE PHY and UE software. The initial focus of UE
management is to define management specifications for the UE link layer and the UE PHY layer. The
following management aspects are covered in the management specifications:
1. PHY configuration for speeds and auto-negotiation.
2. PHY statistics including FEC statistics.
3. Link level retry (LLR) configuration and statistics.
4. Credit-based flow control (CBFC) management including VC mapping, counters,
VC/buffer/credit/scheduler configuration, and PFC co-existence.
5. CSIG management.
6. LLDP management including support for options TLV, CBFC TLV, etc.
7.2 High-Level UE Management Architecture
UE management architecture is focused on Ultra Ethernet fabric, switch, and endpoint management.
The UE management architecture includes management protocols, transport, and data models. UE
management protocol specifications cover baseline operations for management data, topology
discovery, transport(s) for management data, security of transports, and streaming support for
telemetry data. UE management data models define Ultra Ethernet configuration, state, and events. The
UE management schema describes the structure of UE data models.
Figure 7-1 provides a high-level architecture of the UE management stack. The UE Management
Controller (UEMC) is a logical entity that manages UE components including UE fabric endpoints, ports,
NICs, and switches. The UEMC communicates with one or more UE Management Server (UEMS)
instances to access management data and perform management operations. An instance of UEMS can
reside on a server or a switch.
Each UEMS exposes a management data model via a protocol over a transport. The UEMS exposes the
Redfish data model via a RESTful protocol over HTTPS for a server platform. The UEMS exposes the
YANG (Yet Another Next Generation) data model via an OpenConfig protocol over gNMI/gRPC for a
switch platform.

Figure 7-1 - UE Management Architecture
The UE management stack is supported by a variety of industry management standards. To drive
interoperability and common management functionality, UE management specifications leverage
industry standards, Redfish (internationally recognized by the IEC), YANG, and SAI that is prescribed by
the OCP, to cover server and fabric components of Ultra Ethernet.
The Redfish standard specifies an HTTP RESTful interface for exposing system manageability. The Redfish
standard consists of an interface specification and a data model specification. The model primarily
covers managing the physical and logical aspects of multiple systems. The Redfish data model is
described by a schema that is available in OpenAPI, JSON schema, and CSDL formats. The Redfish data
model has been extended by other standards to use Redfish in their management domains. Redfish has
data models for network endpoints and network fabric. The Redfish data models are extended to
manage UE endpoints at the server.
Redfish maps well onto internal facing data models specified by standards Network Controller Sideband
Interface (NC-SI), Platform Level Data Model (PLDM), and Security Protocol Data Model (SPDM). These
internal-facing data models may be extended for the UE.
YANG defines vendor-neutral common data models for switch configuration and management. YANG
supports vendor-neutral automation that can be leveraged for testing and compliance. Any applicable
configuration of a UE fabric switch including LLDP, LLR, UET, or INC can be specified using YANG data
models. Reference YANG models are specified for the UE. UE reference YANG models can be leveraged
by other organizations to create domain-specific YANG models for managing UE fabric switches (e.g.,
OpenConfig).

PAGE 754

754

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Switch Abstraction Interface (SAI) is widely supported by switch vendors as the abstraction layer to
program switch hardware. The following are the benefits of using SAI as an interface specification for
UE-capable network switches:
•
SAI is an abstract API schema consisting of “C” language header files. It has well-defined
conventions, and it provides, at its core, a CRUD abstraction based on tables and attributes.
•
Nearly every switch vendor offers SAI implementation. Using SAI, UE extensions can be
implemented in existing switches.
•
SAI does not impose any restrictions on the kind of network operating system (NOS) using SAI
API for any HW programming.
•
SAI can be programmatically transformed into other schemas such as gNMI, gRPC, etc.
•
The SAI ecosystem contains numerous tools to parse SAI headers and perform various checks
and transformations, such as breaking change detection from previous versions.
•
The SAI ecosystem has at least two popular test frameworks: SAI-PTF and SAI-Challenger.
Thousands of test cases already exist to verify compliance and performance of traditional
networking features. Adding test cases for UE enhancements can be a straightforward,
incremental effort.
To support Ultra Ethernet features requiring UE switch programming, the SAI specification requires
augmentation and updates. UEC works on the SAI enhancements for UE specifications and collaborates
with the OCP SAI community for adoption.
7.3 UE Fabric Management
UE fabric management can be viewed as a logical function that sits on top of management interfaces to
UE NICs and switches. The UE fabric manager provides a coherent view of a UE fabric and provides a
single management entity for creating connections between server NIC endpoints and switch endpoints.
Figure 7-2 shows a conceptual view of the UE fabric manager. The specification of UE fabric manager is
outside the scope of UE management specifications.
In Figure 7-2, the fabric manager manages a UE NIC using an out-of-band interface and/or an in-band
interface. The Redfish data model is used to manage UE endpoints when an out-of-band interface is
used. The fabric manager uses YANG data models to manage a UE switch. Within the UE switch, the
control plane uses SAI to communicate with the data plane. A vendor-specific SDK is used by the layers
below SAI to directly communicate with the switch ASIC pipeline.

Figure 7-2 - UE Fabric Manager
7.4 Redfish for UE Endpoint Manageability
Remote management of the server can be done via two manageability paths, as shown in Figure 7-3: in-
band or out-of-band management. The in-band path uses the same resources that hosts the operating
system. The out-of-band path uses dedicated resources that are operationally independent of the state
of the in-band resources. This path enables the system to be managed before the OS is operational or
when the OS is non-operational (hung or shutdown). The BMC (baseboard management controller) is
the component that exposes the Redfish interface to two management entities. The out-of-band
interface is accessed by the remote client. The in-band interface (host interface) is accessed by the in-
band entities (BIOS, OS, software agent).

Redfish Interop Validator (open source) to verify the conformance of an implementation.

7.5 YANG Model for UE Network Manageability
7.5.1
Network Switch Planes
As shown in Figure 7-4, network switches operate on different planes: management, control, and data
planes.


PAGE 757

757

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

Figure 7-4 - Network Switch Planes
•
Management plane runs management protocols (e.g., OpenConfig) and manages configuration
of routing protocols. The management plane is also responsible for IP and interface
management.
•
Control plane runs routing protocols (e.g., OSPF) and manages routing and forwarding tables.
The control plane uses SAI to interface with switch ASIC.
•
Data plane handles forwarding or routing of data traffic and maintains routing and forwarding
tables. The data plane is responsible for performing per-packet functions (e.g., NAT, stat, ACLs).
7.5.2
UE Switch Manageability Architecture
The UE switch manageability architecture builds on top of a switch management plane.

PAGE 758

758

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.

Figure 7-5 - UE Switch Manageability Architecture
The components of the UE switch manageability architecture can be described as follows.
•
Network switch is a component of the network fabric. Data ports are used for inter-server or
inter-node fabric communications. Management port(s) of the switch platform connect to a
separate and dedicated physical network infrastructure used for managing switches.
•
A remote management client manages the switch and directly communicates over
management ports with the management agent on the switch. The management interface
referenced here is the northbound interface from the NOS on the switch.
•
Management agent resides inside the NOS and exposes the northbound interface for
management. Typically, the management agent is accessed over management ports. Remote
management communication may happen over data ports.
•
SAI is the southbound interface on the switch. SAI is not visible to the remote management
client. SAI is used for configuring and monitoring the switch ASIC.
7.5.3
YANG Model Extensions for UE
YANG (Yet Another Next Generation) is a data modeling language used to define the configuration and
operational state data of network devices for management and automation. YANG provides a
hierarchical, tree-based structure to model data, including configuration data, operational state, remote
procedure calls (RPCs), and event notifications. YANG is protocol-independent and can be accessed by
various protocols including OpenConfig and Netconf. YANG models can be serialized into various
formats such as XML and JSON, facilitating automation and communication between network devices

PAGE 759

759

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
and management systems. UE YANG model specifications will provide a reference model that can be
used for UE switch management.
7.6 Switch Abstraction Interface (SAI) for UE
SAI is a subproject under the OCP Networking Project. Figure 7-6 shows the architecture of SAI.

Figure 7-6 - SAI Architecture
7.6.1
SAI Enhancements for UE
SAI enhancements for UE leverage the SAI pipeline and SAI objects. SAI enhancements for LLR, CBFC,
and CSIG are specified.
7.6.1.1
SAI Enhancements for LLR
Link layer retry (LLR) is a hop-by-hop mechanism that provides the capability for local retransmission of
frames lost due to link errors, thereby avoiding the impact on application performance. LLR uses
sequence numbers and periodic acknowledgements to track Ethernet frames. LLR is a new feature in
SAI. To support LLR, new attributes and statistics are added to the SAI port object. Additionally, a new
object called a Port LLR profile is introduced to model the LLR parameters of a port.
7.6.1.2
SAI Enhancements for Credit-Based Flow Control (CBFC)
In CBFC, the sender ensures that the receiver has enough buffer before transmitting a frame. The
receiver advertises its buffer availability to the sender using credits that represent the amount of buffer
space available. The sender can transmit frames only if it has sufficient credits—ensuring that the
receiver has space to accept the incoming data. Periodically, the receiver sends back to the sender the
credits for the frames that have left the buffer. CBFC supports up to 32 virtual channels (VCs) per port.
Each VC can be configured as either lossless or best-effort, and this configuration can be changed
dynamically.
Create standardized C API to program ASICs

PAGE 760

760

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
Credit-based flow control (CBFC) is a newly introduced feature in the Switch Abstraction Interface (SAI)
that enhances link-level flow control without impacting the existing SAI logical pipeline. The following
SAI enhancements are done for CBFC:
•
Three new objects:
o Virtual channel: Contains per-VC attributes associated with CBFC sender and CBFC
receiver functions on a port.
o CBFC credit profile: Attributes for management of receiver credits (i.e., receiver’s
buffer) on a per-VC basis.
o CBFC credit pool: Used to provide isolation of credits (i.e., receiver’s buffer) between
groups of VCs.
•
New attributes for CBFC to the port object.
•
New QoS map types for VC derivation from TC, queue, or packet’s dot1p DEI.
•
New attributes to enable/disable enqueue and dequeue, which are needed for lossless VC
initialization and deinitialization.
7.6.1.3
SAI Enhancements for CSIG
Congestion signaling (CSIG) is a simple and efficient network telemetry method that collects fine-grained
signals that describe the network fabric’s congestion state. The central insight underlying CSIG’s design
is that for many telemetry signals useful in congestion control and performance analysis, the result of a
simple aggregation function computed over the congestion state at switches along a packet’s path is of
interest. For example, for several signal types, the congestion state is of interest only at a single switch
along a path, where the switch of interest is the one where a signal’s value is an extremum (maximum or
minimum) among the signal’s values at all switches along the path.
CSIG does not alter the forwarding behavior of a packet in the SAI logical pipeline. This means that the
SAI logical pipeline does not require any changes for CSIG packets. SAI already provides an existing
infrastructure that uses the telemetry and management (TAM) object. This TAM infrastructure currently
supports in-band network telemetry, streaming telemetry, events, transport for reporting, and various
reporting formats. The TAM infrastructure has been enhanced to support CSIG.

761

Copyright © 2026 Ultra Ethernet ConsortiumTM. All rights reserved.
8 UE Compliance
To assist implementors in efforts to comply to this UE specification, the UEC provides test collateral
including profile matrices, compliance checklists, and a best practices document describing suggestions
for establishing a testbed.  The profile matrix and compliance checklist should be used by implementors
to self-attest for compliance.
These documents are located at: https://ultraethernet.org/compliance/
The profile matrix states which features are mandatory, conditional, or optional for each Ultra Ethernet
profile.  UE defines three profiles: AI Base, AI Extended, and HPC.  The profile matrix also specifies which
items in the compliance checklist need to be tested if the feature or technology is implemented.  Figure
8-1 shows an excerpt from the profile matrix.
The compliance checklist contains a list of the items to test for each specification. The checklist includes
the TestID, TestName, Criteria, and the reference to the specification.  Figure 8-2 shows an excerpt from
the compliance checklist, each row identifying a testable item.
In order to attest compliance to the specification, implementers should run tests to confirm the
behavior that is targeted by the checklist items, either by themselves or with the help of a third party.
Implementers making a compliance statement should provide the information listed in the Compliance
Statement as follows, to indicate that they have tested and are compliant to the profile and features
they are claiming support for.
8.1 Compliance Statement
A vendor can claim UE support by performing a self-attestation and declaring the supported features
and profiles in their product literature.

Figure 8-2 - Example of Compliance Checklist

Figure 8-1 - Example of Profile Matrix

8.1.1
UE Support Requirements
Implementers SHALL call out supported features and associated profiles [e.g. LL-LLR, AI-BASE].
Implementers SHALL execute the checklist tests, corresponding to the profile line items [e.g. LL-LLR-1.1].
8.1.2
Declaration Format
The declaration format is:
<Complies to UE Specifications: [spec ver # - section], [profile + optional/conditional], tested against
[checklist doc ver #]>
It is RECOMMENDED that the declaration statement lists the optional/conditional profile features that
were tested.
Declaration example: “Complies to UE Specifications: UE Specification v1.0 – Section 5.1, AI-BASE, CT LL-
PHY Specifications 1.0”.
Non-mandatory features can be enabled during compliance tests, but it must be possible to disable non-
mandatory features if they can cause interoperability issues with other implementations using the same
UE profile without the optional features.
8.1.3
Compliance verses Support Terminology
Support is synonymous to Comply.   A statement of compliance with UE Specifications should be
accompanied by a declaration stating what was tested.
